## In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka
## Pañcapakaraṇa-mūlaṭīkā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Dhātukathāpakaraṇa-mūlaṭīkā
## Explanation of the Introduction to the Text

Having paid homage to the Blessed One, who has transcended the collection of the three elements—the sense sphere (kāmadhātu), the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu), and the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu)—and who teaches the distinctions of the elements; to the ten noble Dhamma that are the means of transcending the collection of the three elements; and to the eightfold noble Saṅgha of ultimate sense who are without interval; and being respectfully requested by disciples who desire the long-lasting of the three kinds of True Dhamma (Saddhamma), for the benefit of those with weak wisdom, although there have been many word-for-word translations (nissaya) in the past, I shall properly compose the commentary (ṭīkā) on the seven books of Abhidhamma from the beginning according to the order taught by the Buddha, with correct meaning and essence, by consulting the Mūlaṭīkā and Anuṭīkā without omitting this Dhātukathā-ṭīkā, as I have already exerted effort in the Burmese word-for-word translation (yojanā) from the very start.

The Teacher of the Dhamma (Aṭṭhakathā-ācariya) spoke the words beginning with "Aṭṭhārasahi" to show the time when the Blessed One taught the Dhātukathā treatise, and to show that the treatise taught immediately after the Vibhaṅga is indeed named Dhātukathā. In those words, the Blessed One alone is praised as the "Mārabhañjana" (Vanquisher of Māra) because He crushed the five Māras at the foot of the Bodhi tree: Devaputta-māra, by means of crushing his power and transcending his domain of the sense sphere; Kilesa-māra and Abhisaṅkhāra-māra, by means of making them non-existent in His own continuity; and Khandha-māra and Maccu-māra, by means of abandoning the truth of origin (samudaya-sacca) and through full understanding. This crushing is unsurpassed and independent of others. In the term "Mārabhañjana," He is so called because He crushed the five Māras such as Devaputta-māra. Alternatively, He is called Mārabhañjana because He only crushes the five Māras and does not crush enemies such as rival kings. He is called "Mahāvīra" (Great Hero) because He possesses great endeavor and great energy.

Phenomena beginning with the aggregates (khandha) and ending with the conflict-free (araṇa) are called "elements" (dhātu) because of their intrinsic nature and because they are the basis for the Abhidhamma teaching; thus, this treatise is called "Dhātukathā" because it is the discourse on those elements. Although those phenomena are taught in other treatises as well, in this treatise all those phenomena are taught in each of the fourteen methods such as inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha). Because they are taught in such an extraordinary manner, this treatise alone is called by this name. In other treatises, only a portion is taught. Alternatively, the methods such as inclusion and non-inclusion of phenomena beginning with the aggregates and ending with the conflict-free are taught by means of aggregates, bases (āyatana), and elements. In those methods, those which have great scope...
2:
It should be understood that the name "Dhātukathā" was spoken (either by the Buddha or the commentators) because it is a discourse by means of elements and concerning elements. He is called "Dhātubhedappakāsana" (Revealer of the Distinctions of Elements) because He reveals the distinctions of elements in various ways, such as twofold, threefold, sixfold, and eighteenfold.

"Tassatthaṃ" means the meaning of that Dhātukathā treatise. It should be understood that the letter 'a', which is a part of the letter 'ā', is elided because of the following letter 'a'. Alternatively, in the phrase "yaṃ dhātukathaṃ," the remaining word "pakaraṇaṃ" (treatise) should be understood. Since the explanation of the seven treatises has arisen in order, by connecting with that remaining word 'pakaraṇa', the elision of the letter 'a' in the phrase "tassatthaṃ" (the meaning of that treatise) should also be understood. "Taṃ" means "listen to that explanation," or it means "contemplate that meaning by listening to the words of that explanation." "Samāhitā" means having minds that are not distracted by various tasks, or it means being well-established in one's own mind.

## The Explanation of the Introduction to the Text is Finished.

## 1. Mātikāvaṇṇanā

## 1. Nayamātikāvaṇṇanā

If it is asked, "What is the scope of this treatise?", that scope should not be stated here (in this Dhātukathā commentary), for the scope of the treatise has already been stated in the Atthasālinī (the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī). To show this meaning, he said: "It is said that it is analyzed by fourteen kinds of methods." The teaching of the aggregates and so on is led or proceeded by these modes such as inclusion; therefore, they are called methods (naya). Or, the aggregates and so on are known or understood by these modes; thus, because of the capacity to make them known, they are called methods. It is called "Nayamātikā" because it is the summary (uddesa) of the methods, or because the methods themselves are the summary. The fourteen terms such as inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha), which should be called the "Root Matrix" (Mūlamātikā) because they are the root cause of these terms, are the root cause and the basis of this Dhātukathā treatise, which analyzes the phenomena such as the aggregates.

## 2. Abbhantaramatikāvaṇṇanā

By the terms such as "five aggregates," terms such as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) are shown. By the statement on Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), the twelve terms which have the meaning of the individual factors such as ignorance (avijjā)—to which the term 'Dependent Origination' applies individually—are shown. By means of those terms (aggregates, etc.) shown as a summary, and the terms such as contact (phassa) shown by their individual nature, he said: "By two hundred and twenty-five terms." Among those (225 terms), the factors analyzed in this Dhātukathā such as kammabhava, upapattibhava, and kāmabhava should be understood as the twelvefold Dependent Origination because upapattibhava is included in 'existence' (bhava) as that which is produced, and kammabhava as that which produces; and because sorrow and so on are included in 'aging and death' (jarāmaraṇa) as they are undesirable like aging and death, and are suffering rooted in aging and death. Here, it should be understood that the commentator, by taking terms such as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) separately even though they are not separately answered in the Pāḷi text, shows that those foundations of mindfulness and so on should also be answered separately.

The matrix (mātikā) from the Nayamātikā to the Lakkhaṇamātikā is called the Dhātukathā-mātikā because it is unique to the Dhātukathā treatise and not shared with other treatises. The summary of the phenomena to be analyzed, stated within that matrix, is called the Internal Matrix (Abbhantaramatikā). To reveal this meaning, he said "Ayañhi" and so on. In that statement, "without saying thus" means without saying as it was said outside of this Dhātukathā-mātikā, such as "all matrices... pe... are matrices." "Only within the Dhātukathā" should be understood to mean only within the Dhātukathā-mātikā. Because it is placed within the unique matrix (tadāveṇikamātikā) of the Dhātukathā, it is indeed placed within that matrix...
4:
It has been stated. Alternatively, without speaking in this way, by the words "All... the Matrix," it means that the Matrix which is external to the Dhātukathā, beginning with kusala and ending with araṇa, and which exists in another text (the Dhammasaṅgaṇī), is stated (as the Matrix of this text). The phrase "only within the Dhātukathā" means because it is shown and established by its own nature only within this text. It should be understood as miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) because it is spread out (in the Khandha-vibhaṅga, etc.) and not included in the Matrix of the entire Abhidhamma.

## 3. Explanation of the Matrix of the Doors to the Methods

The states of inclusion (saṅgaha), exclusion (asaṅgaha), dissociation (viyogī), and association (sahayogī), which are the causes (or doors) for the occurrence of the methods (naya), are called the "Doors to the Methods" (nayamukha); the summary of these states is called the "Matrix of the Doors to the Methods" (nayamukhamātikā). Indeed, the fourteen methods occur by way of the mixing of inclusion, exclusion, association, and dissociation; therefore, those states (aggregates, bases, elements, mental aggregates) because of which those four (inclusion, etc.) occur are called the "Doors" (mukha) of the fourteen methods. In presenting that Matrix of the Doors to the Methods, although inclusion and exclusion are stated as they may occur with truths (sacca), etc., in terms such as "inclusion by what is included" (saṅgahitena-asaṅgahita), they are stated only with those truths, etc., which are the agents (subject) that count, and not with those states which are the means (instrument) of counting. Even in the extraction of states to be questioned and answered, such as "By the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), which states are included by way of aggregate-inclusion and excluded by way of base-inclusion?", the inclusion and exclusion with those truths, etc., which are the agents that count, are stated by restricting them only to the means of counting (saṅgaha) such as aggregates; therefore, it is stated: "There is inclusion by three; there is exclusion by three." Furthermore, in the extraction of states to be questioned and answered, and in the questions and answers themselves, the association and dissociation of states beginning with the matter-aggregate (rūpakkhandha) and ending with araṇa occur only with the four (mental) aggregates as they may apply; therefore, it is stated: "There is association with four; there is dissociation from four."

If it is asked: "Does dissociation not also occur with matter (rūpa) and Nibbāna? Why then is it stated: 'There is dissociation from four'?", the answer is: because dissociation that occurs with matter and Nibbāna also occurs only with the four (mental) aggregates. In fact, matter is not dissociated (vippayutta) from matter or from Nibbāna, nor is Nibbāna dissociated from matter; it is dissociated only from the four (mental) aggregates. Therefore, the dissociation of the four aggregates from matter and Nibbāna is also restricted to the four aggregates which are the dissociating states, because there can be no dissociation without those four aggregates. This aforementioned dissociation does not occur for an objectless (anārammaṇa) state with an objectless state or with a mixed (missaka) state (mixed with the objectless); nor does it occur for a mixed state with an objectless state or with a mixed state. However, it should be understood that for an objectless state and for a mixed state, there is dissociation from a state with an object (sārammaṇa); and for a state with an object, there is dissociation from a state with an object, an objectless state, and a mixed state.

## 4. Explanation of the Matrix of Characteristics

Counting by way of aggregates, bases, and elements is itself called the method of inclusion (saṅgaha-naya). The phrase "similar and dissimilar" (sabhāgo visabhāgo) should be applied separately to the sentence "There is inclusion by three; there is exclusion by three" and also to the sentence "There is association with four; there is dissociation from four." Because they are thus applied separately, it should be understood that inclusion (counting) and exclusion (not counting) have the nature of being similar (sabhāga) and dissimilar (visabhāga); likewise, association and dissociation also have the nature of being similar and dissimilar. Alternatively, it should be understood that the state which has inclusion and exclusion is called similar and dissimilar; likewise, the state which has association and dissociation is also called similar and dissimilar. Among those two (similar and dissimilar), the common nature such as being subject to change (ruppana), etc. (due to opposing causes like cold and heat), by which states such as the matter-aggregate... up to... the mind-consciousness element are counted, is to be known as "similarity" (sabhāgatā) in the method of inclusion; the common nature such as having a common arising (ekuppāda), etc., is to be known as "similarity" in the method of association.

## 5. Explanation of the External Matrix

Because it is placed outside the Matrix of the Dhātukathā, it means "External Matrix" (bāhiramātikā) because it is placed outside (the Matrix) by this manner of placement: "All... the Matrix." Alternatively, it means "External Matrix" because states beginning with kusala and ending with araṇa are not placed in this text of the Dhātukathā by this manner, but are established as the Matrix of this text by the Matrix of another text (Dhammasaṅgaṇī) which is external to the Matrix of the Dhātukathā, and are thus clearly shown.

In sentences such as "inclusion, exclusion," etc., while inclusion is of only one kind, why is it called "fourfold"? It is called fourfold because the word "inclusion" (saṅgaha) is spoken without specifying the exact meaning, and the meaning of the word "inclusion" has not yet been extracted. Among the words "inclusion, exclusion," etc., it should be understood here that the word "inclusion" is first of all fourfold by the power of its own meanings (such as class, etc.). Or, "inclusion" is spoken of in "inclusion, exclusion," etc., because it has reached the state of being taken generally (sāmañña) without the specific (such as class, etc.) being extracted; therefore, there is no fault. Only after the specific (class, etc.) has been shown would its onefold nature exist, not before that. Since the word "class" (jāti) is a relative term, when "inclusion by way of class" (jātiyā saṅgaho) is stated, it is understood as "inclusion by its own class" because no other relatable thing is mentioned; therefore, "inclusion by class" (jāti-saṅgaha) stated in the section on matter (Rūpa-kaṇḍa) means "inclusion by its own class" (sajāti-saṅgaha) (counting what is of the same class as itself).
6:
In this Nayamātikā (Matrix of Methods), these two headings, 'Inclusion (Saṅgaha), Exclusion (Asaṅgaha), Association (Sampayoga), Dissociation (Vippayoga)', are summaries of the methods for questioning and answering regarding the general nature of phenomena, without extracting the specific qualities such as being included (saṅgahita) of the aggregates and so on, which are to be questioned and answered. The remaining headings are summaries of methods shown by extracting specific phenomena. In the phrase 'saṅgahitena asaṅgahitaṃ', although it should be said as 'saṅgahitena asaṅgahitaṃ asaṅgahitaṃ', it should be understood that one word 'asaṅgahita' is elided. By that elided word 'asaṅgahita', there exists a specific excluded phenomenon distinguished by a specific inclusion. The method of questioning and answering called 'exclusion' based on that specific phenomenon is summarized. In the word 'saṅgahitena', the instrumental case should be seen in the sense of an attribute (visesana). This method also applies to the summaries of methods from the third to the tenth, excluding the sixth. In those summaries of methods, by extracting the specific phenomena to be questioned and answered using two words each in the manner already stated, the methods of questioning and answering are summarized using a third word similar to the final word in each respective heading.

Among those summaries of methods, in the fourth and fifth, the use of the instrumental case in the sense of the agent (kattu) should be noted. In the four headings starting from the seventh, the instrumental case should be noted in the sense of association (sahayoga). It should not be noted in the sense of an appositional attribute (samānādhikaraṇa visesana) as in the second and third summaries of methods. The reason is that in the second and third, one distinct nature is used to qualify another distinct nature. However, in these fourth and fifth, one distinct phenomenon is used to qualify another distinct phenomenon. In the four summaries of methods starting from the eleventh, the specific phenomenon is extracted only by the initial word, and the methods of questioning and answering are summarized by the remaining words. Here, the instrumental case should be noted only in the sense of an attribute. This is because the phenomena that are the basis of questioning and answering qualify their own state of being associated or dissociated through the specific quality of being included and so on, which acts as the instrument.

'Vikappato' means because of various considerations or because of classification. 'Sanniṭṭhānavasena' means because of decision by way of association with determination (adhimokkha). The meaning here should be understood as: by way of the connection between the arisings of consciousness (cittuppāda) spoken of by way of decision and all arisings of consciousness. Adhimokkha is taught by way of connection with the arisings of consciousness spoken of by way of decision. The remaining phenomena are taught by way of connection with all arisings of consciousness. Among those phenomena, those that are connected with all are pervasive and evident. Therefore, they are grasped by way of delimitation from the beginning. A summary is made for the purpose of delimiting those phenomena through inclusion and so on. Since even those not connected with all must also be delimited, adhimokkha is summarized to show the delimitation through inclusion and so on of other phenomena that have a wide range of objects among them. The statement 'sanniṭṭhānavasena vuttā' should be understood as being said with reference to the statements appearing in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary and the Paṭiccasamuppāda-vibhaṅga.
7:
When the universal (sādhāraṇa) phenomena connected with all arisings of consciousness and the specific (asādhāraṇa) phenomena not so connected are to be taught, among the specific phenomena, there is determination (adhimokkha) which has a wide range of objects. By the power of that adhimokkha, because of the connection with all the stated arisings of consciousness, contact (phassa) and so on are called 'universals' (sabbasādhāraṇa) connected with all arisings of consciousness; and adhimokkha is also taught as a phenomenon with a wide range of objects among the specific phenomena because there is no other such phenomenon. This is how the meaning should be understood.

In this context, it should be understood that the life faculty (jīvitindriya) is not mentioned because it is mixed with materiality (rūpa). One-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) is also mentioned only by the general term 'cittekaggatā' when the nature of concentration (samādhi) is absent. When the nature of concentration is present, although it is mentioned by both general and specific terms, since there is no other pervasive phenomenon or phenomenon to be excluded that is expressible by a specific term, it is mentioned by terms that merely indicate the variety of that concentration. It is not like feeling (vedanā), which has the nature of pleasure (sukha) and so on, and is mentioned only by general and specific terms that are opposite to the stated characteristic.

Therefore, if this general term 'cittekaggatā' occurs without depending on a specific term in the sense of concentration, it would itself reach the status of a specific term and manifest only the nature of non-concentration, while the other would manifest only the nature of concentration. Thus, cittekaggatā, being twofold, is both specific and has a limited range of objects; therefore, it does not deserve to be summarized (uddesa) here. Or, even if it is not divided, because it lacks the evidentness of contact (phassa) and so on, and because it must be spoken of in dependence on other phenomena, that cittekaggatā and life (jīvita) do not deserve to be summarized and thus are not taught.

## The Explanation of the Matrix is finished.

## 2. Niddesavaṇṇanā
## 1. Paṭhamanaya Saṅgahāsaṅgahapadavaṇṇanā
## 1. Khandhapadavaṇṇanā
Aggregates, bases, and elements are taught as states to be known by higher knowledge (abhiññeyya). However, to show the distinction of being fully understood (pariññeyya) etc. of those states already known by higher knowledge in their own nature, the truths (sacca) are taught; and to show the distinction of functions such as predominance (adhipati) etc., the faculties (indriya) etc. are taught. Just as the distinction of truths etc. is easily understood when taught based on states known by higher knowledge, the distinction of inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha) is also easily understood when taught based on states known by higher knowledge. Therefore, it should be understood that the matrix of the method's opening (nayamukhamātikā), "Inclusion by three, non-inclusion by three," is established. Because the matrix of the method's opening is established based on states known by higher knowledge, association (sampayoga) and dissociation (vippayoga), which are taught as being "by four," are also asked and answered by means of aggregates etc., based on states known by higher knowledge.

In the text "The aggregate of matter is (included) by one aggregate," there is a similarity (sabhāgatā) among the actual states called "aggregate of matter" within the five aggregates by way of being the aggregate of matter. Therefore, the inclusion (saṅgaha) as a count is shown by the means of counting called the state of being the aggregate of matter, or by the means of counting called the term "aggregate of matter." Because the counting is shown by the means of counting called the state of being the aggregate of matter, the commentator (Saṅgahakāra) says the meaning beginning with "Whatever (matter there is)." By the text "aggregate of matter," the state to be included (counted) is shown. The showing of the means of counting by which it is counted is the phrase "by one aggregate." The meaning here is that among the five means of counting called aggregates, it is counted by one means of counting called an aggregate. Since counting is expressed by terms such as aggregates, [the Teacher] will say in the following (second method etc.), "They are included by the inclusion of aggregates," and so on.

This phrase "Asaṅgahanayaniddesa" (Exposition of the Method of Non-inclusion) should be understood as being taught as a part of this very first method, "Saṅgaho Asaṅgaho," and not as a different method. By the statement that only the dyads (duka), triads (tika), and tetrads (catukka) having the aggregate of matter as their root are shown here, it is shown that when states having the aggregate of feeling as their root are joined with the preceding term "aggregate of matter," there is no distinction; therefore, they are joined only with the subsequent [aggregates of] perception, formations, and consciousness, obtaining three dyads, two triads, and one tetrad. It is shown that two dyads and one triad are obtained with the aggregate of perception as the root, and one dyad with the aggregate of formations as the root. It should be understood that the asking and answering of these, according to their divisions, should be done after the asking and answering of the pentads (pañcaka); it is a summary, or it should be understood that they are not included in the Pali text because they can be known by the method already stated.

## Āyatanapadādivaṇṇanā
In the sentence "Yasmā ca dukatikesūti," although the answer is the same in the single method (ekakanaya), it is seen that the eye-faculty, ear-faculty, pleasure-faculty, etc., which have the same answer in the single method, have different answers in the dyads (duka) etc. In this exposition of the faculties, a similar answer is not found between the eye-ear dyad and the eye-pleasure-faculty dyad, nor between those dyads and the triads (tika). However, in this exposition of the truths, it is found that the answers for the suffering-origin dyad and the suffering-path dyad are the same as each other and also the same as the triad. Therefore, the fact that the answer is the same only in the dyads and triads is stated as the reason for teaching the path truth (maggasacca) immediately after the origin truth (samudayasacca).

## 6. Paṭiccasamuppādavaṇṇanā
Although it should have been written as "Ignorance is (included) by one aggregate; with ignorance as condition, formations are (included) by one aggregate," it should be understood that the sentence "Ignorance is by one aggregate" was not written due to the negligence of scribes. Alternatively, by applying the method of "sarūpeka-sesa," it should be understood that the answer for ignorance is already shown by the word "ignorance" in the sentence "with ignorance as condition, formations." In the sentence "Sabbampi vipākaviññāṇaṃ," there is no need to qualify it with the word "resultant" (vipāka). This is because wholesome consciousness etc. are also included in the Dhatukatha by terms such as "with formations as condition, consciousness." In the exposition of states included and not included by dissociation, the answer for those consciousnesses is shown by an answer similar to that of the term "resultant states" (vipākā dhammā). Also in this first method, according to the teaching that name-and-form is included by the eleven bases, the inclusion of name-and-form that is not born of kamma can also be known; therefore, qualification with the word "resultant" is not necessary.

Because they are merely the states of arising, maturing, and breaking up of the material and mental states that are currently arising, maturing, and breaking up, birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa) cannot be separated in the ultimate sense (paramattha) and are merely the nature of ultimate realities. Those instances of birth, aging, and death of matter (rūpa) are the arising, maturing, and breaking up of matter, and since they are taken by the nature of "deformation" (ruppana), they share the nature (sabhāga) of the aggregate of matter. As for the birth etc. of mental states, although they occur individually like the birth of material clusters (rūpakalāpa), they occur individually because they are the arising, maturing, and breaking up of the group of four mental aggregates that arise together. They cannot be taken by the exclusive ultimate functions of feeling, perceiving, or cognizing, but are taken only by the non-exclusive ultimate function of "conditioning the conditioned" (saṅkhatābhisaṅkharaṇa); thus, they share the nature of the aggregate of formations. Likewise, both types of birth etc. cannot be taken by exclusive ultimate functions such as the eye-base, but share the nature of the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) and the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu) in the sense of being void of a being (nissatta). Therefore, intending that those instances of birth etc. are included by the aggregate of matter, the aggregate of formations, the base of mental objects, and the element of mental objects, [the Teacher] taught, "Birth is (included) by two aggregates," and so on.

## Paṭhamanaya Saṅgahāsaṅgahapadavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 2. Dutiya-naya: Saṅgahitenāsaṅgahita-pada-vaṇṇanā

In the exposition of the terms 'Included' and 'Excluded' (Saṅgahitenāsaṅgahita-pada-niddesa), those phenomena are extracted which are to be questioned and answered as 'excluded' (asaṅgahita), but are distinguished as 'included' (saṅgahita) and are excluded by bases and elements. To show this first, it is said: "With the eye-base, which states are included by aggregate-inclusion but excluded by base-inclusion and element-inclusion?"

In all methods, the general counting by aggregates and so on always expects a distinction, and because the questions and answers depend on such distinctions, the counting by specific aggregates such as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) is pure (or without remainder), without being mixed with modifiers.

In this second method, since the specific phenomena have already been extracted by the mere words "included and excluded," there are certain states which are included by one or two of the three modes of inclusion—aggregates, bases, and elements—and are excluded by the others. These states alone should be shown by the mere words "included by aggregate-inclusion, excluded by base-inclusion and element-inclusion." However, because it is not possible to show them without extracting them as the eye-base and so on, and because the Method-Matrix (Naya-mātikā) depends on the Internal Matrix (Abbhantara-mātikā) and External Matrix (Bāhira-mātikā), it should be understood that in the Summary (Uddesa), whatever phenomenon among those from the aggregate of matter to the end of the Araṇa [triad] is the 'includer' (saṅgāhaka), the 'included and excluded' is extracted in relation to that specific includer. Therefore, to show the phenomena extracted by those respective includers like the eye-base, defining them by the term "those states" (te dhammā), it is said: "With the eye-base..." and so on.

In methods where there is no extraction of specific phenomena to be questioned and answered, such as in the first and sixth methods, the phenomena from the aggregate of matter to the end of the Araṇa [triad] are shown as the objects to be questioned and answered. In other methods, they are shown as the determinants (niyāmaka) of whatever phenomena are extracted to be questioned and answered.

In that Pali, in the phrase "With the eye-base... up to... with the tangible-object element," the indication by the instrumental case should be understood as being in the sense of the agent (kattu). In the phrase "by aggregate-inclusion... by element-inclusion," it should be understood as being in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa). In this text of the Dhātukathā, whatever agent (kattu) such as the eye-base exists as an includer, there is another phenomenon among the modes of inclusion like aggregates which is included or excluded by that respective mode; only that phenomenon is extracted as being included or excluded. However, by the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha), there is no other phenomenon to be included in aggregate-inclusion; the same applies to the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and so on. Furthermore, a phenomenon itself cannot be its own includer or excluder. The statement "The aggregate of matter is included by one aggregate" was not said with the intention that it is included by that very aggregate of matter itself; rather, it was said with the intention that it is taken as the aggregate of matter or by the term "aggregate of matter." This meaning has already been explained by me.

If a phenomenon itself could be included by itself, then in the exposition of the terms 'Included, Associated, and Dissociated' (Saṅgahitena-sampayutta-vippayutta-pada-niddesa), it would have to be said: "With the aggregate of feeling, those states which are included by aggregate-inclusion..."
11:
...those states included by base-inclusion and element-inclusion are associated with 3 aggregates, 1 base, and 7 elements, and so on. But the Buddha did not teach it so. Therefore, just as consciousness (citta) is not associated or dissociated with itself, the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) is not included (saṅgahita) or excluded (asaṅgahita) by the aggregate of matter itself. Likewise, the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and so on are not included or excluded by themselves. This is because a phenomenon itself is not its own similar (sabhāga) or dissimilar (visabhāga) counterpart.

For that very reason, just as parts do not include or exclude the whole, the whole does not include or exclude the parts. For example, the aggregate of matter does not include or exclude the eye-base and so on; the mental-base (dhammāyatana) does not include or exclude the aggregate of feeling and so on; and the states with taints (saraṇā dhammā) do not include or exclude the four aggregates. Because there is no distinction between the parts contained within a whole and the whole itself, those parts cannot be the similar or dissimilar counterparts of the whole, and likewise, the whole is not the includer or excluder of the similar or dissimilar counterparts of the parts.

For example, the mental-base does not include by aggregate-inclusion the part of the aggregate of matter that is similar to subtle matter (sukhuma-rūpa) and dissimilar to feeling and so on. The life-faculty (jīvitindriya) also does not include by aggregate-inclusion the part of the aggregate of matter and the part of the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) excluding the life-faculty, which are similar or dissimilar to the physical and mental life-faculty. A phenomenon similar to a part is not similar to the whole, nor is a phenomenon dissimilar to a part dissimilar to the whole. Therefore, even if there is an excluder (asaṅgāhaka) of something other than itself, or other than what is contained within itself, or other than what is similar to its own part, the state of being an includer (saṅgāhakatva) does not exist in these cases such that they could be excluders of what is included. It should be understood that such phenomena are not taken in the second method precisely because of the absence of the state of being an includer (saṅgāhakatva).

The statements "The mental-base, excluding the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) from the aggregates, is included by 4 aggregates" and "The eye-base and the ear-base are included by 1 aggregate" do not show the parts including the whole or the whole including the parts. Rather, they show the fivefold distinction of the mental-base according to the different counts of the four aggregates as being countable or uncountable, and the single nature of the eye-base and so on because they are countable by the count of one aggregate. The first method (Paṭhama-naya) is merely the showing of counting through respective counts of phenomena that are countable or uncountable, regardless of includers or excluders, because it consists only of the object (kamma) and the instrument (karaṇa). The second method and others, however, show the non-counting and so on of phenomena included or excluded by includers and excluders, and thus they consist of the triad of agent (kattu), instrument (karaṇa), and object (kamma). Likewise, in the first method, the state or non-state of the respective aggregates and so on, known as the state of being countable or uncountable in various ways...
12:
Homogeneity (sabhāgatā) and heterogeneity (visabhāgatā) mean: in the demonstration of the states as specified in the second method and so forth, homogeneity is the state of having the same aggregates etc. between the classifying states (saṅgāhaka) and the states to be classified (saṅgahetabba); the absence of that is heterogeneity. In the questions and answers, it is only the presence or absence of those respective aggregates etc. that constitutes the distinction between these methods.

States similar to the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) and the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) are only those that are to be classified by them; since there are no states that, having been classified, are then not classified, they are not extracted because they lack the status of being a classifier (saṅgāhaka). States similar to the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) are classified by the many aggregates which are heterogeneous groups through aggregate-inclusion; since there are no states that are not classified by the remaining bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), they are not extracted because they lack both the status of being a classifier and the status of being a non-classifier. Thus, it should be understood that because of the absence of the status of being a classifier, the absence of the status of being a non-classifier, or the absence of both, the aforementioned states similar to the truth of the origin etc. are not extracted, and only the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so forth are extracted because they possess both the status of being a classifier and a non-classifier. In that second method, the statement "Those states which are included by the eye-base in terms of aggregate-inclusion" should be understood as referring to the material states remaining after the eye-base is excluded, and not to the entire aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). It has already been shown that a part does not classify the whole.

In the Commentary, however, "khandhapadena" means by way of inclusion of the term 'aggregate' (khandha-pada), and does not refer to the classifying agent (kattar). This statement is made by bringing in the phrase "by some classifying agent." The meaning of the statement that this answer is not suitable for the aggregate of matter etc. is that it is not suitable when the aggregate of matter etc. are the classifiers. If it were objected: "By the method 'included by the aggregate of matter...', only the aggregate of matter is included by the eye-base, and there is no such thing as that aggregate of matter being not included by the eleven bases and elements; thus, the eye-base etc. should also not be taken"? No, that objection does not hold. For the meaning of the word 'eva' (only) is not merely to exclude other states, but to exclude states other than the classifying agent. The phrase "so ca" (and that) etc. is also not a statement made without regard to others, but is a statement made with regard to the classifying agent. How? When it is said, "Only the aggregate of matter is included by the aggregate of matter," just as there are states other than the eye-base that are included by the eye-base through aggregate-inclusion, which are also not included through base and element inclusions, so too there are no states other than the aggregate of matter that are included by the aggregate of matter through aggregate-inclusion, which might be not included through base and element inclusions. Only the meaning that "only the aggregate of matter is included by the aggregate of matter through aggregate-inclusion" is suitable here. If it were said, "Let that same aggregate of matter be not included by the aggregate of matter through base and element inclusions," then, wishing to prohibit that, it is said: "And that aggregate of matter is not such that it is not included by the eleven bases and elements..."
13:
In saying "there is not" (natthi), here too, the term "by the aggregate of matter" (rūpakkhandhena) should be brought in and stated. In that sentence, it is appropriate to say that the absence of the state of being not included is stated by this method: the aggregate of matter is neither a classifier nor a non-classifier of the aggregate of matter itself or of its parts such as the eye etc., through base and element inclusions. It is not appropriate to say that the absence of the state of being not included is because the aggregate of matter or its parts are included by the aggregate of matter through the eleven base and element inclusions. For such a state of being included does not exist. If it did exist, the aggregate of matter would also have to be extracted in the exposition of terms associated and dissociated with the included (saṅgahitena sampayutta vippayutta pada-niddesa). Indeed, by those three inclusions (aggregate, base, element), the aggregate of matter or its parts would be included, and the state of being dissociated (vippayuttatā) also exists for those states.

Thus, because of the absence of the state of being not included, in the phrase "these terms and others," the meaning is that, like the eye-base etc., because of the absence of the state of being not included for the states included by these aggregate of matter etc. and by other states, these terms and other terms, however they may be, have unsuitable answers like these terms, and thus such terms are not taken as having the status of a classifier.

In that context, the statement "Only the aggregate of matter is included by the aggregate of matter" is refuted by showing the absence of the state of being included or not included of that aggregate of matter by itself. The reason given here for not taking it—"because of the absence of the state of being not included even though there is the state of being included"—would be suitable for the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) etc., because if there were a state included by those truths of the origin etc., there would be an absence of the state of being not included for that state. However, by the aggregate of matter etc., there is no state that is included at all; how then could there be a state of being not included for it? Therefore, it is appropriate to say that the absence of the status of being a classifier is the only reason for not taking it here. Although the state of being not included does not exist because the state of being included does not exist for the aggregate of matter etc. in relation to itself, its internal components, or its homogeneous parts, it does exist for other aggregates like the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) etc. Therefore, the absence of both (being included and not being included), as in the case of the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) etc., is suitable to be the reason for not taking it here. Although the mind-object base (dhamma-āyatana), the life faculty (jīvitindriya), etc., have the status of being classifiers of the four aggregates, two aggregates, etc., it is not that the state of being not included by base and element inclusions does not exist for those included states by those mind-object base, life faculty, etc. (it does exist). Therefore, the absence of the state of being not included is inconclusive (anekantika). Thus, the reason for not taking the states that are not taken, and for taking the states that are taken, should be understood only by the method previously stated.

## "Anidassanaṃ punadeva sappaṭighaṃ"
In this phrase, the term "anidassanaṃ" (invisible) is joined with the word "sappaṭighaṃ" (with impact) mentioned in the phrase "sanidassana sappaṭighaṃ" (visible and with impact)...
14:
The states that are non-visible and with impact (anidassana-sappaṭigha) have been shown. By the word 'puna deva' (again), in that very sentence of non-visible and with impact, the remaining term 'visible' (sanidassana) is taken again to show the 'visible dyad' (sanidassana-duka). It is not possible to say, 'By the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), only the eye-base itself is included.' This is because it should not be said that 'by the eye-base, the eye-base is included' or 'is not included' by way of inclusion as a base; thus this method is shown.

In this way, in all sections, the status of being 'not-sayable' (avattabbata) should be applied to the expressions 'includer and included' and 'non-includer and non-included' regarding the whole and its parts. Indeed, because of the absence of the state of being a non-includer, the eye-base and so on are not said to be 'not included' by the eye-base and so on, and not because of the absence of the state of being an includer.

## The explanation of the second method: Not included by what is included, is finished.

## 3. The Third Method: Explanation of the term 'Included by what is not included'

In the description of the term 'included by what is not included' (asaṅgahitena saṅgahita), among the states not included in the aggregate-group by the form-aggregate (rūpakkhandha), although there is a similarity in nature as bases and elements for the three aggregates such as feeling (vedanā) and for Nibbāna along with subtle form (sukhuma-rūpa), yet because subtle form alone is not the form-aggregate, there is no similarity in nature as bases and elements with the form-aggregate. Therefore, those states are not included by that form-aggregate through the groups of bases and elements. Not only are they not included, they are also not 'not included' by that [form-aggregate] through those inclusions. This is because there is a similarity in nature as bases and elements with the subtle form which is a part of that form-aggregate. However, here, only the absence of the state of being included is intended.

Those states which are not included by the consciousness-aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha), eye-base (cakkhāyatana), and so on, are not included by those consciousness-aggregates etc. in any way because they do not mix with them in any manner. Nibbāna, which is not included in the aggregate-group by the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) etc. which are the collection of the five aggregates, is not included by the groups of bases and elements, just like by the form-aggregate.

Therefore, it should be understood that such states are not taken as non-includers only because of the absence of the state of being an includer. But in the case of indeterminate states (abyākata-dhamma) etc. which are the collection of the five aggregates along with Nibbāna, it is precisely because of the absence of the state of being a non-includer. For there is nothing that could be a non-includer of them by way of aggregate-inclusion. And a part of oneself, or what is similar to a part of oneself, is not 'not included' by oneself. However, the taking of the feeling-aggregate (vedanākkhandha) and so on is done because of the state of being an includer of states that are not included.
15: In the commentary, the statement "those things which are included by the mind-object base (dhammāyatana)" should not be said as such. This is because the mind-object base is a collection of dissimilar aggregates and Nibbāna, and thus there is no phenomenon that is included by any inclusion. This method is shown because the mind-object base does not include itself within the inclusion of aggregates, nor does it have the nature of an includer through bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu). Therefore, the meaning of this statement should be understood as "included by the count of the mind-object base". By the words "yāni...pe... gahitāni", it is shown that terms such as the bases of power (iddhipāda), which indicate a portion of the mind-object base mixed with consciousness, are taken; terms such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), which indicate a portion of the mind-object base mixed with gross matter (oḷārika-rūpa), are excluded; terms such as the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) and the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), which do not indicate the mind-object base at all, are excluded; and terms such as the mind-object base (dhammāyatana), which indicate the entire mind-object base, are excluded. It shows that only those terms which indicate a portion of the mind-object base without being mixed with other bases are taken.## The commentary on the terms 'Included by the Unincluded' of the Third Method is finished.## 4. The Fourth Method: Commentary on the terms 'Included by the Included'In the explanation of the terms 'Included by the Included', the second and third methods were taught as 'Unincluded by the Included' and 'Included by the Unincluded' through the distinction of inclusion and non-inclusion of the three inclusions (aggregates, bases, and elements). However, the fourth and fifth methods are not like that. 'Included by the Included' is taught only by way of the mode of inclusion. 'Unincluded by the Unincluded' is taught only by way of the mode of non-inclusion. Therefore, these two methods are independent of the distinction of inclusion and rely only on the distinction of included phenomena and unincluded phenomena. In this fourth method, a specific phenomenon that is further included by another specific included phenomenon is questioned and answered in terms of being included. Desiring to show that very specific phenomenon according to the manner extracted, it is said: "Those phenomena which are included by the Truth of Origin (samudayasacca) as aggregates...pe...; by those phenomena, which phenomena are included as aggregates...pe...". Here also, phenomena such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), the mind-object base (dhammāyatana), and the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca) are not includers by all three (aggregates, bases, and elements). Just as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) etc. are not included by the two inclusions of bases and elements, and just as the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) etc., the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca), the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) etc., and the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu) etc. are not includers by the single inclusion of aggregates or elements, these phenomena are not extracted as includers because they lack the nature of being an includer.
16:
Those things that are classifiers through classifications are extracted in this Fourth Method because of the evident absence of the state of being a classifier. Indeed, those things that are included by those classifying factors certainly become the classifiers of their own classifier. The inclusion of that which is the classifier of oneself is again to be questioned and answered.

In the Commentary, the phrase 'sakalena hi khandhādipadena' means by a term such as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) which expresses the entire meaning. Regarding the statement, 'Having included the factor that classifies oneself, one should again reach inclusion by that very factor,' it cannot be said that there is no such included thing of that nature without associating it with the terms such as aggregates. This is because the inclusion of a thing is not questioned or answered by the very thing that includes it; nor is it only about that (classifying) thing itself. In fact, only the inclusion of the thing that is included by that factor is questioned and answered.

Unlike feeling (vedanā) and sound (sadda) which are distinct aggregates and distinct bases, subtle matter (sukhumarūpa) is not like that. That subtle matter is merely a portion of the aggregates and bases. Therefore, instead of saying 'a portion of subtle matter' (sukhumarūpekadesaṃ vā), it is stated in the manner of a classifier as 'subtle matter' (sukhumarūpaṃ vā). In all terms, it should be associated as 'unmixed with other aggregates.' The statement, 'That very thing is included by those things by way of aggregates etc.; with reference to those things,' also cannot be said in that manner. This is because in this Fourth Method, the inclusion of an included thing by another included thing is not questioned or answered; rather, it is only the inclusion itself that is questioned and answered. Therefore, 'ekena khandhena' should be understood only as 'by one classifying factor called an aggregate.' It should not be understood as 'by a classifying aggregate.' This is because a single aggregate does not classify its own component parts.

## The Explanation of the Terms 'Included by the Included' in the Fourth Method is Finished.

## 5. Fifth Method: Explanation of the Terms 'Unincluded by the Unincluded'

In the description of the terms 'unincluded by the unincluded,' the things shown through extraction should be understood in the same manner as already stated. In this Fifth Method, the groups of things together with subtle matter and consciousness, being similar to the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), non-visible and non-impinging (anidassana-appaṭigha), mental factors (acetasika), and unacquired (anupādā), even if they do not classify some things by one or two classifications, they are not 'non-classifiers by complete classifications' because there is no thing that is not included by all three classifications. Being similar to indeterminate states (abyākata), they are not 'non-classifiers' simply because there is no thing that is not included by any single classification. Therefore, they are not extracted by way of being non-classifiers. The remaining things, however, are extracted for the opposite reason.
17:
In the Commentary, the statement 'By such a term, Nibbāna would not reach even the mere inclusion within the aggregates' is said with reference to the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca). It should be understood that Nibbāna is contained within the non-visible and non-impinging (anidassana-appaṭigha) states which are non-classifiers, and it is not that those very states do not classify that Nibbāna. The first question, such as the question on mind and matter (nāmarūpa-pucchā), together with the second question and others which are combined by way of terms having similar answers, total thirty-four. By the words 'that very term which is extracted in the question,' it refers to a specific term such as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha), and not to the things to be questioned that are determined as 'unincluded by the unincluded.' Those things are shown only by their characteristics (lakkhaṇa) and not by their own nature (sarūpa) through the term.

In the term 'tadeva' (that very thing), the word 'eva' shows the certainty of the state of being 'unincluded by the unincluded' only for the extracted thing—meaning that the extracted thing is never not unincluded by an unincluded thing (i.e., it is always unincluded)—and it shows the uncertainty for other non-extracted things. In the phrase 'that very thing is unincluded by which things,' the remaining word 'certainly' (niyamato) can be connected. Alternatively, 'tadeva' means only that which is extracted in the question; the word 'eva' has the meaning of defining the state of being 'unincluded by the unincluded' by virtue of being extracted in the question, and it should be regarded as not having the meaning of prohibiting the state of being 'unincluded by the unincluded' for other things. A thing extracted in a question, whether it is with other things or not, is 'unincluded by the unincluded.' For instance, the aggregate of matter and others exist with other things like the aggregate of consciousness, while the aggregate of consciousness and others do not exist with other things.

'The remaining things are included' should be understood as 'the remaining things are not unincluded.' The meaning is that those material things are unincluded by those states of consciousness through the three classifications; thus they are extracted in the question and, being non-classifiers by the three classifications, they are 'unincluded.' Indeed, even the non-extracted things like feeling (vedanā) and others are also 'unincluded.' Here, in the first method, it is said that feeling and others are also unincluded by consciousness; in the second method, it is said that only material things are unincluded; this is the distinction. When it is said that feeling and others are unincluded in the classification of aggregates etc. only by matter and consciousness, it means they are unincluded by the three classifications by gross matter (oḷārikarūpa) and by consciousness. Here, by taking 'matter' (rūpa), gross matter which is a part of matter is taken.

In the fourth question, 'the visual base by the four [aggregates] starting with feeling' (cakkhāyatanaṃ vedanādīhi catūhi), it should be regarded that the term 'visual base' (cakkhāyatanaṃ) shows the non-classifier extracted in the question. The things that are unincluded by the unincluded visual base are the ten gross bases (oḷārikāyatana), not just the visual base alone. By the words 'matter and the mind-object base' (rūpañca dhammāyatanaṃ) etc., that thing which is unincluded by those things through the three classifications is consciousness alone; by the unincluded...
18: That consciousness, along with all phenomena other than consciousness that are unincluded, is brought together in the Pali text within those very phenomena such as the aggregate of form. Terms with similar answers should be shown by bringing them together. Among those summary verses (uddāna), when terms with answers similar to the first aggregate of form are brought together and shown, other terms with dissimilar answers are considered shown by way of providing the method. Therefore, it is said: "The form and the mind-object base...pe... are shown in summary by another manner". In that context, "two existences" (dve bhavā) refers to the existence of unconscious beings (asaññasatta) and the existence of one constituent (ekavokāra). The word "two" is said with reference only to external phenomena (bāhiradhamma) and derived phenomena (upādādhamma). That phenomenon such as the aggregate of form, by which the unincluded phenomenon is questioned and answered as unincluded, is called the "object" (visaya) because it is the basis for those questions and answers. However, because the shown summary verse is merely the providing of a method, it is called a "method" (naya). There is also a Pali reading "dvevīsanayo ca", which means this method consists of twenty-two terms.## The commentary on the terms 'Unincluded by the Unincluded' of the Fifth Method is finished.## 6. The Sixth Method: Commentary on the terms 'Associated and Dissociated'In the terms 'Associated and Dissociated', it should be understood that the statement "all that is obtained and all that is not obtained is taken in the question" is not said with reference to terms such as the aggregate of form, but only with reference to the terms 'associated' (sampayoga) and 'dissociated' (vippayoga). For among the aggregate of form etc., any term such as the mind-object base that is not obtained is also not taken in the question. However, the term 'associated', even if not obtained among the aggregate of form etc., is taken in the question as "With how many aggregates, bases, and elements is the aggregate of form associated?". It is obtained in the aggregate of feeling etc. The term 'dissociated', however, is obtained in all phenomena. For material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma), there is no such thing as association with other matter or with Nibbāna, nor for Nibbāna with matter, because they lack commonality such as arising together (ekuppāda). The commentator, while negating association, should be understood as also negating dissociation, because that very lack of arising together etc. is the dissimilarity of those phenomena. The arising together etc. present in the four mental aggregates constitutes their mutual similarity, and their dissimilarity with matter and Nibbāna. Neither a portion of matter nor Nibbāna possesses that arising together etc., which would constitute dissimilarity between a portion of matter and another portion of matter/Nibbāna, or between Nibbāna and matter. For that very reason, it is said: "It is dissociated from the four aggregates".
19:
In presenting phenomena that are not dissociated (avippayutta) from even one of the seven consciousness elements (viññāṇadhātu), the meaning is as follows: it is not like showing phenomena mixed with the objectless (anārammaṇa) matter, such as the form existence (rūpabhava) being dissociated from three consciousness elements (nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness elements); or phenomena that are neither resultant (vipāka) nor having the nature of resultant being dissociated from five consciousness elements (fivefold sense-consciousness); or phenomena without thought and examination (avitakka-avicāra) being dissociated from one consciousness element (mind element). Instead, it means showing those phenomena that are associated (sampayutta) with all seven consciousness elements, or showing those seven consciousness elements themselves, when there is no dissociation from even one consciousness element.

The term 'avippayutte' means phenomena that are not dissociated; it does not mean only those that are associated. Therefore, it means the non-inclusion of all those terms that indicate phenomena mixed with objectless matter and Nibbāna, such as: terms like the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana) which indicate association with those consciousness elements; terms like non-mental (acetasika) which are not to be spoken of as associated or dissociated; and terms like the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca) which are not to be spoken of as associated. This is because there is no association (sampayoga) or dissociation (vippayoga) with any of the aggregates, bases, or elements for the collection of all consciousness elements mixed with objectless matter and Nibbāna, the mental factors associated with those consciousness elements, or the combination of both.

If it is argued that in the exposition of the terms 'dissociated and not dissociated' (vippayutta-navippayutta), one should not say: 'Those phenomena which are dissociated from wholesome phenomena (kusala-dhamma), from those phenomena, those phenomena are dissociated' (because unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena are both mixed with the objectless). It is not that it should not be said; it indeed should be said. This is because the statement regarding the absence of association and dissociation with aggregates and so forth refers only to the aforementioned collections. For the aggregates and so forth are parts of that collection, and they are also collections of other parts of that collection. Since the collection and its parts cannot be separated, there is no state of being similar (sabhāgatā) or dissimilar (visabhāgatā). Therefore, there is no association or dissociation of those phenomena with the aggregates and so forth.

However, wholesome phenomena are distinguished from unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena. Those unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena are also distinguished from wholesome ones. There is no relationship of part and whole between those phenomena. Therefore, in presenting the phenomena as set forth in the Pāḷi text by the mere fact of being dissociated, without considering the aggregates and so forth, the dissociation of other (unwholesome and indeterminate) phenomena from wholesome phenomena, and of wholesome phenomena from other phenomena, is not non-existent; it indeed exists. This is because the state of being dissimilar (visabhāgatā) is evident. Therefore, the mutual dissociation of those phenomena is taught. This method applies to all such cases.

In the summary verse (uddāna), where it says 'eighteen,' it should be said as 'sixteen.' Where it says 'twenty-three,' it should be said as 'twenty-one.' In all places, there are the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), the base of mental objects (dhammāyatana), and the element of mental objects (dhammadhātu), which are collections of many phenomena, both free and not free from the distinctions of time (kāla) and continuity (santāna). Parts of these, such as the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) and the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), and those mixed with parts such as the bases of power (iddhipāda), and the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) which is not mixed with objectless phenomena, and those not mixed with phenomena having an object (sārammaṇa)...
20:
The Buddha has taken the truth of origin, the aggregate of feeling, and so on, as being distinguished by parts that share the same time and the same continuity, as well as by the state of being associated or dissociated. Therefore, these [states like] the truth of origin and those [states like] the aggregate of perception obtain association (sampayoga) and dissociation (vippayoga) accordingly through certain distinguished parts. For those [aggregates of feeling, perception, etc.], there exists commonality (sabhāgatā), such as arising together, and difference (visabhāgatā). Because association and dissociation are obtained through such commonality and difference, it is stated in various places in the Dhātukathā: 'Associated with certain states through one aggregate, one base, and one element,' and 'Dissociated from certain states through one base and one element.'

The aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness are merely collections of parts from different times; when they arise, they occur only as individual states. Therefore, because there is no nature of being distinguished parts at the same time for the aggregate of feeling and others, the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) and so on cannot differentiate the aggregate of feeling. Likewise, the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇadhātu) and others cannot differentiate the aggregate of consciousness or the mind base (manāyatana). Since the faculty of pleasure and the eye-consciousness element cannot differentiate the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of consciousness, and the mind base, the Buddha did not state such things as 'the faculty of pleasure is dissociated from certain states through one aggregate' or 'the eye-consciousness element is dissociated from certain states through one aggregate and one base.' However, although consciousness is not differentiated by aggregate or base, the Buddha did teach its differentiation by way of element. Thus, it is stated: 'The states from the eye-consciousness element... up to the mind-consciousness element are dissociated from sixteen elements.' In the same way, regarding the faculties like the faculty of pleasure which are distinguished by way of faculty-division, dissociation should be understood accordingly in such passages as 'those states which are dissociated from the faculty of pleasure,' but not for the undifferentiated aggregate of feeling.

If it is asked: 'Just as the Buddha taught "the truth of origin is associated with three aggregates" with reference to its association with those aggregates, why did He not similarly teach "it is dissociated from three aggregates" with reference to its dissociation from those three aggregates such as feeling?' [The answer is:] It is because it is inappropriate to speak of dissociation from those three aggregates, such as feeling, which are devoid of differentiation. If there were differentiation, it would be proper to say that the truth of origin is dissociated from the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, and the faculty of grief, as well as from consciousness elements other than the mind-consciousness element; this is because difference is properly grasped only through differentiation. However, it is not appropriate to say it is dissociated from the aggregate of feeling and others which are devoid of differentiation. This is because there is no state of difference between the existing truth of origin and the existing aggregate of feeling and others. Unlike unarisen states which have a distinction of time that can be grasped, the Buddha points out the conditioned states (saṅkhata) that are extracted based on their present existence, through the state of being associated or dissociated. Such extraction is performed based only on the present existence of conditioned aggregates and others that are devoid of differentiation, because one must rely only on the existence of the nature in a time that is not distinguished. There is no association between a non-existent state and another non-existent state, or between a non-existent and an existent state, or between an existent and a non-existent state. As for dissociation, when a distinction indicating non-existence is taken, the state of difference is also taken by that very distinction.
21:
When the distinction of non-existence is not taken, because the state of being dissimilar is not taken by the grasping of those various aggregates like feeling, etc., and because the state of being similar exists, the existence is shown by defining the similarity of states. Thus, similarity, known as the state of arising together (ekuppāda), etc., is indeed taken. Because that similarity is taken, only association (sampayoga) is obtained, not dissociation (vippayoga). Therefore, the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca) is stated as being associated with the feeling aggregate, etc., and not as being dissociated. This method should also be understood for the Truth of the Path (maggasacca), etc.

The commentary statement, "Excluding sustained application (vicāra) in the second jhāna, the remaining states are those without initial application and with sustained application only (avitakkavicāramatta)," shows that those prominent states which, like initial application (vitakka), are not hidden in other portions of mental arisings, are intended here as states without initial application and with sustained application only. Because those states with initial application are not taken, in the immediately following seventh method, they follow the same course as the Truth of the Origin; they do not follow the course of states with both initial and sustained application, and thus those states without initial application and with sustained application only are not taken. In the ten methods ending with the tenth, the dissociation of those states that are dissociated from those states without initial application and with sustained application only, and the dissociation of those states dissociated from them with the sixteen elements, and the counting by eighteen elements, are stated.

Even if those states without initial application and with sustained application only, which occur with initial application, are taken, all of them are associated with sustained application. Therefore, it is possible to say, "Some states are associated with one aggregate (vicāra)." That group of states without initial application and with sustained application only, excluding sustained application, is not associated with any other state. This is because the association of initial application, which is a part of that group, with a state other than sustained application, is not the association of the group of states without initial application and with sustained application only. Just as the association of the three aggregates with the base of power of desire (chandiddhipāda), etc., which are parts of the group of four bases of power (iddhipāda) arising in various mental arisings, is not the association of the group of bases of power, so it should be understood here as well.

However, just as the association of the group of bases of power with those states is stated because not even one of those four bases of power is dissociated from the feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, and a part of the formations aggregate, so too here, because there is no state among the group of states without initial application and with sustained application only that is not associated with sustained application, it is not impossible to state the association of that group with that sustained application. It is not that the association of states without initial application and with sustained application only should not be stated, like the association of states with roots to be abandoned by vision (dassanenapahātabbahetuka), etc. Among states with roots to be abandoned by vision, some are associated with delusion (moha), which is a part of the formations aggregate, and some are not. Therefore, that group is not associated with delusion, and since there is no other state that can be associated with that group, it is stated, "There are no states associated with states with roots to be abandoned by vision." The same should be understood for states with roots to be abandoned by development (bhāvanāyapahātabbahetuka), states with roots (sahetuka), etc. It is not that there is no state that can be associated with the group of states without initial application and with sustained application only; among the states without initial application and with sustained application only, in any one state...
22:
...because there is no state that is not associated with sustained application (vicāra), it is not that those states should not be called 'associated states' (they should indeed be so called). In all terms, even for a single state, the plural designation 'with some states' is made because there is no intention to limit the number.

## The Explanation of the Sixth Method: Terms of Association and Dissociation is finished.

## 7. The Seventh Method: Explanation of the Terms Associated and Dissociated

In the description of the terms 'associated' and 'dissociated', the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha), etc., are not taken because there is no state associated with that form aggregate, etc. Although the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca), etc., have states associated with them (mental arisings accompanied by greed), and although there are states dissociated from those associated states (wholesome, unwholesome, indeterminate), they are not taken because there is no dissociation of the associated and dissociated states from the aggregates, etc.

Indeed, among the aggregates, etc., there is no dissociation from any aggregate, base, or element for those other states like wholesome states, etc., which are dissociated from the mental arisings accompanied by greed that are associated with the Truth of the Origin. If it is asked, "Are those mental arisings themselves not the four aggregates, one and a half bases (mind-base and a part of the dhamma-base), and one and a half elements (mind-consciousness element and a part of the dhamma-element)? Therefore, should it not be said that there is dissociation from those states?"—the answer is that it should not be so stated. This is because other states are also aggregates, etc. It is not that only those states are the four aggregates; rather, those states and other states besides them are also the four aggregates. Similarly, they are also the one and a half bases and one and a half elements. Other states are not dissociated from those other groups, because there is no dissociation between the parts of a group and the parts of another group. This method is the same for the Truth of the Path (maggasacca), the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya), etc. Even when the states without initial application and with sustained application only (avitakkavicāramatta) are intended without remainder, no reason is seen for the Buddha not taking them, as they follow the same course as the states with both initial and sustained application.

In the Commentary, "states of such nature" means that just as the answer is not appropriate for the form aggregate, so too the answer is not appropriate for other states like the Truth of the Origin, etc.; thus, they are called "states of such nature" because of the inappropriateness of the answer. It should be understood that it is not said because of the absence of associated states. By the words, "Which terms show states associated with the dhamma-element," the terms such as the feeling aggregate (vedanākkhandha), etc., are shown. By the words, "Consciousness is also not mixed with other states," terms such as the consciousness aggregate (viññāṇakkhandha), the mind-base (manāyatana), etc., are shown. Therein, "not mixed with other states" means not mixed with dissociated states. Terms associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha vedanā) are also taken here because they show consciousness mixed with associated states. By this characteristic, it is shown that only states of such nature are taken; it does not show that states of such nature are definitely taken.
23:
Because terms such as Samudaya-sacca and Iddhipāda are not properly included in the way they are taught. Although there is an ancient reading, "Atha phassasattakaṃ cittaṃ saha yuttapadehi sattā," considering this reading to be deficient, the reading was made as: "Atha phassasattakaṃ, tike tayo satta mahantare ca."

In the inquiry, the word "vasena" is stated with the consideration that those things which are dissociated from the terms extracted in the inquiry are also dissociated from the terms extracted for the purpose of that inquiry. In the Uddāna verse found in the Pāḷi, "Dve ca manena yuttā, vitakkavicāraṇā" indicates the Savitakka term and Savicāra term by means of the two, Vitakka and Vicāra, which are invariably associated with the Manodhātu.

## The explanation of the term "Associated with the Dissociated" (Sampayuttena-vippayutta) in the Seventh Method is finished.

## 8. The Eighth Method: Explanation of the term "Associated with the Dissociated" (Vippayuttena-sampayutta)

In the explanation of the term "Associated with the Dissociated," since there is no associated state among those dissociated from the Rūpakkhandha etc., according to the determined manner, it is not stated as "Ye dhammā rūpakkhandhena vippayuttā, tehi dhammehi ye dhammā sampayuttā," but rather as "Ye dhammā rūpakkhandhena vippayuttā, te dhammā katihi khandhehi... pe... sampayuttāti natthi." By that sentence "rūpakkhandhena... sampayuttā," it is shown that because there is no association with any aggregate etc. for those things dissociated from the Rūpakkhandha, there is no "associated state with the dissociated" to be extracted; how then could there be association of that "associated state with the dissociated" again with aggregates etc.?

## The explanation of the term "Associated with the Dissociated" (Vippayuttena-sampayutta) in the Eighth Method is finished.

## 9. The Ninth Method: Explanation of the term "Associated with the Associated" (Sampayuttena-sampayutta)

In the explanation of the term "Associated with the Associated," the term "yaṃ khandhādivasena" should be understood as a compound (samāsa); it means "by the power of whichever aggregate etc." And "tasseva" means "of that very aggregate etc." This is the meaning: whatever association is mentioned here, among the states from Rūpakkhandha to Araṇanta, it is associated with whichever aggregate such as Vedanākkhandha etc.; then, after inquiring about the association of that very Vedanākkhandha etc. with the aggregates etc., the answer...
24:
...the answer to that inquiry has been given. That state is determined as "associated with the associated" because of its association with the state associated with itself. By the term "rūpena vā" (or by form), it should be understood that dissociation (ayoga) from Nirodha-sacca, Appaccaya-dhamma, and Asaṅkhata-dhamma is also stated. Similarly, by the term "rūpamissakehi vā" (or by those mixed with form), it should be understood that there is no association with states mixed with Nibbāna, such as Anupādinna-anupādāniya etc. For it will be said in the Sangaha: "Nibbāna is of the same nature as subtle form (sukhuma-rūpa)." "Sabbārūpakkhandhasangāhakehi" (by those that include all mental aggregates) means that since association is obtained only for states that are presently occurring, it refers to Arūpabhava etc., which include the four aggregates without deficiency, not excluding even a single state among those presently occurring. The summary of this Ninth Method is: all those such as Rūpakkhandha etc. which do not obtain association are not taken; however, all the remaining ones such as Vedanākkhandha etc. which do obtain association are taken.

## The explanation of the term "Associated with the Associated" (Sampayuttena-sampayutta) in the Ninth Method is finished.

## 10. The Tenth Method: Explanation of the term "Dissociated from the Dissociated" (Vippayuttena-vippayutta)

In the explanation of the term "Dissociated from the Dissociated," among the states not taken, states such as Dhammāyatana etc. are not taken because there is no state dissociated from them, due to their being states occurring in all consciousness-arisings (cittuppāda) mixed with those without objects. This distinction should be known: states such as Dukkha-sacca, the four Mahābhava, and Abyākata are not taken because there is no dissociation from the aggregates etc. which are dissociated from them.

## The explanation of the term "Dissociated from the Dissociated" (Vippayuttena-vippayutta) in the Tenth Method is finished.
