## 11. The Eleventh Method: Explanation of the term "Associated and Dissociated with the Included" (Sangahitena-sampayutta-vippayutta)

In the explanation of the Eleventh Method, the words "And those [states] with the remaining three aggregates, one Manāyatana, and seven Viññāṇadhātus" should be connected with the words "are called associated." To show the meaning of the word "kehi-ci" (some), by the statement "saṅkhārakkhandhe dhammāyatana-dhammadhātūsu ca ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ" (excluding craving from the Saṅkhārakkhandha, Dhammāyatana, and Dhammadhātu), the states included in the aggregates etc. by Samudaya-sacca, referred to as "te ca" (and those), are distinguished; and of those distinguished states, with the craving in the remaining Saṅkhārakkhandha other than itself, and with the craving in the Dhammāyatana and Dhammadhātu, and with the Vedanākkhandha and Saññākkhandha...
25:
With reference to the state of being associated with those dhammas that are capable of association, it is stated: "Because of being associated with the remaining dhammas, they are called 'associated with some'."

## The explanation of the terms 'Associated' and 'Dissociated' as comprised by the eleventh method is finished.

## 12. Explanation of the terms 'Included and Not Included by the Associated' (Sampayuttena-saṅgahitāsaṅgahita-pada)

In the twelfth method, just as in the ninth method, only those dhammas capable of association are obtained; with this intention, it is stated: "Only those dhammas are extracted."

## The explanation of the terms 'Included and Not Included by the Associated' in the twelfth method is finished.

## 13. Explanation of the terms 'Associated and Dissociated by the Not Included' (Asaṅgahitena-sampayutta-vippayutta-pada)

In the explanation of the thirteenth method, the dhammas that are not included by the three types of inclusion—namely aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)—are only consciousness (viññāṇa). Those twenty-two dhammas shown in the Pali text by the summary verse (uddāna-gāthā) beginning with "rūpañca dhammāyatanaṃ" are called "dhammas with questions similar to the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha)." Those dhammas which are not included by the three types of inclusion are only the gross bases (oḷārikāyatana), as in the formless realm (arūpabhava). All those remaining dhammas extracted in this method are called "similar to the formless realm."

Regarding the word "sesā" (the rest), the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and so forth, which appear in the fifth method, are not extracted because, although they are non-includers (asaṅgāhaka), they do not reach the point of being an answer in this method. As for dhammas such as the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca), which are not even non-includers, there is nothing to be said. To show how the aggregate of feeling and so forth do not reach the point of being an answer, the text beginning with "vedanākkhandhena hi" is stated. In that Pali, the phrase "there is no so-called association (sampayoga) of those dhammas" means that there is no association because of the mixture with the non-associations of material and mental dhammas.

If those dhammas were sometimes mental dhammas and material dhammas not associated with all consciousness elements (viññāṇadhātu), it is not that their dissociation (vippayoga) does not exist (it does exist). Therefore, it is not stated that "dissociation also does not exist." It should be understood that it is not because of the existence of dissociation of dhammas not included by the aggregate of feeling that it is not stated. Because of the absence of both association and dissociation, the aggregate of feeling and so forth do not reach the point of being an answer in this method.

In this context, it might be thus: "By the aggregate of feeling, the seven consciousness elements, which are mixed with objectless (anārammaṇa) dhammas by way of aggregates etc., are not included; and of those dhammas..."
26:
In saying "there is no association and dissociation," it refers to all consciousness elements (viññāṇadhātu) mixed with objectless (anārammaṇa) matter and Nibbāna, the mental factors (cetasika) associated with those consciousness elements, and both of these dhammas. Because they are not counted by the three types of inclusion such as the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), and the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), the absence of association and dissociation is the reason for not being included (in this method). Dissociation is of four types: dissociation by kind (jāti-vippayoga), dissociation by plane (bhūmi-vippayoga), dissociation by time (kāla-vippayoga), and dissociation by continuity (santāna-vippayoga). Among them, dissociation by kind refers to "wholesome dhammas, unwholesome dhammas," and so forth. Dissociation by plane refers to "sense-sphere dhammas, fine-material-sphere dhammas," and so forth. Dissociation by time refers to "past dhammas, future dhammas," and so forth. Dissociation by continuity refers to "internal dhammas, external dhammas," and so forth. Thus, dissociation should be known as fourfold.

## The explanation of the terms 'Associated and Dissociated by the Not Included' in the thirteenth method is finished.

## 14. Explanation of the terms 'Included and Not Included by the Dissociated' (Vippayuttena-saṅgahitāsaṅgahita-pada)

In the fourteenth method, it should be understood that dissociation does not apply because the mental base (dhammāyatana) and so forth are dhammas included in all arisings of consciousness (cittuppāda) mixed with objectless matter and Nibbāna. In this method, because the three types beginning with kind (jāti) are merely the nature of dhammas (dhamma-sabhāva), and because internal and external dhammas are the combination of all dhammas, and because the invisible and non-reactive (anidassana-appaṭigha) and so forth are all arisings of consciousness mixed with objectless matter and Nibbāna, association and dissociation do not apply in any way. In this method, only the state of inclusion and non-inclusion of dhammas dissociated from the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) and so forth is taken.

In the Pali summary verse (uddāna-gāthā), the phrase "samucchede na labbhanti" means they are not obtained in the final method (the fourteenth method). The phrase "moghapucchakena ca" means that although those dhammas are not obtained, it is because the question is a futile question (mogha-pucchā). Alternatively, the "futile questioner" (moghapucchaka) refers to the eighth method; together with that method, in the final method, these dhammas are not obtained in any way because of the absence of even dissociation.

## The explanation of the terms 'Included and Not Included by the Dissociated' in the fourteenth method is finished.

## The Mūla-Ṭīkā of the Dhātukathā-pakaraṇa is finished.
27:
## Puggalapaññatti-pakarana-mūlaṭīkā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Mātikāvaṇṇanā
In the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, the Buddha showed the classification of dhammas by way of triads (tika) and dyads (duka). In the Vibhaṅga, he showed the analysis of those dhammas by way of aggregates (khandha) and so forth. In the Dhātukathā, he spoke of the distinctions such as inclusion (saṅgaha) and non-inclusion (asaṅgaha) of those dhammas thus collected and analyzed. Then, in order to show the various distinctions of the designations (paññatti) by which those dhammas are designated—both according to their ultimate nature (sabhāva) and by way of derivation (upādāya)—the Blessed One undertook the Puggalapaññatti, beginning with the words "Six designations" (cha paññattiyo).

In that Puggalapaññatti, the designation of individuals (puggalapaññatti) such as "person, woman, man, deity, human" occurs by way of derivation, based on a collection that is not an ultimate nature (asabhāva-samūha), from those dhammas that occur in a sequential order. The designation of the five types, such as the designation of aggregates (khandhapaññatti), should be understood as the designation of intrinsic nature (sabhāvapaññatti). This is the making known of those [aggregates], as well as other external matter and Nibbāna, by way of a collection that possesses an intrinsic nature (sasabhāva-samūha) and by way of distinctions that possess an intrinsic nature (sasabhāva-bheda). Through that sabhāvapaññatti, all designations of intrinsic nature analyzed in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī and other books are included.

However, the designation of individuals (puggalapaññatti) is a designation of non-intrinsic nature (asabhāvapaññatti). Because it occurs by way of derivation from the ultimate dhammas—such as those to be fully understood (pariññeyya)—which exist within the continuity of beings and have distinctions such as "liberated in due time" (samayavimutta), all designations of non-intrinsic nature such as "monastery, bed" are also included by this principal [puggalapaññatti].

To this extent, what is called designation (paññatti) consists of the designation of the existent (vijjamāna-paññatti) and the designation of the non-existent (avijjamāna-paññatti). Only when these two—the existent and the non-existent—are mixed, do the other four designations arise. Therefore, it should be understood that by showing these [six], all designations are shown in this book. Among the six designations such as the designation of aggregates, the name of this book is called "Puggalapaññatti" (Designation of Individuals) because it is based on the designation of individuals, whose distinctions are not shown in other books but are shown only in this book. The phrase "desiring to designate certain dhammas here" means desiring to show them as the basis (vatthu) of designation. Indeed, in this book, one does not create the designation, but rather shows the designations through their bases (vatthu).
28:
The designation called "aggregate" (khandha) refers to all general designations (sāmañña-paññāpanā) and specific designations (visesa-paññāpanā) such as "matter" (rūpa) and "earth" (pathavī). It should be understood that this is said with reference to such communication. The meanings of this term "paññāpanā" (designation/communication) are "dassanā" (manifesting/showing) and "ṭhapanā" (establishing/placing). The meanings of those terms, dassanā and ṭhapanā, are "pakāsanā" (explaining/illustrating) and "nikkhipanā" (depositing/setting down).

Among those meanings, the act of making veneyya beings understand by placing [dhammas] into their respective groups—such as "material aggregate... faculty of one who has known, liberated in due time"—saying "this is named thus, that is named thus," is called "nikkhipanā" (setting down). It is not the kind of setting down like arranging a bed or such things in a physical location. The teacher has made the designation of the subject (kattu) as "the name-designation (nāmapaññatti) both shows and establishes." This should be understood as being said with reference to the fact that the name-designation, being either the state (bhāva) or the instrument (karaṇa), is the cause for those various dhammas being seen by the eye of wisdom and being established.

By the words "designation of the existent" (vijjamānapaññatti) and so forth, the phrase "independent of the Pali" (pāḷimuttaka) is said with reference to the fact that they do not appear [in this specific way] in the Pali Canon. The phrase "kusalākusalasseva" means "as in the case of the wholesome and unwholesome." The meaning of the word "vijjamānassa" is "sato" (existent), and the meaning of that "sato" is "sambhūtassa" (manifested/arisen). Alternatively, "vijjamānassa sato" means that which exists and has come to be. Desiring to show that very meaning, he said "sambhūtassa." By that term, he rejects the state of non-existence.

Likewise, "avijjamānassa" (of the non-existent) does not mean that they exist with distinct intrinsic natures, as wholesome dhammas are distinct from unwholesome natures, or as contact (phassa) and so forth are distinct from the nature of feeling (vedanā). Rather, it refers to the perception of "woman, man" based on the five aggregates. If those five aggregates are removed, there is no intrinsic nature of "woman" or "man" distinct from those aggregates; thus, it means "asambhūta" (not truly manifested). Regarding this term "avijjamānassa," some teachers say: "it is non-existent in that [ultimate] manner, but existent in another [designatory] manner." What should be said regarding that view has already been stated in the Paññattiduka.

Although it does not exist by way of ultimate nature (sabhāva), because the perception of "woman, man" exists through a mind free from wrong clinging while following worldly usage, it is said to be "established merely by worldly usage" (lokaniruttimatta-siddha). However, things like a "fifth truth" (pañcamasacca) grasped with a mind full of clinging are not established by ultimate nature, nor are they established by worldly convention; therefore, it is said they are "not obtainable in any way."

Among those designations, it is said with reference to the fact that three types appear in their own form in this Puggalapaññatti book. The views of the teachers (ācariyavāda) should be applied without contradicting the method of the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) mentioned above. Therefore, the meaning of the statement "this is a designation because of the meaning to be made known" is that it is a designation merely by way of the meaning to be communicated, as it is non-existent by way of ultimate nature. For even the meaning to be communicated, because it obtains its respective ultimate name through its own nature, is not from another...
29:
It receives the name "designation" (paññatti) which is to be obtained. However, a thing devoid of ultimate reality (nissabhāva) does not receive a name by its own nature because of the absence of such nature. It receives the name "designation" merely in the sense of being made known by names such as "being" (satta) and so on; and beings etc. are devoid of ultimate reality. Indeed, for a thing that possesses its own nature, there is no nature that cannot be apprehended by way of identity with or difference from form (rūpa) and so on.

"Kiriṭa" means a crown; because that crown belongs to him, he is called "Kiriṭī" (one who has a crown). In this teacher's view (ācariyavāda), one should include all six types of designations, such as the designation of the existent (vijjāmāna-paññatti) and the designation of the non-existent (avijjāmāna-paññatti), as having complete characteristics. It is appropriate to say that the "comparative designation" (upanidhā-paññatti) and "derivative designation" (upanikkhittaka-paññatti) of such types as "second" and "third" are included among the six designations because the countable (saṅkhyeyya) is predominant. Other designations also belong to their respective categories as appropriate. Since there is no such thing as a number like "second," "third," "two," or "three," the author of the Saṅgaha said, "The remaining designations belong to the class of the non-existent (avijjāmāna) and the class of the non-existent by means of the non-existent (avijjāmānena-avijjāmāna)," considering the nature of "derivative designation" (upādā-paññatti) and "continuity designation" (santati-paññatti) as designations of the non-existent, and other comparative designations as shown as designations of the non-existent by means of the non-existent. He considers only the nature of the non-existent by means of the non-existent for comparative and derivative designations such as "second," "third," "two," and "three." That which is made known by depending on "first" etc., or by placing "one" etc. nearby—that number does not exist at all. Likewise, he considers only the nature of the non-existent by means of the non-existent for the designation of continuity (santati-paññatti). Neither the meaning of "eighty years" nor the meaning of "a person eighty years old" is clearly existent.

Regarding the phrase "some designations of planes" (bhūmi-paññatti), it refers to designations such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). The meaning is that the sense-sphere etc. are ultimate realities (sabhāva-dhamma). If the word "kāma" is taken as the location (plane/bhūmi), this designation should be "designation of the existent by means of the non-existent" (avijjāmānena-vijjāmāna-paññatti). If the aggregates produced by kamma are taken, it should be "designation of the existent by means of the existent" (vijjāmena-vijjāmāna-paññatti). Just as the designation of a person as a "reciter" (bhāṇaka) by means of the action called speech or the volition that produces speech belongs to the class of "designation of the non-existent by means of the existent" (vijjāmānena-avijjāmāna-paññatti), so too, making known a person etc. by means of the shape called the form-base (rūpāyatana) as "thin" or "fat" should be "designation of the non-existent by means of the existent." Alternatively, if shape is not taken within the form-base, it is "designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent." Designations of the existent such as "form" (rūpa) and "contact" (phassa) should be included in "designation of function" (kicca-paññatti) by power of functions such as being deformed (ruppana), or in "individual designation" (paccatta-paññatti) by power of the names of individual dhammas. When the designations of the existent and the non-existent are mentioned, their...
30:
When the designations of the existent and the non-existent are mentioned, other designations (such as the designation of the non-existent by means of the existent, etc.) that arise by way of their mixture are also considered mentioned. It should be understood that this teacher's view (ācariyavāda) is a comprehensive view that encompasses everything.

Desiring to show the meaning of the sentence "As many as the five aggregates" (yāvatā pañcakkhandhā) and so on, the author of the Saṅgaha said "By as much making known" (yattakena paññāpanena) and so on. In that context, "as many as the five aggregates" means "as many as the form aggregate ... etc ... the consciousness aggregate"; there is the designation of aggregates (khandha-paññatti) for the aggregates. By this much extent, there is the designation of aggregates for the aggregates. Thus, by making the Pali construction (yojanā), it should be understood that this meaning is stated by way of brevity and detail. The meaning of this sentence "As many as the five aggregates, the designation of aggregates for the aggregates" is shown by the statement "Briefly, as 'five aggregates' by as much making known." However, the meaning of the Pali "As many as the form aggregate" etc. is shown by the statement "By way of detail, 'form aggregate'" and so on.

In that context, the sentence "form aggregate ... etc ... consciousness aggregate" is merely an indication of the details. Even though not directly stated by that sentence, all the details of the aggregates are encompassed. Therefore, it is said, "Even therein, the form aggregate is of the sense-sphere" and so on. Alternatively, the meaning in this Pali should be construed thus: connecting the word "yāvatā" (as many as) with all the words—as many as there are five aggregates, so many are the designations of aggregates for the aggregates. As many as there are details of the five aggregates and their subdivisions such as the form aggregate, so many are the details of the designation of aggregates for the aggregates. Thus, he shows the details of the designation of aggregates by way of the details of the objects (vatthu) as stated in other texts (such as the Dhammasaṅgaṇī). This method also applies to sentences such as "As many as the bases" (yāvatā āyatanānaṃ).

"By a part only" (ekadeseneva) means "merely by way of summary" (uddesamatteneva).

## The Commentary on the Matrix is finished.
31:
## 2. Commentary on the Description (Niddesavaṇṇanā)
## 1. Commentary on the Description of the Ones (Ekakaniddesavaṇṇanā)
With the intention that "only the factors of absorption (jhāna) are called liberation (vimokkha)," [the author] stated: "By the mental body (nāmakāya) associated with liberation."

By the words "together with which," etc., he first explains the meaning of being endowed [with the mental body]. By the words "only that which is touched by contact (phassa) is called 'name' (nāma)," he explains the second meaning, which is "touching by contact," as stated in "it is also thus," etc. With the remaining words, he explains the other causal meanings. This is because being endowed, touching, and being a cause are all called "touching" (phusanā). Again, because the first meaning (being endowed) is difficult to understand, he explains it further by saying "to him in that [jhāna]," etc. Intending to show that among the more than fifty states remaining after excluding those [jhāna] factors, the feeling (vedanā) and the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) are included, he says: "The four aggregates come to be."

If this is so, since pleasure (sukha) is touched by feeling and the faculty of joy, and since those three are not different (they are one), does it follow that feeling itself touches that [same] feeling? It should be answered: No, it does not. This is because it is stated that the state of close contemplation is obtained through the predominant nature of experiencing. Alternatively, the plural form is used in "excluding those factors" because there are many factors. Among those factors, each should be applied individually, such as "excluding initial thought (vitakka)," etc. Among those applications, in the application "excluding pleasure (sukha)," the remaining three aggregates come to be; in the other applications, four aggregates come to be. In all applications, including at least three within, it is stated: "The four aggregates come to be."

The person who is liberated from certain taints (āsavas) by the non-temporary liberation (asamayavimokkha, i.e., the Path of Arahantship) and is endowed with the superior temporary liberation (the eight attainments) by obtaining the powerful support of non-temporary liberation—only such a person is called "temporarily liberated" (samayavimutta). For a trainee (sekha) who has attained jhāna and is liberated by that attainment, who does not return from the fine-material or immaterial realms to the sense realm, and who is thus liberated from sensual lust, etc. [through suppression and eradication], is worthy of receiving the designation "temporarily liberated." However, a worldling (puthujjana) who has attained jhāna is of a nature to return [to the sense realm], and because they can again be overwhelmed by sensual lust, etc., they are not called one liberated from the taints; thus, they are not worthy of the designation "temporarily liberated." Therefore, such a worldling is not called "temporarily liberated." For an Arahant, there are no remaining taints from which to be liberated. The eight liberations (vimokkhas) of that Arahant are merely pleasant dwellings in this very life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra). Therefore, for that Arahant, the possession of the eight liberations is not the cause for being designated as "temporarily liberated" or "non-temporarily liberated." To show that it is not the cause...
32:
It should be understood that the teaching "Na heva kho... pe... viharati" is not intended to show that only a dry-insight (sukkhavipassaka) Arahant is non-temporarily liberated (asamayavimutta). This is because every Arahant is indeed non-temporarily liberated (one liberated at all times). "External" (bāhirānaṃ) means those that are outside the supramundane (lokuttara), i.e., mundane (lokiya) states. To show that the word "arūpa" does not only denote the four mental aggregates and Nibbāna, he said "other than form (rūpa)," etc. "Casket of the mind" (cittamañjūsaṃ) refers to concentration (samādhi). Because it is the basis for states such as direct knowledge (abhiññā), concentration is like a casket. "To pervade the duration" (addhānaṃ pharituṃ) means to pervade for a long time, or to maintain [the state].

It should be understood that a breach of duty (vattabheda) occurs when one thinks "it should be swept" but does not respectfully exert effort in that task. An attainment (samāpatti) lost merely through such a breach of duty is not like an attainment destroyed by sensual desire, etc., which is difficult to recover; because the obstacles are minor, it can be recovered simply by fulfilling the duty. Thus it is said: "He sat down while entering [the attainment]" (appento va nisīdi). Even for those who spend time with negligence appropriate to themselves, the attainment does not perish, so they are not called "one who has fallen away" (parihīna). This is because they are capable of re-entering the attainment as soon as those various distractions (byāsaṅga) are removed.

"Venerable Sir, why are gain, honor, and fame (lābhasakkārasiloka) an obstacle to a monk whose taints are destroyed?" [The Buddha replied:] "Ānanda, I do not say that gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle to that unshakeable liberation of mind (akuppā cetovimutti) which he possesses. But, Ānanda, I say that gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle to those pleasant dwellings in this very life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra) attained by that monk who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute." This is found in the Sutta from the Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 2.179). In that Sutta, gain, honor, and fame are called an obstacle because the bliss of the attainments, which should be entered from time to time, does not arise during those periods of distraction. With this meaning, it should be understood that there is no contradiction between the Commentary and that Sutta.

In the passage "dhammānaṃ... pe... pi," it should have been said "dhammehi." Here, it refers to the person's falling away (parihāna) or non-falling away from those various attainments. In that context, the perishing of the attainments due to the person's negligence is called "the shaking of the states" (dhammānaṃ kuppanaṃ). It should be understood that the "falling away of the person" and the "shaking of the states" are merely different ways of expression (pariyāya) with slight differences in wording or literal meaning.
33:
7-8. Volition (cetanā) refers to the volition that causes the occurrence of and entry into the attainment (samāpatti), as well as the volition that exerts effort for that attainment. Preservation (anurakkhaṇā) is mindfulness (sati) accompanied by wisdom (paññā) that grasps what is beneficial or unbeneficial to the attainment. Persons who are worthy of the attainments that are exerted and protected by the aforementioned volition and mindfulness are called 'cetanā-bhabba' (capable through volition) and 'anurakkhaṇā-bhabba' (capable through preservation).

'Puthujjanagotta' (the lineage of worldlings) means the transcending of the three trainings (sikkhā)—higher virtue (adhisīla), higher mind (adhicitta), and higher wisdom (adhipaññā)—that exist within worldlings. These are called 'worldling trainings' because the three fetters (saṃyojana)—personality belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), skeptical doubt (vicikicchā), and attachment to rites and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa)—have not yet been cut off.

A person standing on the path to Arahantship (arahattamaggaṭṭha) is also called 'bhayuttarata' (restrained by fear) because they are terrified by the dangers of the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭabhaya) through wisdom and abstain from the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana). Therefore, it is said, 'The seven learners (sekkha) are those restrained by fear (bhayuttarata).'

Persons devoid of wisdom associated with the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-paññā) are included under the phrase 'endowed with the obstruction of [karmic] result' (vipākāvaraṇa). Therefore, to show that even some with triple-rooted rebirth (tihetuka-paṭisandhi) should be taken by the term 'duppaññā' (lacking wisdom), it is said, 'those who have not yet obtained the support (upanissaya) for the path and fruit.' Indeed, without wisdom, that support for the path and fruit cannot exist.

Only where there is a mixed occurrence of the fixed (niyata) and the unfixed (aniyata) can there be fixed states (niyata-dhamma). To show that there is no such thing as 'fixed' among the inhabitants of Uttarakuru because such a mixture does not exist there, the words beginning with 'For the inhabitants of Uttarakuru...' are spoken.

Among the thirteen 'heads' (sīsa), those such as the 'head of obstacles' (palibodha-sīsa) and the 'head of occurrence' (pavatta-sīsa) are states to be exhausted (pariyādiyitabba) [by the path]. Those such as the 'head of resolution' (adhimokkha-sīsa) are the states that exhaust (pariyādaka). The result of the path that exhausts is the 'head of range' (gocara-sīsa). That 'head of range' is indeed the liberation of the fruit (phala-vimokkha) which is an internal object (visayajjhatta). The 'head of formations' (saṅkhāra-sīsa), which is the object of the path and fruit that exhausts, is cessation (nirodha/Nibbāna), the seclusion from formations. Thus, to show the state of 'samasīsi' (attaining the end of defilements and life simultaneously) by demonstrating the simultaneous completion of the states to be exhausted, the states that exhaust, the results, and the objects, thirteen 'heads' are mentioned in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. However, in this Puggalapaññatti-aṭṭhakathā, because it is stated that 'the exhaustion of taints (āsava) and the exhaustion of the life-faculty occur neither before nor after but simultaneously,' the author wishes to connect them only by the power of the 'head of defilements' (kilesa-sīsa/avijjā) and the 'head of occurrence' (pavatta-sīsa/jīvita) among those heads. Thus, it is said, 'Among those heads, the head of defilements is...' In that statement, although the path that rises out of the cycle of rebirth exhausts the 'head of occurrence' by making it not occur again after death (cuti), since the nature of occurrence still exists until death, it is said 'head of occurrence...'
34:
"...the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is exhausted together with the death-consciousness (cuticitta)," it is said. The stages of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-vāra) that are completed as if immediately after the exhaustion of defilements should also be regarded as the stages of the exhaustion of defilements. For, according to the word, "When liberated, the knowledge 'it is liberated' arises," the exhaustion of defilements is said to be completed by the conclusion of the reviewing knowledge. If that completion occurs with the death-consciousness, then the completion of the life-faculty also occurs with that same death-consciousness. Therefore, because of this equality of the stage and death, the exhaustion of defilements and the exhaustion of the life-faculty reach the state of occurring neither before nor after, as expressed by the phrase 'vāra-samatāya' (by the equality of the stage).

In the phrase "descending into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), he attains Parinibbāna," it should be understood that only the death-consciousness, which is the cause of Parinibbāna, is spoken of as 'descending into the life-continuum.'

'Mahāpayogo' (great effort/action) refers to the destruction of the world of space (okāsaloka) characterized by a heavy downpour of rain that causes the ruin and transformation of the world. 'Tiṭṭheyya' (should stand) means that destruction should not occur.

'Araṇīyattā' means because of being worthy of being approached and served (payirupāsitabba).

When that supreme knowledge (aggavijjā) by which one's task is done is attained, the state of 'te-vijjā' (threefold knowledge) is called 'non-metaphorical' (nippariyāyata). That knowledge is also a 'te-vijjā' that is accomplished through arrival (āgamana) and is endowed with excellence; thus it is said, 'the burden of arrival itself' (āgamanīyameva dhuraṃ).

In the word 'tattha ca,' the locative case (bhummavibhat) applies either in the sense of a cause (nimitta) or in the sense of being the basis for the attainment of omniscient knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). For it is in that [knowledge] alone that one is said to have attained omniscience.

'Ananussutesu dhammesu' means in the truths (sacca) that have not been heard before.

Although it is stated in the Mahānidāna Sutta, after mentioning the eight liberations (vimokkha) ending with the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) such as 'Possessing form, one sees forms,' that 'Ananda, when a bhikkhu dwells having touched these eight liberations with his mental body (nāmakāya), and his taints are exhausted by seeing with wisdom, this bhikkhu, Ananda, is called liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta),' that statement was made with reference to the most excellent 'liberated in both ways' person. Here, however, for the purpose of including all 'liberated in both ways' persons according to the Kīṭāgiri Sutta, it is said, 'He dwells having obtained the eight attainments with the co-nascent mental body.'
35:
In the Kīṭāgiri Sutta, it is taught: "Monks, here a certain person dwells having touched with the mental body those peaceful deliverances that are immaterial, transcending form, and their taints are destroyed by seeing with wisdom. Monks, this person is called one liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta)." In accordance with this, four [types of] those liberated in both ways are taught by way of the immaterial attainments. Among those liberated in both ways, the most excellent person is such because of possessing the aforementioned characteristics. The same method applies to the body-witness (kāyasakkhī).

In the sentence "their taints are destroyed by seeing with wisdom," it is not that the taints see with wisdom; rather, the taints that reach destruction because of the cause of seeing are said to be "destroyed by seeing." This is because destruction is dependent on seeing, and thus seeing is the preceding action for the destruction of taints.

In the sentence "this person is one dependent on the mental body (nāmanissitako)," it means that this person liberated in both ways, having been freed from the material body (rūpakāya) and remaining dependent on the mental body (nāmakāya), is then freed from that mental body; thus they are called "nāmanissitako." By citing the Sutta as evidence for liberation from both the mental and material bodies, it is meant that "they are called liberated in both ways because they are well-freed from both bodies." In the Sutta, the Buddha declared the Brahmin Upasīva, who attained the sphere of nothingness, to be a sage liberated in both ways, being freed from the mental body.

In the first Theravāda (Elder's view), one is called "liberated in both ways" because of being liberated by two parts. In the second Theravāda, one is called "liberated in both ways" because of being liberated from two parts. In the third Theravāda, one is called "liberated in both ways" because of being liberated twice by two parts. This is the distinction between these Theravādas. In that text, "liberated" (vimutta) should be understood as being liberated from defilements, or being liberated from the collection of both the material body and the mental body through the suppression and eradication of defilements.

That the immaterial sphere attainment is liberated from the mental body means it is liberated from the mental body known as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Because that immaterial attainment is liberated from the mental body by being far from the hindrances, and from the material body by the suppression of craving for form, it is called "liberated in both ways" in a partial sense. Therefore, the intention is that it is suitable to be the cause for obtaining the name "liberated in both ways," which is the basis for the path of Arahantship.

The reason is that among these persons, not even one is an attainer of the eight deliverances (vimokkha); therefore, even a single instance of liberation from the material body, which is the cause of being liberated in both ways...
36:
...means not having attained liberation (vimokkha). Indeed, one who attains even one of the immaterial jhanas is called a "possessor of the eight liberations" (aṭṭhavimokkha-lābhī) because they have acquired the cause for being liberated in both ways, and that attainment is capable of bestowing that name by way of a portion of the eight liberations. Therefore, it was said, "But in the immaterial jhanas..." and so forth.

In the sentence "He realizes the end of what is touched" (phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikaroti), the end of the touched immaterial jhanas is called 'phuṭṭhanta'. It means the time immediately following the touched immaterial jhanas. Here, the word 'phuṭṭhantaṃ' should be understood as using the accusative case in the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyoga). It means he realizes through the means to be realized only for the duration of the time immediately following the touched immaterial jhanas. Alternatively, as in passages like "he sat down to one side" (ekamantaṃ nisīdi), this term is an adverbial derivative (bhāvanapuṃsaka).

In truth, the person who is liberated from the material body and from a portion of the mental body through the liberation of displacement (vikkhambhana-vimokkha) by means of immaterial jhana, for him, the liberation known as cessation (nirodha) is as if contemplated and made manifest, but it is not yet realized with the mental body. However, when some taints are destroyed by making cessation the object, he is said to have realized it. Therefore, because he realizes the cessation that is to be realized with the mental body just as it was contemplated, he is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī). He is not yet called "liberated" (vimutta) because some taints have not yet been exhausted.

By the words "attained through seeing" (diṭṭhattā patto), it shows the attainment of cessation through vision (diṭṭhi), which is the seeing of the Four Noble Truths. Alternatively, there is a reading "attained the end of vision" (diṭṭhantaṃ patto), which means he has reached the state immediately following the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga-ñāṇa), which is called vision. Indeed, from the fruit of stream-entry up to the highest path (arahatta-magga), a person is called "one attained through vision" (diṭṭhippatta).

In rejecting this method with the word "No," it should be understood that the rejection was made upon seeing this flaw: that only the diversity of wisdom among those who have reached the states of 'attained through vision' and 'liberated by faith' (saddhāvimutta) was mentioned, but the specific reason by which that distinction was reached was not mentioned. By the words "in the Āgama commentaries" (āgamaṭṭhakathāsu), it should be known that it only strengthens the conclusion regarding the diversity of the means of attainment.

By the words "liberated while having faith" (saddahanto vimutto), it shows the state of being liberated by mere faith, even if not liberated in every respect. Alternatively, "liberated by faith" (saddhāvimutta) means one who is resolved through faith.

"He sets wisdom in motion" (paññaṃ vāheti) means he carries on wisdom to an extraordinary degree. "Wisdom carries this person" means it leads him towards Nibbāna.
37:
In this way, regarding the phrase 'even at the moment of the Path,' why is this word 'api' (even/also) used? Does it not lead to the objection: 'If one is endowed with the Path consisting of the eight noble factors, it occurs only at the moment of the Path; therefore, is one not called a Sotāpanna only at that moment of the Path?' It does not lead to such an objection. This is because the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga) gives the name 'Sota' (Stream) to its corresponding Fruition of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), which consists of either eight factors or seven factors (excluding Right Intention). Therefore, one is a Sotāpanna because of being endowed with that Fruition; or, one who stands in Fruition is also said to be endowed with the Path called 'Stream' which has not yet diminished from its function. However, such a person in Fruition is not currently attaining the Stream (the Noble Path) as in the first moment of the Path. Therefore, because of the state of having well-attained the Stream, it is appropriate to be called a 'Sotāpanna' (Stream-enterer) starting from the first Fruition.

Indeed, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, whoever has unwavering faith in me, all of them are Sotāpannas. Among those Sotāpannas, for five, the end (of saṃsāra) is here in this world; for five, the end is after leaving this world (in a higher realm).' Among those Sotāpannas, since those standing in the Fruition of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-phala), etc., have distinct names, only the person standing in the Fruition of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phalaṭṭha) should be distinguished from others and called a 'Sotāpanna'; it is this person who is intended here. By the phrase 'knows by the Path already attained,' it shows that the attained Path is the sufficing condition (upanissaya) for the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths and so on. Because the Sotāpatti-magga, which knows the Four Noble Truths, is the supreme support for this person, they are called 'Sambodhiparāyaṇa' (bound for enlightenment). According to the second meaning, because the Eightfold Path that knows the Four Noble Truths is the supreme destination (gati) for this person, they are called 'Sambodhiparāyaṇa.'

Since the word 'kula' (family) alone refers only to a great family, the author states the meaning as 'one is reborn only in families of great wealth.'

'Khandhabīja' (seed of aggregates) refers to rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa). In this context, a Sotāpanna who possesses jhāna, even if they have not yet completely cut off the lower fetters, is similar to an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) and does not have the nature of returning to the sense sphere; thus, they are not included in this classification of Sotāpannas. The teacher of the Commentary intends that only a Sotāpanna with inferior jhāna, who wanders between the lower sense sphere and the upper Brahma realms and returns to the sense sphere, is included here.

'What should be said' means the explanation that should be stated, such as 'the thinning (of defilements) should be understood through two reasons.'

'Immediately after being reborn' means that after this person is reborn in a new existence, they produce the Noble Path immediately after that rebirth-linking. 'Before reaching the middle of the lifespan' means that within this interval, before reaching the middle of that person's lifespan...
38:
...they produce the Noble Path; this is the meaning of the Pali here. In the Commentary, however, just like the phrase 'a river that has not reached the mountain,' it should be understood that because of the connection with the subsequent word in the phrase 'before reaching the middle of the lifespan,' the word 'hutvā' (being/having been) is applied as a grammatical ellipsis.

Regarding the word 'Upahacca,' the meaning is 'having approached.' By this, it encompasses both the passing of the middle of the lifespan and the approaching of death. Therefore, it is said, 'having surpassed the middle,' and so on.

One is called 'Uddhaṃvahi' (Upward-streamer) because one is carried upwards. It is called 'uddhaṃvāhibhāvena' because of the state of being carried upwards through the stream of craving or the stream of the round of rebirths. Even if an 'Uddhaṃsota' person in the Aviha realms does not attain Parinibbāna there, and regardless of which higher realm they go to for Parinibbāna, because that person who will attain Parinibbāna has the states of 'Asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī' (attaining Nibbāna without exertion) and 'Sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī' (attaining Nibbāna with exertion), ten types of Anāgāmīs are mentioned in that Aviha realm. The same method applies to the Atappa realm and others. 'Anupahaccatala' means one who has not reached the ground. The quick or slow destination of the Asaṅkhāra and Sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī persons should be understood as being like a flame that burns a small or large amount of grass and wood. It should be understood as having a duration greater than a flame that goes out as soon as it arises, or a duration less than a flame that goes out only upon reaching the ocean; and as having a greater or lesser duration than the Antarā-parinibbāyī, Upahacca-parinibbāyī, and Uddhaṃsota persons. Indeed, those very persons are the Asaṅkhāra and Sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī. The phrase 'greater than that' serves to illustrate the flames capable of burning grass and wood, not to show the specific degree of being greater or lesser.

Regarding the sentence 'No cassa no ca me siyā,' the meaning is: 'If the group of five causes such as ignorance (avijjā) and formations (saṅkhāra) were not, then this group of five results such as consciousness (viññāṇa) currently occurring in this life would not be mine.' By that text, because it shows the occurrence of this present suffering (dukkha-sacca) due to the origin (samudaya-sacca) which is the cause of suffering established in the past life, the practice of seeing the arising of the aggregates in the sense of arising through conditions is stated. Regarding the sentence 'Na bhavissati na me bhavissati,' the meaning is: 'If the group of five causes does not exist in the present life, the group of five results will not be mine in the future life.' By this Pali, the practice of seeing the cessation of the aggregates in the sense of the cessation of conditions is stated. Alternatively, the practice of emptiness (suññatā) by way of prohibiting 'self' and 'what belongs to self' in the present and future is stated by all four of those sentences. 'Yadatthi' is analyzed as 'yaṃ atthi' (that which exists). 'Bhūtaṃ' means the group of five aggregates which exist with their ultimate nature, or which have arisen, which have arising and falling as seen, or which are empty as seen; it means mere mind and matter (nāmarūpa) devoid of the state of imagined woman, man, being, and so on. With the mind directed towards the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) through the contemplation of cessation (vivaṭṭānupassanā), that true reality...
39:
By the thought "I shall abandon," one attains equanimity; it means one becomes equanimous through the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa).

"Not attached to existence (bhava), not attached to becoming (sambhava)" means not being attached to either ordinary existence or distinguished and noble existence, as some teachers say. However, it should be understood that present existence is called 'bhava', and existence that encompasses the birth (jāti) to occur in the future is called 'sambhava'. Alternatively, the manifest five aggregates (bhūta) are called 'bhava', and the cause of those aggregates is called 'sambhava'. By showing non-attachment to both, the practice of the trainees (sekha) is demonstrated. Indeed, detachment from the five aggregates along with their causes is the practice of the trainees. Therefore, the Venerable Sāriputta said: "Venerable Sir, I see these five aggregates as 'what has come to be' (bhūta) as they really are with correct wisdom. Having seen them thus as 'what has come to be' as they really are with correct wisdom, I practice for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what has come to be. I also see 'becoming' (sambhava), the source of what has come to be, as it really is... and practice... I see the five aggregates that arise due to the cessation of that cause as 'states subject to cessation' as they really are... and practice... In this way, Venerable Sir, one is a trainee (sekha)." (Saṃyutta Nikāya, Nidāna-vagga).

"Athuttarī" means when one is thus unattached, one properly sees the peaceful state of Nibbāna above through the sequence of insight with path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). However, that state is not yet fully realized in every respect, because that Nibbāna, which is to be realized only by the fourth path (arahatta-magga), has not yet been realized by that trainee.

## The Commentary on the Description of the Ones is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Description of the Twos

Sensual existence (kāma-bhava), from which one cannot be removed due to the inability to abandon certain defilements or from which one is not liberated in some way, is a specific cause for the grasping of a self; therefore, it is called "internal" (ajjhatta). A bond in that internal state is an internal fetter (ajjhatta-saṃyojana); a person associated with that fetter is called an internal-fetter person (ajjhatta-saṃyojana-puggala).

One who has a mind desiring the welfare of others that arises without a cause (without expecting a return) is called "unconditionally affectionate" (akāraṇa-vacchala). Even if one expects a future benefit, if one is grateful based on a previously received favor, they are merely "grateful" (kataññū), not a "prior benefactor" (pubbakārī). Therefore, it is said "he will do for me," etc. A person heading from darkness to light (tamo-joti-parāyaṇa) is called a "prior benefactor" (pubbakārī) because they perform meritorious deeds without depending on the fruits of merit. They form the perception "I am paying a debt." Even if they do not consciously form this perception, it is as if they do.
40:
In the phrase "having obtained bear meat, he has no remorse thinking it is pork," it means that even though he knows it is bear meat, he has no remorse thinking it is pork, and thus he tramples upon and transgresses (the training rule).

"A satisfied person" (titta) is one who is free from exertion because their task is completed.

## The Commentary on the Description of the Twos is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Description of the Threes

"By the failure of the remaining restraints" means by the failure of the restraint of the mind (mano-saṃvara), or by the failure of the restraint of mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), and so on. "By being endowed with unwholesome virtue" means being endowed with those things described as: "Householder, what are unwholesome virtues? Unwholesome bodily action, unwholesome verbal action, and evil livelihood." For such a person... (pe)... "one whose conduct is thus repulsive" means one whose conduct is repulsive.

By way of showing the distinction among persons who have similar objects, "body-witness" (kāya-sakkhī), etc., are taught.

In the phrase "concentration is the beginning, etc.," the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) are primarily called the "Dispensation" (sāsana). Therefore, the foundational concentration (pādaka-samādhi), which has those supramundane states as its goal, is called the beginning of the Dispensation. Insight (vipassanā) is also called the beginning because of its proximity to it, and the Path (magga) is called the beginning because it is a part of the root of that Dispensation.

"A person with lap-like wisdom should be known" means that because of having wisdom like a lap, the person is also like a lap, just as the wisdom is like a lap. This is said with the meaning that teachings do not remain long in that person. It will be said later: "The meaning is one with wisdom similar to a lap."

Just like lap-like wisdom, upturned-pot-like wisdom (nikkujja-kumbha-paññā) should also be known, because teachings do not remain in that wisdom.

Because of lasting a long time and being firm, a person who has marks of anger caused by the faults of others, which are like inscriptions on stone, is called "one like an inscription on stone" (pāsāṇa-lekha), being endowed with anger like an inscription on stone. In this same way, the others should also be understood.
41:
Conceit that is empty and devoid of substance such as learning is called 'naḷa' (reed) because it resembles a reed. A person in whom this reed-like empty conceit has arisen is called 'unnala'.

To show that the initial effort, such as the occurrence of talk on virtue mentioned here as 'There will be talk on virtue for us,' cannot happen with an immoral person, it is said: 'Talk on virtue simply does not occur.'

In the phrase 'tatttha tattha' (in this and that), it means that one supports through wisdom—which has arisen depending on superior virtue—those various states that should be supported, purified by wisdom, and developed by wisdom.

By the phrase 'immorality is like a cesspool,' the author shows only the similarity of immorality (dussīlya) to excrement.

'They are unable to properly make [others] understand' is said with reference to the fact that they are generally unable to do so. Or, it refers to the inability of one who, having disregarded the Tathāgata when He has appeared, strives to produce meditative attainments (samāpatti). Alternatively, it refers to the six sectarian teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa.

## The Explanation of the Description of the Triads is finished.

## 4. Explanation of the Description of the Tetrads

Immorality committed by another's command is done through the command of the other and through one's own effort; therefore, the one who commands is called 'the heir to half of that evil committed by the other.'

By the word 'ayaṃ' (this), the method beginning with 'the first person among them' is stated.

In the teaching, making the states such as virtue appear to knowledge is called 'ñāṇugghāṭana' (the opening up of knowledge). 'Saha udāhaṭavelāya' (together with the time of utterance) should be understood as meaning 'at that very time, without exceeding the time of preaching.'

The word 'taṃ' (that) refers to the immediately preceding statement. When asked 'What is the world?', the statement that stands encompassing a vast meaning as 'the five aggregates of clinging' is called 'atthayutta' (meaningful) because it is endowed with meaning. The statement 'It is called the world (loka) because it disintegrates (lujjati)' is called 'kāraṇayutta' (logical) because it is endowed with a reason.
42:
'Sahitāsahitassa' means words connected with reason and words not connected with reason. Alternatively, it means in the discernment of what is connected and what is not connected with reason. 'Dveyeva' (only two) refers only to the second and fourth persons. Because of the fulfillment of the speaker and the listener, they are able to make [the Dhamma] known; thus they are called 'sabhāvadhammakathika' (speakers of the Dhamma according to its nature) or 'saccadhammakathika' (speakers of the Dhamma of the Truths), meaning those who teach the Four Noble Truths.

The perfuming or development of the mind with wholesome states is called 'vāsadhura'. The statement 'This person is an evil person' refers to the fourth person, not the first. This is because the first person is intended to be like the Brahmin of Verañjā, who desires not to be deceptive.

'Puggale'pi ariyānaṃ abhikkamanādisadisatā' means that in a person, the manner of walking forward and so on is similar to the walking forward and so on of the Noble Ones. Alternatively, it means the state of having a similar manner of walking forward and so on because of the person's similarity to the Noble Ones' walking forward and so on.

Calling an immoral person 'immoral' is speaking what is factual (bhūta). Instead of saying one is immoral due to taking what is not given, saying 'one is immoral specifically due to taking life' when it is because of the act of taking life, is speaking the truth (taccha). Regarding the phrase 'at the proper time,' to show what kind of person is meant by 'one who speaks at the proper time,' the text says 'he is one who knows the time' and so on. To show this, it is said: 'In that statement "at the proper time," the person who...'

'Āgamanavipatti' (failure of arrival/conception) is kamma, while 'pubbuppannapaccayavipatti' (failure of previously arisen conditions) refers to the semen and blood [of the parents]. Conditions during the course of existence (pavatti) are nutriment and so on. It is called 'joti' (light) because it shines; it refers to radiance. A person who shines through the fulfillment of family lineage and so on is also called 'joti' because they are like a light.

Reviewing the defilements that have been abandoned and those that remain is also simply 'vimuttidassana' (the vision of liberation) by way of seeing which defilements one is liberated from and which one is not. Therefore, it was said: 'The knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana) is the nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa).'

'Yāni kānici tantāvutānaṃ' means any unspecified cloths among those woven on a loom. 'Sāyatatiyo' means having the evening as the third. Constant application is 'anuyoga'. In the sense of 'one devoted to that application,' the phrase 'taṃ anuyutto' should be seen as using the accusative case, or it is a neuter abstract noun (bhāvanapuṃsaka).
43:
In this context, 'sikkhanabhāvena' means by way of practicing in the training (sikkhā) and in the livelihood (sājīva). 'Sikkhaṃ paripūrento' means fulfilling the restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara). 'Sājīvañca avītikkamanto' means being one who does not transgress the training rules (sikkhāpada), which are the words of the Blessed One described as the body of names, the body of words, the body of language, and the body of syllables. Both of these are called 'sikkhana'. Among those two, non-transgression of livelihood is the cause for the fulfillment of training. This is because, through that non-transgression of livelihood, the fulfillment of restraint is achieved up to the Path. 'Vināsanabhāvato' means due to the nature of harming and destroying. In the phrase 'haliddirāgo viya na thirakatho hoti' (like turmeric dye, his talk is not firm), it should be understood that the similarity to turmeric dye refers to the instability of the talk, not to the person.

'Dārumāsako' refers to objects that enter into commerce; the word 'iti' indicates such various types. 'Aññaṃ dassetvā aññassa parivattanaṃ' (showing one thing and exchanging it for another) means showing a pair of clothes worth ten units and giving a cloth worth five units to an ignorant person.

'Avikiṇṇasukhaṃ' means undistracted happiness by way of considering beauty (subha), etc., in forms and so on.

Insight (vipassanā) occurring by way of impermanence (anicca), etc., in the phenomena of the aggregates (khandha) is said to be "attained" by the attainment of the Path and Fruit (magga-phala); it is because of the lack of stability without that attainment. Therefore, only one who has attained the Path and Fruit is called 'adhipaññādhammavipassanālābhī' (one who has attained insight into phenomena with higher wisdom). 'Adhipaññādhammavipassanā' should be understood as such because the knowledge of the Path and Fruit is itself the higher wisdom, and because it is the distinguished seeing of the Four Noble Truths, or of Nibbāna, which is the most excellent among all dhammas.

'Sutena anupapanno' means one who is not endowed with the text (Pāḷi) or the meaning (attha) according to what was heard.

## The Explanation of the Exposition of the Fours is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Exposition of the Fives

In the first group of five, the classification of persons is understood by the table of contents (uddesa) alone. Therefore, wishing to classify them according to how one should practice towards those persons, he said 'tatra yvāyaṃ', and so forth. 'Ārambhasaddo' means the word that expresses the act of exertion.
44:
Since the task of the Path (maggakicca) is completed by the arising of the Fruit (phala), he said, "The Fruit alone is spoken of by way of Path-duty." 'Āyācanasādhū' means good through entreaty, not good through praise and so on.

That which should be placed from the beginning is called 'ādheyya'. Acceptance (gahana) occurring like a mouth by way of seeing, hearing, replying, and giving should be understood as 'mukha'. One who places that 'mukha' of acceptance at the beginning, or one whose natural mouth is placed for the sake of acceptance, is 'ādheyyamukha'. It means one who has established acceptance based on the initial talk without investigation.

'Rajaggasmiṃ' means in the state of the tip of dust.

"Milk from a cow is said to be the best"—this should not be connected directly in this way. Rather, according to the order of production, having shown the five cow-products (gorasa), the phrase 'gavā khīraṃ', etc., is said to show the excellence of the cream of ghee (sappimaṇḍa) among them. Therefore, he said, "From a cow, there is what is called milk," and so forth.

## The Explanation of the Fifth Exposition is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Sixth Exposition

In the group of six, wishing to show that the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha) and others, who are absolutely well-known, are persons endowed with the qualities already mentioned, he said, "The Fully Enlightened One should be known by that [knowledge]," and so forth. In that text, 'tena' (by that) refers to the whole collection: the self-realization of the truths, the attainment of omniscience, and the mastery over the powers (bala). When it is said "by omniscient knowledge" (sabbaññutañāṇena), all of this is included, because omniscient knowledge does not exist without the self-realization of the truths and the mastery over the powers. Therefore, in the Commentary, only this much—"by omniscient knowledge"—was said. In that Commentary, by the words "produced by oneself without a teacher," he prohibits the state of having a teacher and the arising from another for omniscient knowledge. He does not prohibit omniscient knowledge that is produced by others who have a teacher. This is because there is no such [omniscient knowledge] that needs to be prohibited.

## The Explanation of the Sixth Exposition is finished.
45:
## 7. Commentary on the Seventh Exposition

Faith (saddhā) is said to have a good acquisition; in the phrase "it emerges," faith is included among wholesome states (kusala dhamma), or it reaches the state of decision (adhimokkha) among the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya dhamma). Because it is excellent, it shows the wholesome state that emerges. The same applies to shame (hiri) and so on. In the phrase "in wholesome states," it should be understood in the locative sense (bhumma), either because it is included within them or because it supports those wholesome states. Here, with the phrase "Faith emerges well in wholesome states," etc., it shows the arising of faith and others through the wisdom of emergence (ummujjana-paññā). For this very reason, it was said: "His faith is not yet stable," and so on. Alternatively, after showing the benefit of emergence with "Faith is excellent in wholesome states," it should be understood that the word "emerges" shows the emergence which is specifically called faith.

"Cankavāre" refers to the basket used by dyers for filtering liquid. The sequence of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti) produced by a single kamma is called one thought-process (cittavāra). Since it means the second thought-process occurs exactly as taken immediately after death, it was said "by the second thought-process" (dutiya-cittavārena). The four types of persons, such as those who emerge and stay, should be understood as many individuals who do not realize the fruit of Arahantship in various births. As for the one who realizes it, although he is a single individual, he reaches the state of the third person in the initial stage and becomes the seventh person at the end.

## The Commentary on the Seventh Exposition is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Tenth Exposition

In the passage, "Five persons reach the end in this very life; five persons leave this life and reach the end in another," those such as Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) who will attain Parinibbāna after being born in the fine-material or immaterial realms belong to the side of "leaving this life to reach the end." However, they are not included here in the place common to worldlings (puthujjana) because their internal fetters (saṃyojana) have not yet been fully eradicated. It should be understood that only persons such as the "one who attains Parinibbāna in the interval" (antarā-parinibbāyī) are called "those who leave this life and reach the end" by virtue of being born in realms exclusive to Noble Ones (ariyas).

## The Commentary on the Tenth Exposition is finished.

## The Puggalapaññatti-mūlaṭīkā is concluded.
47:
## Kathāvatthu-pakarana Mūlaṭīkā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Commentary on the Introduction to the Text

By the phrase "Because of being the basis of discourses," it refers to the status of the text, which is a collection of discourses, as the basis for its own parts, the individual discourses. Indeed, the parts are included within the whole. To show the manner in which the Blessed One taught in brief, the teacher said, "established only by the setting down of the Matrix (mātikā)."

## Commentary on the Narrative

In the sentence "He attains Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna-element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu)," the act of attaining Parinibbāna itself is stated in the instrumental sense (karaṇa) to distinguish it from the other Parinibbāna with residue (sa-upādisesa). Alternatively, that Nibbāna-element, by the attainment of which the final consciousness becomes one without further rebirth, is stated as the cause (karaṇa) for that cessation of rebirth.

"Weak faction" means a faction that was not powerful like King Kālāsoka, but rather, ancient teachers say it was a faction that ruled only a single region. Specifically, it is called weak because of the absence of wisdom capable of distinguishing between those who speak Dhamma and those who do not.

"Only those" refers only to the Bāhuliya sect; they are also known by the name Bahussutika. "Those who are divided" means those who have split from the original council (mūla-saṅgīti) or from the original sect (mūla-nikāya), meaning they have reached a state of being different in terms of views (laddhi), Suttas, and appearance and practices (liṅga-kappa).

"Mūla-saṅgaha" refers to the First Council performed by five hundred Arahants. In the phrases such as "recited in another collection," it means that they took various Suttas out from the collection of Suttas other than the Dīgha Nikāya and so on, and placed them elsewhere. Or it means they placed Suttas not included in the Council elsewhere, or they created other Suttas. "The meaning and the Dhamma" refers to the meaning of the Pali and the Pali text itself. "In the Vinaya and in the five Nikāyas" means in the Vinaya Piṭaka and in the remaining five Nikāyas.
48:
"Ānanda, I have also taught feelings as two in a figurative sense (pariyāya)," and so forth, is the teaching taught figuratively. Indeed, the Blessed One's teaching of equanimity (upekkhā-vedanā) as a peaceful and sublime happiness (sukha) is the figurative method (pariyāya) in this context. "Monks, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling," and so forth, is the teaching taught literally (nippariyāya). Indeed, the fact that the nature of feeling is threefold is the literalness (nippariyāya) in this context. "Pleasant feeling is also impermanent and conditioned," and so forth, is a sutta of explicit meaning (nītattha). "Whatever is felt, all that is suffering (dukkha)," and so forth, is a sutta of implicit meaning (neyyattha) that must be understood by drawing out another sentence. "Monks, in three ways the people of Jambudīpa surpass the people of Uttarakuru and the Tāvatiṃsa gods," and so forth; they took such a sutta spoken with reference to one meaning and substituted another meaning. Even for the sutta, "There is no practice of the holy life (brahmacariya) among the gods," and so forth, although it was spoken with reference to one meaning, they substituted another meaning; thus should the meaning be understood here. "A certain person (puggalā) practices for his own benefit," and so forth; by the shadow of the words, they destroyed many subtle and profound meanings such as emptiness (suññatā).

"Vinayagambhīra" means having discarded a profound portion of the Vinaya Piṭaka. Or, it means having discarded a profound portion of the Suttas concerning the removal of defilements (kilesa-vinaya). "Patirūpa" means a sutta that conforms to one's own desire, or a non-sutta that resembles a sutta. Some discarded only the Commentary section (Aṭṭhakathā-kaṇḍa), while others discarded the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka; thus the former teachers said, "They discarded the six treatises of the Abhidhamma." Although the Kathāvatthu treatise is a subject of dispute (regarding its authorship), the six undisputed treatises of the Abhidhamma should be recited and contemplated; it is said "six treatises" (sappakaraṇa) to show that those six treatises no longer persist. Or, it is called "six treatises" by virtue of those existing before the Third Council. "Aññāni" refers to other Abhidhamma treatises and so forth. "Nāma" refers to names not connected with the Buddha and others, such as Mañjusirī; it refers to the names of such sects as the Mahāsaṅghika. "Liṅga" refers to the specific appearance created by the manner of dressing and robing, and requisites such as rosaries. The specific manner of positioning the limbs in standing and so forth should be known as "ākappa." "Karaṇa" refers to specific activities such as sewing robes.

Because they were divided by the sect or view known as Saṅkantika, they are called "Saṅkantika." From the Saṅkantikas, the Suttavādīs gradually split off; this is the meaning. "Bhinnavādena" means that divided views exist in this; by that view...
49:
It means that together with the undivided Theravāda, there are eighteen (schools) in total. Or, 'bhinnavāda' means that by way of divided views, if all those views are counted together, they are eighteen. In the phrase 'theravādānamuttamo', the word 'thera' is an uninflected designation. It belongs to the Elders (Theras), hence it is 'Thera'. What is that? It is the view (vāda). The meaning here is that the view of the Elders is the best among all views.

With reference to a view that has arisen, it is said, 'the crushing of the views of others' (parappavādamathana). Because it has the characteristic of prohibiting views that will arise in the future, it is called 'the sign for the future' (āyatilakkhaṇa).

## The Description of the Introduction (Nidānakathā-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
50:
## Mahāvagga
## 1. Puggalakathā
## 1. Suddhasaccikaṭṭha
## 1. Anulomapaccanīkavaṇṇanā
Through magic, pebbles, potsherds, and stones that appear in the form of gems and so forth are called "māyā" (illusion). Magic objects and mirages (marīci) that are perceived in the false form of gems, water, and so forth, are "asaccikaṭṭha" (not real in the ultimate sense) because they have a nature that is known falsely. To show that whatever is not like that is "saccikaṭṭha" (real in the ultimate sense), he said: "māyā...pe... bhūtattho" (illusion...pe... true meaning). A meaning perceived by way of hearsay (anussava) and so forth might be as heard or it might be otherwise. Therefore, such a known meaning is not the ultimate sense (paramattha). However, the meaning known by personal realization is the ultimate sense; to show this, he said: "anussavā...pe... uttamattho" (hearsay...pe... highest meaning).

"Chalavādassa" refers to the meaning of the word connected with form (rūpa) and so forth, which are said to "exist" by the general usage of the word "exists." However, because of the statement, "That person...pe... having taken up a view, confesses 'It is so'," it cannot be called "chalavādassa" (of a deceptive view). This is because a view (laddhi) is not a deception (chala). "Okāsaṃ adadamāno" means cutting off the ground of the opponent's proposition. The intended meaning is: If a person (puggala) were found in the true sense, they should be found like form (rūpa) and so forth; since they are not found in that way, your view cannot stand; thus he refutes it. By the words "taṃ sandhāya," he shows that the true sense mentioned here in "yo saccikaṭṭho" refers to the various phenomena (dhamma) such as form (rūpa) that appear in the Pali texts like "Form is found," which are explained as being with causes and so forth.

Having said "tena saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena," the intention of the commentator in saying "tenākārena" is: if it is found by way of the characteristic of the real and ultimate sense, it is said to be found by the real and ultimate sense. Otherwise, if the characteristic (ākāra) and the possessor of the characteristic (ādhāravanta) were different, it should be said "tato...pe... tenākārena." What is the distinction between this (second) question and the first question? In the first question, it was asked whether the person is found in the same way as the fifty-seven types of phenomena are found by their true individual nature. But in this (second) question, it is asked whether the person is found by the same characteristics, such as being subject to deformation (ruppana) and being with causes (sappaccaya), by which those phenomena are found in their true nature. By that very characteristic...
51:
## 
The point that a person is also apprehended [by wisdom] is a distinction. However, just as feeling, which is apprehended by its true nature like form (rūpa), is not apprehended by the characteristic of deformation (ruppana), so too, a person, who is apprehended by his true nature like the various categories of phenomena (dhamma), is not apprehended by the characteristic of deformation, etc., or by the characteristic of being conditioned, etc. The opponent (Paravādī) could say this; this would be a point that should not be challenged. Since the opponent's rejection is appropriate, he should not be refuted (niggaha). However, because a reality (saccikaṭṭha) other than the various categories of phenomena is not established, [the Sakavādī] challenges him only by way of the categories of phenomena. Through the very act of rejection, he shows the refutation. The sides of acceptance and rejection are called the sides of affirmation and denial by way of general and specific characteristics. The sides of forward (anuloma) and reverse (paṭiloma) order are the first and second methods; this should be understood as the distinction between these questions.

One who says, 'Therefore, indeed, O sir, you should say,' brings blame upon the one who does not say what should be said; with this intention, it should be understood that it is said, 'because he is brought to refutation.' Thus, it is said, 'Because the refutation and the fourfold censures by way of forward and reverse order are stated, it is called the fivefold forward sequence (anulomapañcaka) beginning with "is apprehended".' However, by way of forward and reverse order, there should be seven parts including the two propositions (ṭhapanā); otherwise, the reason for excluding those propositions should be stated. It will be said later: 'A proposition (ṭhapanā) is merely a setting up of the opponent's view to show "this is your fault"; it is not the making clear of a refutation or a rebuttal.' With that intention, the two propositions are excluded here as well. Just as in that fourfold rebuttal (paṭikammacatukka), the fourfold rebuttal will be stated without mentioning the fivefold rebuttal, so too, in this case, the fourfold refutation should be stated. However, it should be understood that in the pure refutation, because the refutation is primary, the refutation taught as a summary (uddesa) is stated separately. It follows that the proponent (Sakavādī) intends only conventional truth (sammutisacca) as reality. If both truths were real and ultimate (saccikaṭṭhaparamattha), then one who desires the apprehension of a person by a portion of reality (conventional truth) should not inquire, 'Is a person apprehended in a real and ultimate sense?' etc., nor is an inquiry by a portion of reality appropriate. For feeling, which is apprehended by the characteristic of experiencing (vedayita), should not be inquired into as to whether it is apprehended by the characteristic of deformation (ruppana). The opponent does not desire a person who has the nature of deformation, etc., but rather desires a person who is real and ultimate. If there exists a reality other than ultimate truth, one should not inquire into his being ultimate truth.

In the view of the teachers who say that the opponent inquires by attributing the term 'reality' to what is not reality and referring to that attributed reality, it is not appropriate for that attributed reality to be the reality intended by them. If it is said that both the attributed reality and the primary reality are 'reality', the fault is the same as previously stated. That which is apprehended by way of conventional truth may or may not be apprehended by way of its true nature (bhūtasabhāva). If it is apprehended by way of its true nature, then the Sakavādī who admits 'a person is also apprehended in a real and ultimate sense' should not be questioned. If it is not apprehended by way of its true nature, then the real and ultimate characteristic of conventional truth, which is devoid of that true nature, should not be stated, because it is not established (asiddha). It will also be said later: 'Just as form, etc., exist by way of individual characteristics (paccattalakkhaṇa) and general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa), a person does not exist in this way.' Therefore, the intention of the Commentary should be investigated here.

In the phrase 'of the two truths' (dvinnam saccānam), since a person is not apprehended by way of both truths (conventional and ultimate), this non-apprehension should be admitted, or nothing at all should be said. How so? Just as the non-apprehensibility by way of the ultimate characteristic, which is a portion, is not a reason for admission, so too the apprehensibility by way of the conventional characteristic, which is a portion, is not a reason for rejection. It is not that the opponent desires identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi); rather, it is appropriate to say they reject it because of the fear that it would become eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi). Among identity views, only five are annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi), while the remaining are eternalism. In this context of "aññatra rūpā", it should be understood that the meaning "the person possesses form" (rūpavā puggalo) is also included.

"This is a mere view" means that it is not the case that the same person is both the doer and the enjoyer, nor is it that one person acts and another enjoys. Therefore, for one who holds such a view, it means he falls into the fault of "not created by oneself" and so forth. Alternatively, this is shown: the inquiry "Does he act?" and so forth is not stated merely by the will of another. Rather, for one who does not desire one of the views such as "He acts," he falls into another; and if he does not desire that, he falls into yet another. Thus, while standing on the view that there is a doer and an enjoyer, it is shown by the power of falling into those respective views because of not desiring them. Or else, it shows that this inquiry is made not only because of falling into all the views such as "He acts," but also because of falling into each one individually. By the words "only in the previous manner," he shows that all reasons such as the acknowledgment "He rejoices in this world" and so forth should be combined together.
