This Sutta is not the basis for the view that there is falling away for an Arahant; rather, it is only the basis for the view of falling away for those such as Non-returners (Anāgāmīs). Therefore, in the statement that they desire falling away even for an Arahant, the word "pi" (even/also) should be applied to the Non-returner and the Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī) as well.

"In the third Sutta also, only those Arahants with dull faculties (mudindriya) are intended; for all of them, falling away does not occur"—this is the old reading of that person's view. However, if only those with dull faculties were intended, then a rejection should not have been made, yet a rejection was made. Therefore, the teachers read: "In the third Sutta also, only those with sharp faculties (tikkhindriya) are intended; for all of them, falling away does not occur"—this is the view of that person.

"Taking the meaning improperly" means taking the meaning as: "Only the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) is said by the Blessed One to be 'fixed' (niyata); therefore, only that Stream-enterer does not fall away, while the remaining Once-returners, Non-returners, and Arahants do fall away." Others say that without taking the meaning stated as "fixed for the sake of attaining the three higher paths," one takes the meaning that "because he is fixed, he does not fall away from the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala)."

## Vādayuttiparihānikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

## 2. Ariyapuggalasaṃsandanaparihānivaṇṇanā

In this context, in the passage beginning with "Yaṃ panettha," this point should be investigated: that one who stands in the path and fruit of stream-entry desires the attainment of Arahantship immediately after, and that one who, having fallen away from that and desiring to stand in that (fruit of stream-entry), does not desire the attainment of Arahantship immediately after through further effort.

"One who has attained jhāna but has not yet reached mastery" should be understood as referring to a trainee (sekha). As for the worldling (puthujjana), whether they have reached mastery or not, they are not included in the lineage of the temporarily liberated (samaya-vimutta) and the non-temporarily liberated (asamaya-vimutta); however, it is said that they may reach the state of being temporarily liberated by way of the defilements suppressed by meditative attainment (samāpatti).

## Ariyapuggalasaṃsandanaparihānivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

## 3. Brahmacariyakathā

## 1. Suddhabrahmacariyakathāvaṇṇanā

Even though it is said "above the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas," according to the words of the Sutta "Tīhi, bhikkhave, ṭhānehi" (A. Ni. 9.21), it should be understood that they do not desire the development of the path even in the deva realms below that.

When asked by way of the location (okāsa) as "Yattha natthi" (where it does not exist), it is not appropriate to prohibit it by way of the person (puggala). If that person's intention is the same as that of the Proponent (Sakavādī), then he should not be refuted.

"Ekantarika-pañhā" refers to the questions asked alternately between the Opponent (Paravādī) and the Proponent (Sakavādī).

## 2. Saṃsandanabrahmacariyakathāvaṇṇanā

It should be considered how this statement—that by the fine-material sphere path (rūpāvacara-magga), that person is called "one whose stay here is finished" (idhavihāyaniṭṭha)—agrees with the description of the view such as "The Non-returner (Anāgāmī) who has developed the path in this realm is called one whose stay here is finished."

In the past, only one who stood in the fruit of non-returning was called a Non-returner, but in this context, it refers to persons such as the Non-returner who has attained jhāna, the Stream-enterer, and so on. One who develops the path of Arahantship in this realm and realizes the fruit in this very realm is called "one who attains Parinibbāna here" (idhaparinibbāyī). However, one who develops the path in this realm and realizes the fruit in that realm is called "an Arahant who attains Parinibbāna there" (tatthaparinibbāyī arahā).

## 4. Jahatikathāvaṇṇanā

## 1. Nasuttāharaṇakathāvaṇṇanā
"Kiccasabbhāvaṃ" refers to the state of having abandoned the fetters (saṃyojana) that are to be abandoned by the three lower paths. If it were held that this task is accomplished only by that path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga), it would not be consistent with the view that sensual lust (kāmarāga) and ill will (byāpāda) are already abandoned even during the state of a worldling (puthujjana). Therefore, the meaning is that although they are abandoned in the state of a worldling, since they do not arise again when the path of seeing (dassanamagga, i.e., the path of stream-entry) arises, the task of the three lower paths is possible.

## 5. Sabbhamatthītikathā

## 1. Vādayuttivaṇṇanā
"Sabbhasmiṃ sarīre sabbaṃ" means that everything exists in every place, just as feet might be in the head or eyes might be in the back. "Sabbhasmiṃ kāle" means that the whole nature exists in all times, just as youth might exist in childhood or childhood might exist in old age. "Sabbhenākārena" means that yellow exists in the mode of blue, or red exists in the mode of yellow. "Sabbesu dhammesu" means that the ear exists in the eye, or the nose exists in the ear. 

By the word "ayuttaṃ," it refers to being devoid of conjunction (yoga). That phenomenon has a single nature. Wishing to show how the state of being devoid of conjunction is possible for a phenomenon with a single nature, he said "nānāsabhāvānañhi," etc. Only two fingers or two rams, which have different natures, can be conjoined with each other; conjunction is not possible for a single object. Therefore, a single nature that is devoid of the conjunction that occurs among things with different natures is called "ayoga" (non-conjunction). Thus he asks.
68:
It means that there is the state of right view (sammādiṭṭhi) in one's own view, which arises by taking the opponent's (paravādī) view as wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi).

## The Commentary on the Logic of the Argument is finished.

## 2. Kālasamsandanavaṇṇanā
In the statement "having set aside the past and future and making only the present matter (rūpa) an indivisible thing," it means that by both the words "paccuppanna" (present) and "rūpa" (matter), only present matter is intended. This point should be understood by the phrase "because the concept (paññatti) is not absent." Just as the concept of matter (rūpapaññatti) is a concept of what exists (vijjamānapaññatti) occurring in a phenomenon defined by its own nature, the concept of an object (vatthupaññatti, i.e., the concept of cloth) is not a concept of what exists. In reality, it is only a concept of what does not exist (avijjamānapaññatti) occurring in dependence on a collection of matter arising in a sequence of before and after. Therefore, while it is appropriate not to say that the concept of cloth is gone when the whiteness of the cloth is gone, it is inappropriate not to say that the nature of matter is gone when the present state of matter is gone.

## The Commentary on the Comparison of Times is finished.

## Vacanasodhanavaṇṇanā
In the statement "whether it be future or present, it exists having become (hutvā hoti)," it should be noted that "exists having become" refers to the future becoming present after having been future, and similarly, when the present comes to be, it exists having become present after having been future previously. In the phrase "does it exist having become so for you?", the meaning that he asks about the non-interruption (anupaccheda) of "existing having become" because that present state is not absent is appropriate. "Because there is no further becoming for a phenomenon that has already become" means that for a phenomenon that has become present after having been future, there is no further becoming present after having been future again.

Since that present which has become has come to be called "exists having become" because it became present after having been future, the meaning is that he admits that the phrase "exists having become" is also applicable a second time. Thus, for one who asserts the non-interruption of "existing having become" in a phenomenon (dhamma), the non-interruption of "not existing without having become" would apply to a non-phenomenon like a rabbit's horn; with this meaning, he said "atha naṃ," etc.
69:
The 'rejected method' refers to the difference in time (kālananatta). The 'accepted method' refers to the non-difference in meaning (atthānanatta). Even if one desires the non-difference in meaning, it should be examined how one acknowledges the state of a future phenomenon being called 'arisen' in the present, and the state of a present phenomenon being called 'having arisen' in the future. For that person only allows the non-difference in meaning, not the state of the present in the future, nor the state of the future in the present.

'By reversing the previously rejected problem' means that since the fault 'having arisen, it arises; having arisen, it arises' has already been stated in the accepted problem, one passes over the fault not yet stated and takes up the rejected problem again to challenge with that rejection. In this context, for one who acknowledges 'having arisen, it arises' due to the non-difference in meaning, how does the fault occur through the rejection 'the future is the present' precisely because of the difference in time? The meaning is that the fault arises because of that person's own acknowledgment and rejection.

'Individually' means that since the future is not 'not having arisen, it does not arise' and the present is also not 'not having arisen, it does not arise', taking both of them, it is said 'individually, not having arisen, it does not arise; not having arisen, it does not arise'. It does not mean only one is 'not having arisen, it does not arise; not having arisen, it does not arise'. This method is the same as the previous statement 'individually, having arisen, it arises; having arisen, it arises'. By combining both the name 'having arisen, it arises' for the future and the name for the present, the challenge is made as 'having arisen, it arises; having arisen, it arises'. Similarly, the challenge is made as 'not having arisen, it does not arise; not having arisen, it does not arise'.

'As if covered by darkness in all directions'—by this phrase, it is shown that if it were not covered by darkness, it should be acknowledged. Here, in the first method, the state of 'having arisen, it arises' for a phenomenon that has already arisen is challenged. In the second method, the state of having the name 'having arisen, it arises' for each one in the future, etc., is challenged. This is the distinction.

For that reason, because the terms 'past' (atīta) and 'exists' (atthi) have the same meaning, and because the meaning of the word 'exists' is not the state of being past, it is said: 'The past is not past, and what is not past is past.' ## 7. Discussion on 'Some Exists' (Ekaccaṃ atthīti-kathā)

## 1. Commentary on the Discussion on 'Some of the Past', etc.

The three groups (tayo rāsī) are: kamma that has not yet matured, kamma that has already matured, and indeterminate (avyākata) phenomena that do not have the nature of maturing. It is examined: 'How should one who asserts the existence of kamma that has not yet matured by way of conventional usage be challenged?' with 'They desire the accumulation of kamma (kammupacaya) which is a formation (saṅkhāra) dissociated from mind'.

## 8. Commentary on the Discussion on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna-kathā)

The phrase 'for the purpose of asking about the supramundane state' means: because right mindfulness (sammā-sati), which is both mundane and supramundane, is a foundation of mindfulness; or because only supramundane mindfulness is the foundation of mindfulness in the ultimate sense; it is for the purpose of asking about the supramundane state by the power of that mindfulness.

'By way of questioning the divisions' (pabhedapucchā-vasena) means by way of questioning the various divisions of the foundations of mindfulness, which are the collection of mundane and supramundane foundations of mindfulness.

'Because of being established unwisely' (ayoniso patiṭṭhāpitattā) means it should be understood as being established because of a reason that should be ignored with an unanswerable reply.

## 2. The Second Chapter (Dutiya Vagga)

## 1. Commentary on 'Assistance by Others' (Parūpahāra)

The observation of the emission of semen in those with overestimation (adhimānika)—those who think they have attained the fruit of Arahantship when they have not—should be examined. For those with overestimation have only suppressed lust through concentration and insight; it is said that even for outsiders who are free from lust for sensual pleasures, there is no emission of semen. Therefore, only those who were previously overestimating should be intended.

'In the sense of speech' (vacasāyatthe) means in the sense of certainty. Specifically, because the reason is asked with 'for what reason?', it is appropriate to say it is in the sense of reason, as in the discussion on the holy life (brahmacariya-kathā).

## 5. Commentary on the Discussion on Breaking into Speech (Vacībheda-kathā)

In the discussion on breaking into speech, 'one who has attained the supramundane first jhāna' refers to the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). Because that person sees through insight as 'suffering' (dukkha), therefore he speaks only the word 'suffering', and not 'origin' (samudaya), and so on—this is the meaning.

The statement "one hears that sound with which sound" is appropriate either when it is desired that one hears that sound only at the moment of speech-origination (vacīsamuṭṭhāpana-kkhaṇa) or when a suitable reason is presented. ## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Duration of Mind

In the Discussion of the Duration of Mind, by virtue of the words beginning with "eighty-four thousand...", it is meant that the opponent rejects it, considering that such a duration for the whole of life is stated only in the formless realm (āruppa) and not elsewhere. Nevertheless, the second commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) which says, "Even they do not remain, being composed of two minds," should also be considered. It should be shown that there is no contradiction with the earlier permission of remaining for a period such as a hundred years. Although the question "moment by moment" is stated as if asked by the proponent (sakavādin), it should be understood as being asked by the opponent.

## 9. Commentary on the Discussion of Gradual Realization

In the Discussion of Gradual Realization, by the words beginning with "Alternatively," this meaning is shown: because the four knowledges constitute a single path, there is no occurrence of a single path becoming many paths; and he admits that the statement "he develops the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) gradually" is appropriate.

"At that time" means at the conclusion of the vision (of the four truths).

In the phrase "with eight knowledges," if the eight are taken together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), it should be reflected how the realization of the fruit of stream-entry occurs through the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of ready wit (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Gradual Realization is finished.

## 10. Vohārakathāvaṇṇanā

In the Vohārakathā, regarding the phrase "or the ear etc. also," there is no reason to say that among the objects (visaya) and sense faculties (visayī) which are strictly mundane, only the sound-base (saddāyatana) as an object is supramundane, while the sense faculties (visayī) are not. Just as the supramundane nature of the sense faculties (visayī) is not established, so too the supramundane nature of the sound-base as an object is not established. Among those objects and sense faculties, just as the supramundane nature of that sound-base, which is not yet established, is arrived at according to your (the opponent's) wish, so too the supramundane nature of the ear etc. is arrived at. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "Are those ear etc. also supramundane?" The meaning "If it impinges on the supramundane, it would be supramundane" should not be taken. It means that even if it is imagined that it impinges on the supramundane, this meaning should not be taken because the supramundane nature of the sound-base does not exist. Although it is extracted as "by mundane knowledge," in the Pali text it is "by consciousness (viññāṇa)." That consciousness is known as ear-consciousness because of its connection with the ear. "Indeterminacy (anekantatā)" means that because the reason "it is mundane because it is known by mundane knowledge" can apply to both mundane and supramundane things, it would be an indeterminate state (anekantabhāva).

## The Explanation of Vohārakathā is finished.

## 11. Nirodhakathāvaṇṇanā

In the sentence "He does not desire the two truths of suffering," it means he does not desire those two truths of suffering which must be brought about by the two cessations. By saying "Those things which do not cease by reflecting with supramundane knowledge" etc., it shows those formations (saṅkhāra) which cease without reflection (paṭisaṅkhā) and which do not occur as "ceased without reflection (appaṭisaṅkhā-niruddha)." It does not show the dissolution (bhaṅga) after arising. By showing thus, it amounts to showing the cessation without reflection (appaṭisaṅkhā-nirodha) and the cessation through non-occurrence (asamudācaraṇa-nirodha).

## The Explanation of Nirodhakathā is finished.

## The Explanation of the Second Chapter is finished.

## 3. The Third Group

## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of Powers

In the phrase "The knowledge of the degree of faculties is uncommon (asādhāraṇa)," although the disciples (sāvaka) do not know the possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭṭhāna), etc., in all aspects and in detail according to the description of the arising of all hindrances, etc., they do know the possible and impossible in brief by way of the summary: "It is impossible, it is not an occasion, that a person endowed with right view should approach any formation as permanent." They do not know the degree of faculties even by way of a mere summary in the manner of "He knows the inclination, he knows the underlying tendency," etc.; therefore, it is called "uncommon."

However, the Elder Anuruddha, referring merely to the knowledge of the sharpness or dullness of the faculties such as faith, etc., said: "I know the degree of faculties of beings as it really is." It should be understood here that the intended meaning is that the knowledge of the degree of faculties as stated is not the power of a Tathāgata (Tathāgata-bala). It is said: "He admits it by way of knowing merely the possible and impossible, etc., in brief." If one admits it in this way, one would also admit that "the power of a Tathāgata is common to disciples." If that is so, how should this opponent be questioned?

The rejection regarding the remaining knowledge of the possible and impossible, etc., is because of the common or uncommon nature of the proponent's (sakavādin) knowledge of the possible and impossible, etc., with the disciples; the meaning is that it refers to the common side among those common and uncommon parts.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Powers is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of the Noble

For one who admits it with reference to formations (saṅkhāra), it should be investigated how the meeting of two contacts (phassa) occurs in the manner already stated. A being is called "panidhi" (fixation/aspiration) because of being placed and established by the power of conception. Because that being is not to be placed and established even in one thing, the state of being devoid of that "panidhi" which is placed and established even in one thing is stated.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Noble is finished.
75:
## 4. Commentary on the Discourse on One Being Liberated (Vimuccamānakathāvaṇṇanā)
It should be examined what fault lies in this view: "A mind liberated by liberation through suppression (vikkhambhanavimutti) by means of jhāna is called 'being liberated' (vimuccamāna) by liberation through eradication (samucchedavimutti) at the moment of the Path." If there were a fault in showing the incomplete action of "being liberated," then in that statement also, because that person is being liberated, it is said "liberated and being liberated." If there were a fault, one should not object to the words "liberated" (vimutta) and "being liberated" (vimuccamāna) as meaning "liberated at the moment of arising (uppāda)" and "being liberated at the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga)"; rather, one should object only to the word "being liberated." It is said to be a "neuter of state" (bhāvanapuṃsaka) because a part of the action of liberation of the mind that is being liberated, either partially or in a part, is the qualifier. "Kaṭādayo" means mats, clothes, and so on. "By a single mind" means by a single fruition consciousness (phalacitta).

## The Commentary on the Discourse on One Being Liberated is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Eighth Person (Aṭṭhamakakathāvaṇṇanā)
The inclusion of "conformity" (anuloma) and "change-of-lineage" (gotrabhū) is made with the intention that the view arises: "If defilements do not occur as active obsessions even at the moments of conformity and change-of-lineage, they should be called abandoned even at the moment of the Path."

## The Commentary on the Discourse on the Eighth Person is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Discourse on the Faculties of the Eighth Person (Aṭṭhamakassa Indriyakathāvaṇṇanā)
"Obtains the faculties" means that because of the state of not having previously obtained the faculties, when one develops the factors leading to liberation (niyyānika) such as faith (saddhā) which were not yet faculties, one obtains the faculties; it does not mean that one develops the faculties themselves.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on the Faculties of the Eighth Person is finished.
76:
## 7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Eye (Dibbacakkhukathāvaṇṇanā)
"Upatthaddha" (supported) means the firm establishment of the power produced by the fourth jhāna, which serves as the condition, in such a way that it becomes distinguished by showing the object within the range of its power. "Only that much" means that the fleshly eye (maṃsacakkhu) that existed previously, before being supported by jhāna, is not the eye supported by the fourth jhāna. "Not come into range" means not reaching the range of the place to be perceived by the fleshly eye.

In this context, the commentator, while speaking of the similarity of the object and the dissimilarity only of the range of power, says "What is the object of the fleshly eye?" This mention of the object is not for the purpose of showing the distinction between the objects of the fleshly eye and the divine eye. Rather, it is shown for the purpose of demonstrating such an object of form (rūpāyatana) in which there are distinctions in the range of power. Or else, it shows the distinction only in the range of power of an object that is similar in terms of being a form-base.

"Does not desire the fleshly eye itself to be the divine eye" means that the proponent of the contrary view (paravādī) does not accept that at the time of being supported by the fourth jhāna, it is only the previous fleshly eye that exists. The statement "The arising of the fleshly eye is the path" is said only to show that the fleshly eye is a supporting condition for the divine eye; it is not said to establish that the divine eye is not-grasped (anupādinna). In the phrase "those belonging to the fine-material sphere" (rūpāvacarikānaṃ), it means that the paravādī intends that the great elements (mahābhūta) produced by the condition of fine-material sphere jhāna are called "belonging to the fine-material sphere." The same method applies to the phrase "those belonging to the immaterial sphere" (arūpāvacarikānaṃ). "He rejects it because there is no fine-material sphere mind at the moment of the immaterial sphere" means the paravādī rejects it, considering that at that very moment of fine-material sphere jhāna, being of the fine-material sphere, it cannot be of the immaterial sphere.

Because of whatever reason the three kinds of eyes supported by the Dhamma would become another kind of eye for the one who says so, therefore, it means he does not desire the state of the eye of wisdom (paññācakkhu) for the divine eye supported by the Dhamma.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on the Divine Eye is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge of Passing Away and Rebirth According to Karma (Yathākammūpagatañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā)
In the statement "With the divine eye, he knows beings passing away and being reborn according to their karma," the instrumental case (karaṇa-vibhatti) is used for the divine eye as the basis (upanissaya) for the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to karma; it is not used for the function of knowing the passing away and rebirth according to karma. However, because the paravādī thinks the instrumental case is used for that very function of knowing, it is said "having grasped it wrongly." By the statement "He holds the view that the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to karma is itself the divine eye," it means that the divine eye is itself the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to karma...
77:
...it should be so. The word "eva" (only/itself), being placed in an inappropriate position, should be joined after the word "dibbacakkhu." This is because that word "eva" excludes the state of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to karma being something other than the divine eye. It does not, however, exclude the state of the divine eye being something other than the knowledge of passing away and rebirth according to karma.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge of Passing Away and Rebirth According to Karma is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Discourse on Restraint (Saṃvarakathāvaṇṇanā)
Because the existence of restraint (saṃvara) and non-restraint (asaṃvara) among the gods of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) is revealed in the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta, it is said "starting from the Tāvatiṃsa gods." This being so, in the Discourse on the Happy Destinations (Sugatikathā), it should be said: "One hears of the drinking of liquor by the Pubbadevas (Asuras) who are included in Tāvatiṃsa, and the prohibition of drinking liquor by Sakka and the gods; that drinking of liquor by those Pubbadevas is not non-restraint."

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Restraint is finished.

## The Commentary on the Third Group is finished.

## 4. The Fourth Group (Catuttha Vagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Discourse on a Layperson being an Arahant (Gihissa Arahatikathāvaṇṇanā)
By the phrase "because of being associated with the fetters of a layperson," it shows the meaning that one is called a "layperson" (gihi) only because of being associated with lay desire and lust (chandarāga), and not merely by outward appearance.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on a Layperson being an Arahant is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Discourse on Rebirth (Upapattikathāvaṇṇanā)
"Ayoniso" means he is spontaneously born (opapātika); it means he takes the sense that he attains final Nibbāna (parinibbāyī) by that very rebirth (upapatti) in that existence.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Rebirth is finished.
78:
## 4. Commentary on the Discourse on Possession
In the Discourse on Possession, the opponent (paravādī) who acknowledges possession with reference to attainment (patti) might say that he does not speak of possession of the four mental aggregates in the same way as possession of the four factors such as contact (phassa). In that case, how the consequence (appasaṅga) of possessing contact, etc., occurs in his doctrine should be stated.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Possession is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Discourse on Possession of Equanimity
With the phrase "in this very way," everything such as "therein, there are two kinds of possession" should be applied. Therein, what is called the state of attainment (pattidhamma) is the acquisition of the first jhāna, etc., by a person reaching one of the planes such as the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) through the power of the first jhāna, etc. Teachers say that even when the first jhāna, etc., have ceased, there is a mental-disassociated formation (cittavippayutta saṅkhāra) which does not cease, and because of this formation, a person who is sleeping or engaged in recitation, etc., is said to be possessed of those jhānas.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Possession of Equanimity is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Discourse on 'Buddha by Bodhi'
"Therefore" refers to the fact that the two previously mentioned types of knowledge (Path knowledge and Omniscience) constitute enlightenment (bodhi). It should be understood that the proponent's (sakavādī) question and inquiry are directed at those whose doctrine is that one who possesses a non-existent bodhi through the power of attainment (pattidhamma), without taking that knowledge, is called a Buddha.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on 'Buddha by Bodhi' is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Discourse on Characteristics
"It is said with reference only to the Bodhisatta" means that this sutta was spoken by excluding those who are not Bodhisattas among those endowed with the marks, and taking only the Bodhisatta.
79:
It is not that there is no one other than the Bodhisatta who is endowed with the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa); there are. However, not everyone endowed with these marks is a Bodhisatta. Therefore, the meaning is that [the sutta] cannot be taken as conclusive evidence.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Characteristics is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Discourse on Entering the Path of Assurance
"Only by fulfilling the perfections (pāramī) are those people called 'assured of enlightenment' (bodhiya niyata)," the commentator shows. By the words beginning with "kevalaṃ hi naṃ," he shows the meaning that the prediction (byākaraṇa) is not given because of the arising of any specific thing called assurance (niyāma).

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Entering the Path of Assurance is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Abandoning of All Fetters
In the phrase "nippariyāyeneva" (without figurative language), it means the opponent (paravādī) holds that because there are no remaining fetters to be abandoned after being abandoned by the Path of Arahatship, the abandoning of all fetters occurs only through the Path of Arahatship, without taking this figurative expression "abandoning of all fetters." In the sentence "appahīnassa abhāvā," teachers say the opponent acknowledges this because there are no remaining fetters to be abandoned after they have been abandoned. Likewise, in the phrase "anavasesappahāna," teachers say the same. If this is the case, the opponent falls into the fault of abandoning his own doctrine and acknowledging the doctrine of the proponent (sakavādī).

## The Commentary on the Discourse on the Abandoning of All Fetters is finished.

## The Commentary on the Fourth Chapter is finished.

## 5. The Fifth Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Liberation
"It is not fruition knowledge (phalañāṇa)" means that it should not be said that they are "liberated" (vimuttāni) due to the nature of liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgavimutti), etc., nor that they are "not liberated" (avimuttāni) because things abandoned by the Path do not arise again...
80:
...the meaning is that they should not be so called. Here, it should be noted that by taking insight (vipassanā), change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhūñāṇa) is also taken.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Liberation is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Adept
By the phrase "na panetaṃ asekhaṃ," the opponent's view is shown that it is an adept's knowledge (asekhañāṇa) because it has an adept (asekha) as its object. It shows the meaning that it is not an adept's knowledge just because it belongs to an adept.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Adept is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Discourse on Perversion
In the text "na paṭhavīyeva," the meaning is that it is not merely the characteristic of earth (lakkhaṇapaṭhavī) nor the composite earth (sasambhārapaṭhavī). The perversion of perceiving the permanent in the impermanent, etc., is called perverted knowledge (viparītañāṇa); it should be noted that the term "knowledge" is applied metaphorically even to what is not knowledge (such as ignorance).

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Perversion is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Discourse on Assurance
428-431. The opponent's doctrine is that there is a knowledge which follows the Path knowledge and is in accordance with the truths, seeing which the Blessed One knows, "He is capable (bhabba) [of attaining the Path]." In the phrase "paṭhamapaññameva catutthaṃ katvā," it is called "the fourth" by counting from the perverted inquiry beginning with "niyatassa aniyāmagamanāya."

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Assurance is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Discourse on Analytical Meditations
432-433. Even the opponent who holds that all knowledge of the Noble Ones (ariya) is exclusively supramundane (lokuttara) cannot say that all knowledge is analytical meditation (paṭisambhidā). This is because the knowledge of worldlings (puthujjana) is also...
81:
...indeed knowledge. Or rather, it should be said that the opponent does not desire the status of knowledge for that person. In the sentence "paṭhavīkasiṇasammutiyaṃ samāpattijñānaṃ sandhāya," it should be understood as referring to this knowledge of the worldling.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Analytical Meditations is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Discourse on Conventional Knowledge
434-435. To show that the opponent speaks by taking both [conventional and ultimate truths] as being the same in terms of truth, merely because of the common name "truth" (sacca), the commentator said the words beginning with "tattha."

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Conventional Knowledge is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Discourse on Mind as Object
436-438. By the phrase "for one who attends to the characteristic of contact (phassa)," it is shown that the previous acknowledgment was made with reference to collective attention (samudāya-manasikāra) as distinct from attention to individual states (anupadadhamma-manasikāra).

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Mind as Object is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge of the Future
439-440. In the passage beginning with "sabbasmimpi," the Buddha taught that there is knowledge of the future through the method beginning with "Pāṭaliputtassa kho." This implies that the opponent desires knowledge even in the immediate future (anantarānāgata) simply because it is the future.

## The Commentary on the Discourse on Knowledge of the Future is finished.
82:
## 9. Paṭuppannañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā
441-442. "Vacaṇaṃ nissāya" (depending on the word) means depending on the word that has arrived by way of meaning, or depending on the word of permission. "Santatiṃ sandhāya" (referring to the continuity) means it is intended to refer to the continuity of contemplation by way of the dissolution of the knowledges of contemplation of dissolution (the knowledges that repeatedly contemplate the cessation and destruction of conditioned phenomena).

## The Commentary on the Knowledge of the Present is finished.

## 10. Phalañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā
443-444. "Buddhānaṃ viya" (like the Buddhas) means that just as the Buddhas know fruition by virtue of knowing the hierarchy of fruition in all its aspects and by their own power alone, it is the same in this case.

## The Commentary on the Knowledge of Fruition is finished.

## The Commentary on the Fifth Group is finished.

## The Great Fifty is complete.

## 6. Chaṭṭhavagga

## 1. Niyāmakathāvaṇṇanā
445-447. "Aniyato nāma na hoti" (he does not become uncertain) means that just as for a person fixed in wrongness (micchattaniyata), there is uncertainty in another life, for a person who has attained this Noble Path, there is never a state of uncertainty. Therefore, the law of certainty (niyāma) called the Path is unconditioned (asaṅkhata).

## The Commentary on the Law of Certainty is finished.

## 2. Paṭiccasamuppādakathāvaṇṇanā
"Kāraṇaṭṭhena ṭhitatā" (standing in the sense of a cause) means simply the state of being a cause. By this, it is shown that the causal state of phenomena such as ignorance (avijjā) is called "dhammaṭṭhitatā" (the stability of phenomena). Likewise, in the term "dhammaniyāmatā" (the certainty of phenomena), only the cause should be understood.

## The Commentary on Dependent Origination is finished.
83:
## 3. Saccakathāvaṇṇanā
452-454. "Vatthusacca" (objective truth) refers to birth (jāti) and so forth, sensual craving (kāmataṇhā) and so forth, and right view (sammādiṭṭhi) and so forth. "Lakkhaṇasacca" (characteristic truth) refers to oppression (bādhana), origin (pabhava), and deliverance (niyyānika), which are the characteristics of oppression and so forth.

## The Commentary on the Truths is finished.

## 5. Nirodhasamāpattikathāvaṇṇanā
457-459. "Kariyāmānā karīyatīti" (being made, it is made) means that the non-occurrence of the occurring mental aggregates (nāma-khandha) is accomplished through the sequence of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā). By saying "because of the absence of conditioned and unconditioned characteristics," the inherent nature (sabhāva) of the attainment of cessation is denied. Purification (vodāna) is also merely a synonym for emergence (vuṭṭhāna). It means that because the inherent nature of the attainment of cessation is accomplished, it does not serve as a cause in the unconditioned state.

## The Commentary on the Attainment of Cessation is finished.

## The Commentary on the Sixth Group is finished.

## 7. Sattamavagga

## 1. Saṅgahitakathāvaṇṇanā
471-472. The words "Saṅgahitā" (included) mean they are connected.

## The Commentary on Inclusion is finished.

## 2. Sampayuttakathāvaṇṇanā
473-474. The meaning that there is no specific distinction is shown by the rejection "It is not so," because even the statement "oil is contained within the sesame" is inappropriate.

## The Commentary on Association is finished.
84:
## 3. Commentary on Mental Factors
475-477. Since there is no co-nascence (sahajāta) devoid of simultaneous arising (ekuppādatā) and so forth in the mental aggregates such as contact (phassa), the author of the Saṅgaha says, "referring to the state of associated co-nascence."

## The Commentary on Mental Factors is finished.

## 4. Commentary on Giving
"To urge by way of the gift (deyyadhamma)" means that if only the mental factor is the gift (dāna), then by the grammatical definition "it is called a gift because it is given," the state of being a gift would apply only to the mental factor (volition/cetanā); this is the meaning intended for the urge.

Regarding the phrase "having an undesirable result" and so forth, it should be understood that this is not said to show that a non-mental phenomenon (the material gift) is the gift, but rather to show the state of giving a result. By saying "having an undesirable result" and so forth, it is as if the result-giving of a non-mental phenomenon is being stated, not its state as a gift; this statement is made to prohibit the result-giving of that non-mental phenomenon. Because of this, it is said immediately after, "Indeed, a non-mental phenomenon such as food cannot give a resultant effect (vipāka) in the future." "To be noted as having a desirable result" means that, unlike the material gift, there is no such thing as a gift having an undesirable result by any figurative method; rather, it means it must be noted that it strictly has a desirable result only.

"By another method" refers to the figurative method "it is called a gift because it is given." In the phrase "not by a single meaning," to refute the Opponent's (paravādī) view that "only the material object is the gift," the Sutta evidence such as "faith, shame" is appropriate in the Proponent's (sakavādī) doctrine. The Sutta evidence such as "here, someone gives food" is appropriate in the Opponent's doctrine to refute the view that "only the mental factor is the gift." Furthermore, to establish the view that "the mental factor is the gift," "faith, shame" etc. are used in the Proponent's doctrine, and to establish that "the material object is the gift," "here, someone gives food" etc. are used. It should be understood that "not by a single meaning" is said referring to this difference in the purpose of refutation and establishment. In that context, just as in the question "It should not be said that the mental factor is the gift" in the Opponent's doctrine, the meaning should be taken as "is it only the mental factor?", so too in the question "It should not be said that the material object is the gift," the meaning should be taken as "is it only the material object?". In the phrase "the material gift has a desirable result," only the absence of a desirable result is rejected; thus, by this text "only the state of having a desirable result is rejected"...
85:
It should be so. Or it should be said: "It is rejected seeing only the absence of the desired result." In the phrase "to free it from a mixed state," it means to free it from the state of giving, both by the sense of the mental factor being what is given and by the sense of the gift having a desired result.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Giving is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Discussion on Merit Consisting in Use

The view is that there is merit consisting in use which is dissociated from consciousness. It means they say, referring to that merit consisting in use dissociated from consciousness, that it increases.

"By the power of that view" means it is by the power of that view. They say that they acknowledge that there would be a combination of these, such as contact and so on, just like the combination of the five consciousnesses. Specifically, it means they acknowledge it referring only to the combination of the five consciousnesses, contact, and so on.

By the words "even if not used," he shows such cases as "the recipient, having received it, does not use it but throws it away." This view that merit consisting in use increases because it is merit even if the gift is not used, is refuted. When that view is refuted, only the view of the Sakavādin is strong. It means that the state of merit is thus established only through the volition of giving. Intending that merit occurs only through the volition of giving even when the gift is not used, he said, "Only the view of the Sakavādin is strong."

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Merit Consisting in Use is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Discussion on What is Given from Here

488-491. "They subsist only by that gift" means they subsist only by that object such as a robe, or it means they subsist only by the giving of that robe and so on, even without their own performed wholesome kamma. "For this reason" means it is the intention of one establishing the view: "If they did not subsist by the robe etc. given from here, how could they rejoice... etc., how could they obtain joy?"

## The Explanation of the Discussion on What is Given from Here is finished.
86:
## 7. Explanation of the Discussion on whether the Earth is a Result of Kamma

Contact has distinctions such as being felt as pleasant. Therefore, having shown all results of kamma through contact, he said "that [contact] and perception etc." to show the association in accordance with the associated states excluding itself. The phrase "and they have those states" is said referring to the conascent states that arise together with eye-consciousness and so on, along with adverting. Among those results, whatever result is a desired result, beings perform kamma by making a wish only for that result; therefore, he shows the wish which is the strong dependence condition (upanissaya) for kamma. Or, he shows craving (taṇhā) which has present feeling as its condition and which produces future suffering by way of producing grasping (upādāna) and so on. By the term "root craving," he shows the previous craving which is the strong dependence condition for the kamma that produces the present round of results. Or, he shows the previous craving which is the companion of kamma and the strong dependence condition for the result.

He said "also by the view of those" etc. to show the appropriateness of the challenge by the power of their own doctrine.

By the phrase "by way of obtaining," he shows that when there is kamma, there is the obtaining of the earth and so on; therefore, kamma is said to be that which leads to [the production of] that earth.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on whether the Earth is a Result of Kamma is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Discussion on whether Old Age and Death are Results

In the phrase "because of the absence of the characteristic of association," it means because of the absence of this characteristic of association called "having a single object."

In the phrase "there is no alternative reason (pariyāya)," it shows that since there is no alternative reason in the state of what should be said by the Sakavādin himself, the question was not asked by way of the indeterminate (abyākata) in order to prevent old age and death of indeterminate states from being results.

Some teachers say, "Having an impure complexion is just old age." That statement is just the same as showing the ugliness of form only, by the words "unwholesome kamma is that which has kamma as its cause..." and so on.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on whether Old Age and Death are Results is finished.
87:
## 9. Ariyadhammavipākakathāvaṇṇanā

"Rounds (vaṭṭā)" refers to the rounds such as the round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa).

## The Explanation of Ariyadhammavipākakathā is finished.

## 10. Vipākovipākadhammadhammotikathāvaṇṇanā

"Tappaccayāpi" means that for whichever result (vipāka) the result is a mutuality condition (aññamañña-paccaya), it is a result because of that condition of being a result which has the mutuality condition, or because of being a mutuality condition. By the words "So hi" etc., it shows the reason for this objection in the point "Result is a result-natured state" which was previously admitted. In the phrase "aññamaññapaccayādīsu," by the word "ādi," conditions such as the conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) are included, showing the manner of assistance by those respective conditions among those conditions.

## The Explanation of Vipākovipākadhammadhammotikathā is finished.

## The Explanation of the Seventh Chapter is finished.

## 8. Aṭṭhamavagga

## 1. Chagatikathāvaṇṇanā

503-504. "Vaṇṇa" refers to color/luster and shape; thus it is said, "of similar form and shape (sadisarūpasaṇṭhānā)."

## The Explanation of Chagatikathā is finished.

## 2. Antarābhavakathāvaṇṇanā

Because of being able to see a place that is very far, distant, and to be reached, he is like one with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). Because of being able to go by piercing through the intervening spaces of the earth via the sky, he is like one with psychic power (iddhimā). "Na sahadhammena" means that if that intermediate state (antarābhava) does not exist between births, there is no reason for the rejection "There is no intermediate state."
88: In that intermediate state (antarābhava), the opponent (paravādī) who does not desire birth (jāti), aging (jarā), and death (maraṇa), nor the succession of death (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), does not desire, by this statement, the intermediate state occurring immediately after death to be 'aggregates' (khandha), the currently occurring state to be 'birth' (jāti), and the disappearance upon entering the mother's womb to be 'death' (maraṇa). Just as in the sensual realm (kāma-bhava) and so forth, there is a succession of death and rebirth-linking by way of repeatedly dying and being reborn in those various existences, it is shown that he does not desire such a succession in that intermediate state. ## The commentary on the discussion of the intermediate state is finished. ## 3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Strands of Sensual Pleasure. It is called 'sensual existence' (kāma-bhava) because of the sense of desiring the sensual realm; it should be understood with this intention that all aggregates of the sensual sphere (kāmāvacara) and so forth are called 'sensual existence'. However, in the Dhātukathā, only the state of sensual existence of the grasped aggregates (upādinnakkhandha) is shown, not the state of sensual existence in the sense of desiring. Relying merely on the words, 'Monks, these five are the strands of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa)', only the five types of sensual objects are called 'sensuality' (kāma); therefore, the term 'sensual element' (kāmadhātu) is not the name of any other state—with this intention, the meaning should be understood by relying merely on the words. ## The commentary on the discussion of the strands of sensual pleasure is finished. ## 5. Commentary on the Discussion of the Material Element. 515-516. In the discussion of the material element (rūpadhātu), because of the term 'material element', the view should be understood that the material element must consist only of material phenomena (rūpī-dhamma). In the Suttas, the delimitation of planes (bhūmi-pariccheda) is only the planes defined by such phrases as 'These three are the existences' (D. iii. 305); they also speak of the delimitation of actions (kamma-pariccheda) by such phrases as 'starting from the Avīci hell below' (Vibh. 182). ## The commentary on the discussion of the material element is finished.
89:
## 6. Explanation of the Discourse on the Immaterial Element

517-518. In the phrase "by this method only," just as in the previous discourse on the fine-material element, phenomena having the nature of matter were called "fine-material element" (rūpadhātu) generally without distinction, so also in this discourse on the immaterial element, phenomena not having the nature of matter (mental phenomena) are called "immaterial element" (arūpadhātu) generally without distinction. Therefore, the method stated in that discourse on the fine-material element is the same in this discourse on the immaterial element.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Immaterial Element is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Discourse on the Bases of the Fine-material Element

The phrase "ghānanimittānipi" should be stated as "ghānādinimittānipi." By the word "sign" (nimitta), it refers to the collection of matter having such a shape that is marked as the location of the nose-base (ghānāyatana) etc.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Bases of the Fine-material Element is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Discourse on Matter in the Immaterial

524-526. Subtle matter exists; because it is the escape from that subtle matter, that [meditative attainment] is called "immaterial" (āruppa).

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Matter in the Immaterial is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Discourse on 'Matter is Kamma'

527-537. "Pakappayamānā" means striving, or performing excessive activity regarding associated phenomena. In the previous section, it refers to this question: "Whatever matter is originated by unwholesome consciousness, all that is unwholesome."

## The Explanation of the Discourse on 'Matter is Kamma' is finished.
90:
## 10. Explanation of the Discourse on the Life Faculty

In the question "immaterial life faculty" (arūpa-jīvitindriya), it speaks by taking the end of the question such as "Is there life (āyu) for immaterial phenomena?" etc. When one desires that there is a continuity of the life faculty dissociated from mind (cittavippayutta) for immaterial phenomena, if one desires that continuity of the life faculty for both material and immaterial phenomena, it is appropriate to say that one desires it for immaterial phenomena; thus it should be understood that "arūpadhammānaṃ" is said.

It should be understood that by the words "Even if material phenomena occur in the continuity of beings" etc., it refers to that same continuity of the life faculty.

In the phrase "referring to the preceding and succeeding parts," it means that because of the proximity to the meditative attainment (samāpatti), even at that time, one is indeed an attainer of the meditative attainment.

544-545. In the phrase "two life faculties," there is the earlier reading: "The question of the proponent (sakavādī), the admission of the other (paravādī)." There is also the later reading: "The question of the opponent (paravādī), the admission of the proponent (sakavādī)"; that later reading alone is appropriate.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Life Faculty is finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Discourse on the Cause of Kamma

By the word "remaining," in stating the cause of kamma such as killing (pāṇātipāta) etc., it speaks of the investigation of persons such as the Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) etc., which occurred before this. In the phrase "handa hi," since this is only the word of admission of the opponent, it is not appropriate to say "to make [him] admit." However, the meaning that the proponent says the words "Of what kamma is it the cause?" in order to make him admit that view is appropriate. "Sampaṭicchāpetuṃ" should be understood not as the meaning of making one admit a doctrine, but as the opponent making the proponent accept his own view.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Cause of Kamma is finished.

## The Explanation of the Eighth Chapter is finished.
91:
## 9. Ninth Chapter (Navama Vagga)

## 1. Explanation of the Discourse on One Who Sees the Benefits

"Vibhāgadassanatthaṃ" means to show the difference in nature between the knowledge that sees the faults in formations (saṅkhāra) and the knowledge that sees the benefits in Nibbāna. It should be considered how it is appropriate to suppress the intention of the opponent (paravādī) who admits [this] by way of various consciousnesses. For the opponent who says that two knowledges occur simultaneously by way of taking an object, it is appropriate to say that this [discourse] is begun to show the non-existence of such [simultaneity]. By the words "anussavavasena" etc., it is shown that not only the knowledge having objects such as impermanence (anicca) etc., is insight (vipassanā), but also the knowledge seeing the benefits in Nibbāna, such as "The non-arising of formations (Nibbāna) is safety," etc., is insight.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on One Who Sees the Benefits is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Discourse on the Deathless as Object

"Suttabhayena" (through fear of the Sutta) should be understood as: because of the fear of contradicting the Sutta passage where the Buddha said, "Monks, that further shore is safety, free from fear; this is a designation for Nibbāna," referring to the state of being free from fetters (saṃyojana) etc., as the state of safety etc.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on the Deathless as Object is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Discourse on 'Matter has an Object'

552-553. "Ārammaṇatthassa vibhāgadassanatthaṃ" means that although there is a distinction between the sense of "condition" (paccaya) and the sense of "clinging" (olubbha), it is intended to show that one should not hold that matter has an object even by way of a clinging-object because of its being conditioned, whether one assumes or does not assume the lack of difference between condition and clinging, without knowing the distinction between those two.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on 'Matter has an Object' is finished.

## 4. Anusayā-anārammaṇā-kathā-vaṇṇanā

## 9. Explanation of the Discussion on the Stability of Phenomena (Dhammaṭṭhitatākathāvaṇṇanā)

"Anantarapaccayatañceva" (and the state of proximity condition) means that ignorance (avijjā) is the proximity condition for formations (saṅkhāra). There is a certain stability (ṭhitatā) of ignorance; because of that stability in the state of proximity condition, the stability known as the state of proximity condition arises. This is the meaning. Here, the taking of the proximity condition should be understood as having the purpose of showing a single condition that is devoid of the state of mutuality condition (aññamaññapaccaya). By that proximity condition, all conditions of such nature are shown. "Aññamaññapaccayatañca" (and the state of mutuality condition) means ignorance is a condition for formations, and formations are also conditions for ignorance. In that case, because of the stability known as the state of ignorance being a condition for formations, the stability known as the state of formations being a condition for ignorance arises; and because of that, the stability of the other [remaining conditions] arises. This is the meaning.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Stability of Phenomena is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Discussion on "Seven Times at Most" (Sattakkhattuparama-kathāvaṇṇanā)

641-645. "Sattakkhattuparama-niyato" means one who is certain by the state of being a seven-times-at-most [Sotāpanna]. "Imaṃ vibhāgaṃ" means this distinction. "Tvaṃ panassa niyāmaṃ icchasi" means do you desire certainty (or the cause of certainty) in the state of being a seven-times-at-most, other than the state of not being subject to fall [into lower realms] and the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry?

"Anantarīyābhāvaṃ" means that because of which anantarīya kamma (or the realization of the Four Noble Truths through path-knowledge), that person is not one who is fit to commit anantarīya kamma; it refers to the absence of that anantarīya kamma. Or, it means the absence of the state of anantarīya in a Sotāpanna person. Regarding the question, "Does that seven-times-at-most person penetrate and know the Four Noble Truths within the seven lives?" —

Some teachers say, "Although the seven-times-at-most person does not exceed the seventh life, there is no prohibition against penetrating and knowing the Four Noble Truths within the seven lives."

Other teachers, however, say, "For the person whom the Blessed One has declared by the power of His knowledge as a seven-times-at-most person, there is no such thing as realization within the seven lives. Nevertheless, because there is no state that makes existence fixed, he is called 'bhabba' (capable of knowing the Truth). For example, just as a wholesome super-knowledge volition (abhiññā-cetanā) is called 'vipākadhamma' because it is capable of giving a result if the cause exists, even if it sometimes does not give a result; likewise, one becomes a seven-times-at-most person because of the weakness of the faculties (indriya), not because of the existence of a fixed nature, nor because of the Blessed One's declaration. And since the weakness of faculties is not a state that makes one incapable of attaining the path, that person cannot be called 'abhabba' (incapable). In this discussion of the seven-times-at-most, 'abbhabatā' (incapability) is rejected because there is no causal factor that makes one incapable of attaining the path; however, it does not mean he is capable of penetrating the Four Noble Truths within the seven lives. If the seven-times-at-most person were to know the Truth within the seven lives, he would become a 'Kolankola' person." Thus they say. It is more appropriate to call him "bhabba" (capable) because of his capable nature without making a distinction. In the phrase "na bhavaniyāmakaṃ kiñci", the remaining word "passitvā" (having seen) should be added, or it should be connected with the word "byākaroti" (He declares).

## The Explanation of the Discussion on "Seven Times at Most" is finished.

## 4. Niyatassaniyāmakathāvaṇṇanā

663-664. In the statement, "The remaining states belonging to the three planes are called undetermined (aniyata)," the phrase "states belonging to the three planes" is said with reference to the states of those who have not yet reached the assurance (niyāma). With reference to those very states, it is said, "Even though one is endowed with those states, one is still undetermined (aniyata)." Thus, taking only this conventional usage, the meaning should be coordinated according to the view of those who hold: "A Bodhisatta in his final existence is destined (niyata) and enters the path of assurance (niyāma) because he is fit (bhabba) to penetrate and descend into the Dhamma."

In this way, the word 'niyata' is spoken because of the existence of mere conventional usage, and the phrase 'enters the path of assurance' is spoken because of the state of being fit (babbatā) to penetrate the Dhamma. However, it is proper to say that the state of being fit (babbatā) alone is the cause for both. The phrase "by another reason" is intended to show that if a destined person were to enter the path of assurance, then one destined for wrongness (micchattaniyata) would enter the assurance of rightness (sammattaniyāma), or one destined for rightness (sammattaniyata) would enter the assurance of wrongness (micchattaniyāma); but such a thing does not exist.

## Niyatassaniyāmakathāvaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.

## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of Conditionality

711-717. "Therefore conditionality is determined" means that a phenomenon which is a root-condition (hetu-paccaya) should not become an object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) and so forth, nor a predominance-condition (adhipati-paccaya) and so forth. Only its status as a root-condition is determined.

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of Mutuality Condition

718-719. "Is it not that ignorance arises together with formations?"—because of this, only demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) are taken. In this context, "by power of co-nascence, mutuality, presence, non-disappearance, and association," the dependence-condition (nissaya-paccaya) is not mentioned separately [by the author of the Compendium] because it is included by taking the presence-condition (atthi-paccaya) while breaking the sequence of conditions; this should be understood because of the uncommon nature of kamma-condition and nutriment-condition. It will be said later: "The three graspings are conditions for craving just as ignorance is for formations." Therefore, here the conditionality of formations is shown to be similar to that of the graspings.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Mutuality Condition is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Third Discussion of the Cessation of Perception and Feeling

In the Third Discussion of the Cessation of Perception and Feeling, in the phrase "with reference to the remaining beings," it should be understood as referring to those beings in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra) who are capable of attaining the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), other than those currently in it. Alternatively, since the opponents desire the death of unconscious beings (asaññasatta) due to the arising of perception, it may be said to refer to all beings remaining besides those in the attainment of cessation. "Bodily nature" (sarīrapakati) means this body is of such a nature that contact with the hand and so forth can affect it.

733-734. "It would be contrary to the Sutta"—this statement should be made after making the opponent admit [the premise].

## The Commentary on the Third Discussion of the Cessation of Perception and Feeling is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Discussion of the Unconscious

In stating the view that "the development (bhāvanā) proceeding by way of dispassion for perception is the unconscious attainment (asaññasamāpatti)," the opponent shows their view that the fourth jhāna attainment proceeding by way of dispassion for perception is not taken as "unconscious attainment," but that state of being unconscious is indeed the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti). Because non-greed and so forth exist for one in the unconscious attainment, here the fourth jhāna attainment established in our own school is called "unconscious attainment."

It is called "unconscious" (asaññita) because it is attained by way of dispassion for perception, not because of the absence of perception; this refers only to the fourth jhāna attainment.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Unconscious is finished.

## 11. Commentary on the Discussion of the Accumulation of Kamma

738-739. In the questions "It arises together with kamma," there is a reading in some versions: "He rejects it with reference to the accumulation of kamma (kammūpacaya), and accepts it with reference to what is dissociated from mind (cittavippayutta)."

In another version, it says: "He rejects it referring to cittasampayutta (associated with mind), and accepts it referring to cittavippayutta (dissociated from mind)." Wise men should investigate both of these readings.

776-779. "Without taking the mind" means without taking the indeterminate functional consciousness (kiriya-citta), which was mentioned as "because of the existence of the occurrence of giving, etc., by functional consciousness."

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion on "There is no Untimely Death for an Arahant"

"Taking improperly" means taking the meaning as: "I (the Buddha) do not speak of the disappearance of kammas that have not yet had the opportunity to give their results." However, some teachers say: "Taking the meaning improperly in this way: 'I do not speak of the disappearance of a person without experiencing the results of kammas.'"

"It does not reach for such a long time" means he rejects it with the view that it does not reach for such a long time, but it reaches after that. In this discussion, it is said that because of the statement "While life still remains, he deprives him of life," teachers say there is no offense of taking life (pāṇātipāta) for one who strikes or cuts off the head of one who is dying according to his own nature (dhamma-tā). The meaning is that even though the factors of a living being, the perception of a living being, the intent to kill, the effort, and death are present, there is no pāṇātipāta because he did not die due to that effort. However, to say that such a dying person does not die even a single mind-moment earlier than death by natural law is very difficult to understand.

## The commentary on the Discussion on "There is no Untimely Death for an Arahant" is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion on "All this is due to Kamma"

In the phrase "Just as a sprout comes from a seed," just as there is no arising of a sprout from a cause other than a seed, similarly, there is no arising of a state occurring in the present from a cause other than kamma (the result of kamma); the meaning is that the opponent rejects it referring to this sense. "He asks about the result of the gift by way of the object to be given" means he asks about the result of that gift (the volition) with which he gives that object by way of the object to be given; it means he does not ask about the result of the object to be given itself.

However, the meaning is that if the recipient's bringing about of the resultant were also through the bringing about of the volition of giving, then in such a case, it would be reasonable to say that one is the doer for another.

## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of Emptiness (Suññata-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

By the phrase 'the characteristic of non-self is for some' (anattalakkhaṇaṃ tāva ekaccaṃ), he speaks of the characteristic of non-self of the mental aggregates (nāma-kkhandha). ## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of Absolute Certainty (Accantaniyāmakathā)

Based on the Sutta "Sakiṃ nimuggo nimuggovahoti" (Once submerged, he remains submerged), the opponent considers the decision made regarding the non-arising of supramundane faith and so forth in that existence as being made with reference to being a stump in the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra-khāṇuka). 883-884. In the Iddhikathā, the sentence "atthi adhippāya-iddhi" means there is a psychic power (iddhi) named "adhippāya" (intention) because of the fulfillment through the power of the intention of the desired person.

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of Phenomena (Dhammakathā)

887-888. In the Dhammakathā, the sentence "rūpaṭṭhato aññassa rūpassa abhāvā" means that since there is no other thing apart from matter (rūpa) which is called the characteristic (niyāma) of matter, namely the nature of being matter (rūpaṭṭha), matter also is not something other than the nature of being matter. Therefore, matter is only the nature of matter and not the nature of feeling (vedanā) and so on; with this intention, it should be said "matter is fixed by the nature of being matter." It does not mean it is fixed in another way by the characteristic called rūpaṭṭha.

In that statement, when it is shown that there is no rūpaṭṭha other than matter, it is already shown that there is no matter other than rūpaṭṭha. Therefore, wishing to show only that there is no rūpaṭṭha other than matter, he said "rūpasabhāvo hi" and so on. "Esa vohāro" means that the nature of matter is rūpasabhāva, and the meaning of matter is rūpaṭṭha; thus, taking matter and its nature, or matter and its meaning, as if they were different through a genitive compound (saṭṭhīsamāsa), the usage of the term rūpasabhāva or rūpaṭṭha is for the purpose of making known that that nature of being matter is indeed distinct from feeling (vedanā) and so on.

Therefore, because matter is not different from the nature of being matter, the statement of the opponent (paravādī) who says "matter is fixed by the nature of being matter" instead of saying "matter is only matter, not the nature of feeling etc." is faulty in the manner already stated. Nevertheless, it should be understood why the teacher, who says "it should be said with the intention that matter is only matter and not the nature of feeling etc. because matter is fixed by the nature of being matter," admits that "matter is fixed by the nature of being matter." If one asks, "Was this not said by himself and not by another, therefore should it not be said that he 'admits' it?", the answer is no, because he speaks of himself as if he were another. Or, "vattabbaṃ" means it should be said by the proponent (sakavādī). If it should be said by the sakavādī and he admits that meaning, then the meaning here is: why does the sakavādī admit it?

"Atthantaravasena" means that by concealing the reason already stated there, he was challenged by another, and thus he prevents the challenge by showing that very reason. "Ito aññathā" means that apart from the mere nature of being matter, there is no fixed thing as imagined by him (the opponent)...
114:
In order to prevent the fixedness imagined by that opponent (paravādī), the proponent (sakavādī) said "micchattaniyata" (fixed in wrongness) and so on, in order to challenge again by that same method.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Phenomena is finished.

917-918. In the phrase "na aniccādibhāvaṃ", matter (rūpa) is referred to as "aniccādibhāva" because it has the nature of impermanence (anicca) and so forth.
