## Yamaka-pakaraṇa-mūlaṭīkā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Description of the Opening of the Text
After preventing the wrong grasp of things (dhammas) through the Kathāvatthu treatise, which was taught in brief, the Buddha undertook the Yamaka treatise for the sake of proficiency in various ways through the power of decision (sanniṭṭhāna) and doubt (saṃsaya) arising based on the dhammas, persons (puggala), and planes (okāsa) already revealed in those very texts such as the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. Showing that Yamaka treatise by way of the time, place, and teacher, and the sequence of its commentary having reached him, the commentator, acknowledging the task of explaining it with the thought, "A burden that has arrived must certainly be carried by the wise," said: "Saṅkhepeneva" and so forth.

In that passage, "yamassa visayātīto" means: when there is birth (jāti), death (maraṇa) occurs; therefore, birth, or the five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā), is the realm (visaya) of death. It has the meaning of having transcended that realm of death by abandoning the origin (samudaya) of craving. Or, it means having transcended death, which is the realm of King Yama, or having transcended the place where his authority extends, namely the realms of sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial. He is called "chaṭṭhānadesaka" because he teaches the six points of impossibility (abhabbaṭṭhāna) which are stated as "incapable of committing the six major crimes." The body hairs of that Blessed One are not in pairs but grow singly, circling to the right, being dark blue in color and free from impurity; therefore, he is called "ayamāvaṭṭanīlāmalatanuruho."

## End of the Description of the Opening of the Text.
## 1. Description of the Enumeration Section of the Root Yamaka
By the words "because it is taught by way of pairs (yamakas)," he shows that each group of yamakas among the ten, and the entire treatise which is a collection of those groups of yamakas, has acquired its name by way of the yamakas.
118:
If it is asked: By this statement "Atthayamaka" (Yamaka of meaning) by way of the two meanings called wholesome (kusala) and unwholesome (akusala) roots, does the meaning of this single forward question (anuloma-pucchā) "Whatever dhammas are wholesome, all those are wholesome roots" itself arrive at the state of being a Yamaka? It does not. Why? Because the state of being an "Atthayamaka" is stated by way of the distinctions of wholesome and wholesome roots mentioned in the second and first questions that are desired to be known, or by way of the wholesome and wholesome roots included in the concluding term (sanniṭṭhāna-pada) in the first and second questions that are desired to be known. In truth, because the prominence here lies in the distinctions that depend on the possessors of the distinction (visesavanta) which are desired to be known, or in the dhammas possessing those distinctions that depend on the distinctions, only one meaning is included in each type of question. Here, the word "attha" (meaning) does not denote an ultimate reality (sabhāva-dhamma), nor does it denote cause and effect, etc.; rather, it denotes the meaning of the Pali text. Therefore, he said: "of those very meanings" and so forth.

The phrase "having made all three terms into one" is said with reference only to the ability of the name-term (nāma-pada) to include wholesome things, etc.; it is not intended to mean including them without remainder. Since the name-term is stated only for the purpose of including all wholesome things, etc., it is said: "in the four terms of the Wholesome Triad Matrix (Kusalatika-mātikā)."

## End of the Description of the Enumeration Section.

## 1. Description of the Exposition Section of the Root Yamaka

In the Mutual Yamaka (Aññamaññayamaka), at the point "without asking: Whatever are wholesome"—just as in the second Yamaka, without asking "Whatever are wholesome roots," the question "Whatever are wholesome" is made; so here too, the question "Whatever are wholesome" should be made. The meaning is that the subsequent Yamaka does not occur by taking a new term distinct from the preceding Yamaka. Some teachers say: "Because it conforms to the reverse question (paṭiloma-pucchā)." However, when the preceding question is made by way of meaning, the subsequent question should conform to that preceding question, because doubt arises in the reverse for one who is free from doubt in the forward (anuloma). Therefore, the preceding question should not conform to the subsequent question; thus, only the former intention is appropriate here. This statement "Because that very meaning is possible even by this phrasing (byañjana)" should not be said in this way. Why? Because the meaning of the phrasing "wholesome" (kusala) is not the same as the meaning of the phrasing "having the same root" (ekamūla) with the wholesome root; therefore, the answer is also not the same. By the phrasing "wholesome"...
119:
If the question is formulated using the term "wholesome" (kusala), then in this context, it should be stated as "the remaining wholesome states" (avasesā kusalā dhammā). Otherwise, if the question is formulated in the manner of "having one root with a wholesome root," it should be stated as "the remaining states born together with wholesome roots" (avasesā kusalamūlasahajātā dhammā). These statements do not have the same meaning because they clarify the meanings of "wholesome" (kusala) and "unindicated matter produced by wholesome states" (kusala-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa-abyākata).

The intended meaning here is as follows: Since the meaning of the phrasing "whatever states have one root with a wholesome root" can also be established by the phrasing "whatever wholesome states," the question is formulated as "whatever states have one root with a wholesome root," without asking as in the second Yamaka. This is because, just as there are other wholesome states besides the wholesome roots, there are no other wholesome states besides those that have one root with a wholesome root. However, there are other states, such as mind-produced matter (cittajarūpa) caused by those wholesome states, which are distinct from the wholesome states themselves.

In the explanation of the reverse question (paṭilomapucchā), it was said that when the question is asked, "Are those states that have one root with a wholesome root...," the answer should be given according to the method stated below: "Those roots that arise together..." However, it is not possible to say it in that way. When it is asked, "Alternatively, whatever states are mutually roots with a wholesome root, do all those states have one root with a wholesome root?", the answer should simply be "Indeed" (āmantā). Among states that are mutually roots with a wholesome root, there is not a single state that does not have one root (i.e., they all certainly have one root). Therefore, it is not necessary to make a distinction as in the forward question (anulomapucchā).

In a consciousness (associated with knowledge/ñāṇasampayutta) where three wholesome roots arise, those roots are mutually roots and also have one root, because each pair is mutually a single root for the other. However, in a consciousness (dissociated from knowledge/ñāṇavippayutta) where only two roots arise, those roots are only mutually roots and do not have one root—if one asks whether the answer should be given as "those roots that arise together..." to prevent such a grasp? No, it is not so. This is because such a grasp can be prevented by the answer "Indeed" (āmantā) itself, and because the fact that two or three roots arising together are mutually of one root has already been determined by the answer to the forward question. By the term "one root" (ekamūla), only the state of having a common root among states that are mutually roots is questioned, not the state of having a mutually common root. There is indeed a state of having a common root for two roots. Among them, each single root has a common root with the other root and with other co-nascent states that have that root.

It should be understood that once the state of being mutually roots is determined, there is no doubt about the state of having one root; therefore, the question "Do all those states have one root with a wholesome root?" is not asked. The term "mutually roots" (aññamaññamūlā) means "these states have each other as roots." The term "having one root" (ekamūlā) means "these states have a single root in the sense of being common." Thus, both terms express only the state of being associated with a root. For this reason, in both cases, it is stated as "by a wholesome root" (kusalamūlena). In that context, although the state of having one root, which is a general association with a root, is determined, the state of being mutually roots, which is a specific distinction of that root, is not yet determined; thus, the forward question proceeds. However, once the state of being mutually roots, which is a specific association with a root, is determined, without...
120:
Because the state of being mutually roots exists, the state of having one root—which is a general association with a root—is already determined. Therefore, without making a separate question as "having one root" (ekamūlā), just as the terms "wholesome root" and "having one root" do not indicate the state of being wholesome, and thus the reverse question "Are all those states wholesome?" was asked in the first and second Yamakas due to the existence of doubt regarding their wholesomeness; similarly, the term "mutually roots" does not indicate the state of being wholesome. Therefore, because there is doubt regarding the state of being wholesome, and because the heading (adhikāra) of "wholesome" continues, the reverse question "Are all those states wholesome?" is asked.

However, in the Pali text where the passage "the rootless name, the rooted name" appears, the word "name" (nāma) is stated for the sake of making it very clear.

## 1. Paṇṇattiuddesavāravaṇṇanā
2-3. In the Khandhayamaka (The Book of Aggregates), within the six time periods such as the present, the arising and cessation of the aggregates, as well as their full understanding (pariññā), should be explained by way of the person (puggala), the location (okāsa), and both the person and location. These aggregates are expressed by five terms such as 'rūpakkhandha' (matter-aggregate), and within these five terms, there are ten component terms (avayavapada). Among these component terms, is the reality (dhamma) denoted by the component term 'rūpa' (matter) the same as the meaning of the collective term (samudāyapada) 'rūpakkhandha'? And is the reality denoted by the collective term the same as the meaning of the component term? To resolve this doubt—showing that a part or the whole denoted by component terms like 'rūpa' is the meaning of the collective terms, and the meaning denoted by the collective terms is indeed the meaning of the component terms like 'rūpa'—the Section on the Purification of Terms (Padasodhanavāra) was taught: 'Is rūpa the rūpakkhandha? Is the rūpakkhandha rūpa?'

Furthermore, since compound terms (samāsa) like 'rūpakkhandha' primarily emphasize the meaning of the latter term (uttarapada), the meaning of the primary term 'khandha' and the adjacent terms like 'vedanā' (feeling) can also occur. In the term 'rūpakkhandha', the status of the meaning denoted by the component term 'rūpa' as being the 'rūpakkhandha' is due to the co-referential (samanādhikaraṇa) nature of the word 'rūpa' and the word 'khandha'. Similarly, in that context, can the meaning denoted by the primary component term 'khandha' be the 'vedanākkhandha' (feeling-aggregate) and so on? Is it possible because the term 'khandha' and terms like 'vedanā' have a co-referential meaning? To resolve this doubt—showing that some realities (collective meanings) denoted by the component term 'khandha' are expressed by a certain collective term, but not everything is expressed by everything—the Root Cycle of the Purification of Terms (Padasodhanamūlacakka) was taught: 'Is rūpa the rūpakkhandha? Are the aggregates the vedanākkhandha?' By showing this, the status of terms like 'rūpa' as qualifiers (visesana), the status of the term 'khandha' as the qualified (visesitabba), and the co-referential (samanādhikaraṇa) nature of the qualifier and the qualified are demonstrated.

Because this has been shown, a doubt arises here: Is there any other 'rūpa' apart from the 'khandha'? This is because 'rūpa', when excluded from 'khandha', acts as a qualifier for 'khandha'. Are all aggregates to be qualified by 'rūpa', which is a qualifier of the aggregate? What is that 'rūpa' which is a qualifier of the aggregate? That 'rūpa' is indeed the primary elements (bhūtarūpa) and derived matter (upādārūpa), because only those primary and derived matters are taken. In the Exposition (Niddesa), the term 'Are the aggregates the rūpakkhandha?' is extracted and answered. Thus, in this matter of doubt, there is no 'rūpa' other than the 'khandha'. For that very reason, that which is denoted by the term 'rūpa' (primary and derived matter) is indeed denoted by the pure term 'khandha'.
122:
Not all aggregates are to be qualified by 'rūpa', which is a qualifier of the aggregate; for that reason, those aggregates should be distinguished (as rūpa-aggregates and non-rūpa aggregates). To show this meaning—that the same applies to the feeling-aggregate (vedanākkhandha) and so on—the Section on Pure Aggregates (Suddhakhandhavāra) was taught: 'Is rūpa an aggregate? Is an aggregate rūpa?'

Thereafter, when it is affirmed that 'rūpa is an aggregate', the doubt arises: 'This term aggregate (khandha) is not only qualified by rūpa, but also by feeling (vedanā) and so on.' After deciding the status of rūpa as an aggregate, a doubt also arises regarding the connection of the aggregates with the qualifier 'rūpa'. In such a case of doubt, to show that not all aggregates are connected with qualifiers like 'vedanā', but only some aggregates are connected with certain qualifiers, the Root Cycle of Pure Aggregates (Suddhakhandhamūlacakka) was taught. Thus, for those aggregates whose arising (uppāda) and so on are to be taught, it should be understood that the Section on Designations (Paṇṇattivāra) was taught to decide those aggregates by purifying their designations.

In the passage 'cattāri cattāri cakkāni bandhitvā' (binding four wheels each), the Yamakas are called 'wheels' (cakkāni) because they are parts of a wheel. The meaning here should be: 'having bound four Yamakas each, having a single aggregate as their root.' Or, the meaning should be understood as: 'four Yamakas each have a single aggregate as their root; thus, organizing them so they arise from each single root reality.' In that text, it should be understood that the status of a wheel is described by making the root term (mūlapada) such as 'Is rūpa the rūpakkhandha?' the hub (nābhi), the term 'aggregates' (khandhā) the rim (nemi), and terms like 'rūpakkhandha' the spokes (ara). It is not called a wheel because of being connected in a circular shape. Even in the sections rooted in the feeling-aggregate and so on, the textual order proceeds only by purifying the terms below, not by connecting in a circular manner. The meaning of the phrase 'teneve ca kāraṇena' is: taking only the acquisition of pure aggregates, and not stopping at the status of pure rūpa in the qualifiers of the aggregate like rūpa, but to show the meaning of rūpa etc. which is called the status of being a qualifier of the aggregate, the term is extracted and the meaning is analyzed in the manner of 'Are the aggregates the rūpakkhandha?' by connecting it with the word 'khandha'.

By the passage 'piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ' (pleasant and agreeable nature): 'The eye in the world is of a pleasant nature... forms in the world... eye-consciousness... eye-contact... feeling born of eye-contact... perception of forms... volition regarding forms... craving for forms... initial thought regarding forms... sustained thought regarding forms is of a pleasant nature in the world.' Thus, it should be understood as the mind, mental factors, and matter arising in the three planes, which are the objects of craving.
123:
The phenomena belonging to the three planes, which are the objects of craving, should be understood. Therefore, whatever agreeable and pleasant nature exists as a collection of the five aggregates, that is partially the aggregate of form; thus it is said: "The agreeable and pleasant nature is form, but not the aggregate of form." Alternatively, because of its agreeable nature, the aggregate of form is included in piyarūpa (agreeable form), but not by way of its nature of being deformed (ruppana); thus it is said: "The agreeable and pleasant nature is form, but not the aggregate of form."

In the Saññāyamaka, first in the term "diṭṭhisaññā", the word "viseso" (distinction) is an ellipsis. There, diṭṭhi (wrong view) itself is saññā (perception), thus it is called "diṭṭhisaññā". For in such verses as: "A person, having personally undertaken vows, goes to high and low states, being a being of perception" (Sn 798), and "For one detached from perception, there are no bonds" (Sn 853), diṭṭhi is also taught as "saññā".

"Are they not aggregates? Is it not the aggregate of feeling? Yes." In this way, it should be understood that because the word 'aggregate' (khandha) does not occur, the word 'aggregate of feeling' (vedanākkhandha) also does not occur; this is merely a clarification of the designation (paññatti). The actual existence of other phenomena is not the primary measure here. For this reason, He will say: "Are they not bases (āyatana)? Is it not the ear-base? Yes," and so on.

In the phrase "others than form, such as feeling," the supramundane (lokuttara) feeling and so on should be understood. The phrase "the remaining phenomena, excluding form and the aggregates" should also be understood as being said merely with reference to the non-occurrence of those words 'form' and 'aggregate'. For this reason, He will say: "The remaining phenomena, excluding the eye and the bases, are neither the eye nor the bases." And that dhammāyatana would not be an object of craving. If it were, it would be form because of its agreeable and pleasant nature, and it would be an aggregate because of the statement: "Is form an aggregate? Yes."

In the Commentary, however, although it is a non-existent designation, it is based on existent ultimate reality; referring to the existence of taking such concepts as 'woman' or 'man', it should be understood that the designation is taken here in the phrase "the remaining phenomena."

## 2. Commentary on the Occurrence Chapter (Pavatti-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

50-205. In the Occurrence Chapter (Pavatti-vāra), taking the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and others as the base (mūla), the Yamakas of three, two, and one are taught by combining them only with subsequent aggregates, not with preceding ones. Why is this? Because in the unmixed time divisions (amissaka-kāla), there is no difference in meaning. Indeed, a Yamaka where a preceding aggregate is combined with a subsequent one would merely be stated in an irregular order of questions if the subsequent were combined with the preceding; however, there is no difference in meaning. Since there is also no difference in the questions and answers, such a combination was not made.

In this context, only six time divisions are taught. The three mixed time divisions—Past with Present, Future with Present, and Future with Past—are just these three as shown; they are not taken separately because they do not exist independently. In various places, time divisions such as Past with Present are shown through inverse questions (paṭiloma-pucchā). In that same way, it is possible to combine them as: "For whom the aggregate of form has arisen, for him does the aggregate of feeling arise?" and so on. For this reason, even in the mixed time divisions, Yamakas are not taught by combining a subsequent aggregate with a preceding one. For the sake of easy comprehension, following the method adopted in the unmixed time divisions, they are taught by combining only with subsequent aggregates.

## By the words beginning with "Imināyeva ca lakkhaṇena," the reason why the names "Purepañha" (Prior Question) and "Pacchāpañha" (Posterior Question) are used is shown. A question whose answer is given by showing its specific form (sarūpa) is called "Paripuṇṇapañha" (Complete Question) because it encompasses the meaning that should be fully answered. It is called "Purepañha" because its meaning is similar to the first part (purima-koṭṭhāsa) of that answer, and "Pacchāpañha" because its meaning is similar to the latter part (pacchima-koṭṭhāsa). The similarity of meaning should be understood in the "Purepañha" merely by the attainment of arising and cessation of the aggregate encompassed by a single term, without investigating the distinction between the antecedent (sanniṭṭhāna) and the doubt (saṃsaya). Alternatively, it is appropriate to say it is called "Purepañha" by virtue of the affirmation of the aggregate encompassed by the antecedent term.

The rejection of the meaning of the antecedent (sanniṭṭhāna) itself is "Paṭikkhepa" (repudiation). The prevention of the meaning of the doubt (saṃsaya) is "Paṭisedha" (negation). This is the distinction between "Paṭikkhepa" and "Paṭisedha." "Pāḷipadameva hutvā" means that the very word "nuppajjati" stated in the Pali of the question becomes that word without the "na" (negative particle). Among those answers, it should be understood that the answer is made according to the course of the Pali for the purpose of negating the negation of arising and cessation, and the answer is made by negation for the purpose of negating arising and cessation themselves.
125:
The inclusion of the four questions and five answers in the twenty-seven places should be understood as being stated by way of including a portion of those questions and answers. Indeed, only the complete question (paripuṇṇapañha) and the answer by way of showing the specific form (sarūpadassana) should be included in the twenty-seven places.

By the phrase "What else can be done from here?", he shows that there is no other possible explanation to be made other than showing this Pali definition (pāḷivavatthāna), etc.

By the answer, "For those born in the Suddhāvāsa realm, the aggregate of matter has never arisen there, and the aggregate of feeling has never arisen there," it is made known that there is no second rebirth even in a single realm among the Suddhāvāsa realms. Indeed, this teaching proceeds by taking the continuity of karma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) from rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) until death (cuti) as a single unit, and by way of its arising and ceasing. When that continuity of karma-born matter is uninterrupted, the arising of wholesome states, etc., occurs; when it is interrupted, they do not arise. Therefore, by that very continuity, the initial arising and the final cessation are shown. Thus, from the arising of the rebirth-linking of that single being until the cessation of death, there is no "past" state; and prior to that rebirth-linking, the continuity of karma-born matter has never arisen before in that Suddhāvāsa realm by way of rebirth-linking. Therefore, it is said of both aggregates, "they have never arisen." Why is it not understood from this Pali text that there is no second rebirth in all five Suddhāvāsa realms? Because of the existence of the Uddhaṃsota Pali text. Indeed, both Pali texts should be taken in conjunction.

In the passage, "For those born in the Asaññasatta realm, the aggregate of matter will arise there," there are also Asaññasatta individuals who are distinguished by the premise (sanniṭṭhāna), "To whomsoever the aggregate of matter will arise in whichever place." Taking only those individuals, it is said, "of the Asaññasatta" (asaññasattānaṃ). Those who are excluded by that premise will go from that Asaññasatta realm to the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra) and attain Parinibbāna; for those individuals, there is no possibility of a second rebirth in the Asaññasatta realm. Therefore, referring to those individuals in their final existence (pacchimabhavika), he said: "For those in their final existence, the aggregate of matter will not arise there, and the aggregate of feeling will not arise there."

Here, just as there is an existence such as the five-constituent existence, is there also some "final existence" where their non-arising will occur? There is not. It is because those in their final existence, staying in any one of the existences such as the five-constituent existence, are included by the premise, "To whomsoever the aggregate of matter will not arise in whichever place." Desiring to allow the fact that for those in their final existence, there is no arising of the aggregate of feeling other than the aggregate of matter in that place, he said: "and the aggregate of feeling will not arise."
126:
The phrase "for those attaining Parinibbāna in Suddhāvāsa" should be understood as being stated by way of the Parinibbāna of the aggregates in those respective realms for Suddhāvāsa individuals, both those with rebirth-linking and those without. Indeed, for all those Suddhāvāsa inhabitants, the aggregate of feeling has never arisen in that realm. Just as the word "will cease" applies even to a person endowed with the present moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa-samangi), the word "has arisen" does not apply to the present; rather, it applies only to the past which has arisen and disappeared. Therefore, because the present continuity (santati) has not yet disappeared, it is said, "it has never arisen for those attaining Parinibbāna." The statement "the world systems are infinite" means that because space (okāsa) is delimited, the arising and cessation mentioned by way of space are also without limit and are intermingled. Therefore, it is said: "In the place where the aggregate of feeling arises, does the aggregate of perception cease there? Yes (āmantā)."

For the author of the Compendium (Sangaha) will say: 'Because the sound-base does not arise at the moment of rebirth-linking, there is no answer for the Yamaka together with it.'

The statement that the second Yamaka has an answer similar to the first, etc., should be understood as being said with reference only to the Section on Persons (Puggala-vāra). However, in the Section on Planes (Okāsa-vāra), it is stated because there is a dissimilar answer; even in the Section on Persons, it is answered in order to make it known that the second Yamaka does not have a similar answer in all sections. The statement that the three Yamakas together with the smell, taste, and tangible-object bases have similar answers is said with reference to the beings of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), because they should be answered in the manner of 'to those who have eyes but no smell,' and so on. Because the seed of rebirth-linking produced by the karma of those beings who are detached from sensual pleasures is of such a nature, the sensitivities (pasāda) such as the nose-base etc., and the objects such as smell etc., do not exist. 'Because of having an answer similar to the Yamaka of the nose-base' means that among the Yamakas based on the eye-base, it has an answer similar to the Yamaka of the nose-base.

In that eye-base-root, the answer occurred as 'to those who are being reborn with eyes but without a nose,' and so on. However, in these Yamakas based on the nose-base, the answer should be: 'For whom the nose-base arises, does the tongue-base arise for him? Yes (Āmantā).' Therefore, one might ask whether there is no similarity in the answers. It is true that there is no such similarity; however, just as among those eye-base-roots, the nose-base Yamaka and the tongue and body-base Yamakas have similar answers, so too in this nose-base-root Yamaka, the tongue and body-base Yamakas have similar answers. Therefore, it should be noted that the similarity of answers in those respective Yamakas is the reason for not being included in the Pali text. To show that the answer of the Yamakas with similar answers based on the eye-base, which were taken as examples, is the reason only by way of being an example, it is said: 'Because of having an answer similar to the Yamaka of the nose-base.' The similarity of answers in these nose-base-roots should be understood by way of majority (yebuyya). For, in those tongue and body-base Yamakas, by the answer 'Yes' (Āmantā) to the three questions...
129:
In the subsequent question, there should be an answer such as "For those who have the body-base but not the nose-base..." etc. Alternatively, just as in the Yamakas of the perception aggregate etc., which have the feeling aggregate etc. as their root, among the three unmixed periods, the answer "Āmantā" (Yes) is given to acknowledge the previously stated words as the answer; since there is nothing new to be said, no [new] answer is made. Similarly, in this Yamaka of the tongue-base with the nose-base as the root, because there is nothing new to be said, it does not enter the Pali text—this meaning is clear.

However, the body-base Yamaka should be answered by way of the second question; and that second question has an answer similar to the nose-base Yamaka among those with the eye-base as the root. Therefore, for whichever question an answer should be made, that question has an answer similar to the nose-base Yamaka; thus, the remaining ones do not enter the Pali text—this is how the meaning should be understood here. The word "Tathā" (likewise) is stated only because of the similarity in not entering the Pali text, not because the reasons are the same.

The nose, tongue, and body bases, whether they occur in beings who are not womb-born, or in womb-born beings at the time when the bases are complete, occur together. Because there is no difference or only a slight difference, it should be understood that once one nose-base Yamaka is answered, the other two are not [separately] answered; and once those with the nose-base as the root are answered, those with the other two as roots are not answered.

"Together with the form-base and mind-base" means together with the form-base and mind-base stated in this question: "To whom the form-base arises, to him does the mind-base arise?" The reason is that among those with the form-base as the root, the similarity of the answer of the first question in the mind-base Yamaka with the first questions in the smell, taste, and tangible-base Yamakas is stated as the reason for not answering those Yamakas. Just as the answer should not be made in the manner previously stated for the second questions, the first questions also should not be made.

In the phrase "Heṭṭhimehi sadisavissajjanattā" (because the answer is similar to the ones below), the answers for the taste and tangible-base Yamakas with the smell-base as the root, and the tangible-base Yamaka with the taste-base as the root, should not be made in the same manner as previously stated. For whichever Yamakas the answers are made, those mind-base and dhamma-base Yamakas with smell, taste, and tangible bases as roots have the same answer as the mind-base and dhamma-base Yamakas with the five bases starting with the eye-base as roots—this is the meaning. All the sound-base Yamakas with the eye-base etc. as roots, and all those with the sound-base as the root, by not being answered...
130:
By showing that an answer cannot be obtained, the sixty-six Yamakas are said to be answered; thus [the teacher] said: "Sixty-six Yamakas are said to be answered."

In the phrase "one born blind, one born deaf," it should be understood that by taking "one born deaf," one who is both born blind and deaf is also included. The phrase "those with the nose-base and eye-base" is stated with reference only to spontaneously born beings (opapātika) with complete bases. In this context, the word "eva" should be connected after the word "vuttaṃ" (stated). Just as the phrase "those with the nose-base but without the eye-base" is stated with reference to those with incomplete bases, the phrase "those with the nose-base and eye-base" is not stated with reference to such [incomplete ones]; rather, it should be understood that it is stated only with reference to those with complete bases. By saying so, it does not exclude the reference to those who are born deaf.

22-254. In the question "In which place the eye-base...", it is stated by seeing only the simultaneous arising of the eye and the ear in the Rūpa Brahma realm, as it invariably asks about that realm. However, in the Okāsavāra (section on location), because the person is not being considered in that realm, it is said "Āmantā" (Yes), meaning that in whichever Sense Sphere (Kāmadhātu) and Fine-material Sphere (Rūpadhātu) the eye-base arises, the ear-base also certainly arises there.

Why is it affirmed: "Or else, to whom the form-base will arise, to him will the eye-base arise? Āmantā"? For one who will attain Parinibbāna after entering the womb, the form-base will arise at rebirth, but will the eye-base not [fail to] arise? It is because for the person to whom the form-base will arise, after the arising of the form-base for that person in that state, the initial arising of the eye-base continuum in the subsequent period (pavattikāla) must also be affirmed.

If so, why is it affirmed: "Or else, to whom the form-base will not arise, to him will the eye-base not arise? Āmantā"? For a last-existence person (pacchimabhavika) who is a womb-born being currently at the stage of rebirth and staying within the first 11 weeks (ekādasama-sattāha), the form-base will not arise, but is it not the case that the eye-base will [still] arise? It is because an arising that will occur in that same life is not spoken of as "future" (anāgata). Only the initial arising of various base-continua in another life (at rebirth and during the course of existence) is called "future arising," because it is not included within the current span of time (addhā-paccuppanna). However, what will occur during the course of existence (pavattikāla) in that very same life is not called "future arising" because it is included within the current span of time. Here, the distinction of periods such as the present for the karma-born matter is intended by way of the span of time (addhā). For this reason, in the Indriya Yamaka (Yam. 3, Indriya Yamaka, 368), "To whom the feminine faculty..."
131:
The Blessed One said: "(The female faculty) is arising for that person; will the male faculty arise for that person?" For women in their last existence who are currently undergoing rebirth, for women who will attain Parinibbāna after reaching the fine-material or immaterial spheres, and for women who will attain Parinibbāna after appearing in a few more existences in that very female state—for those women currently undergoing rebirth, the female faculty (itthindriya) is arising, but it is said that the male faculty (purisindriya) will not arise for them. Indeed, it is not that the male faculty will definitely not arise during the course of the present existence for all those women, because the possibility of a change of sex (liṅgaparivattana) exists. However, the statement "the male faculty will not arise for them" is made with reference to the non-existence of the initial arising of the male faculty in a subsequent existence (bhavantara). This is because the future state of the initial arising in a subsequent existence is what is intended. For this reason, the Blessed One used the term 'existence' (bhava) in the phrase "after appearing in a few more existences."

According to the teaching, "The acquisition of the bases (āyatana) is birth (jāti)," if one takes the meaning that the base which will inevitably arise for a person who has taken rebirth through the kamma that produces those respective bases is "arising" until the completion of the bases, then the answers to the two questions are well-suited. If this is the case, in the Pali passages such as, "Or rather, for whom the ear-base (sotāyatana) will not arise, is the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) not arising for that person?", those in their last existence who are womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka) and are currently undergoing rebirth are also included. For this reason, in the Indriya Yamaka, the answer "Āmantā (Yes)" to the question, "Or rather, for whom the pleasant-feeling faculty (somanassindriya) is arising, is the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) arising for that person?" is also appropriate. This is because the kamma that produces the pleasant-feeling faculty can certainly produce the eye-faculty; therefore, even in the womb, until the eye-faculty arises, that answer is highly commendable as it refers to the state of the pleasant-feeling faculty being in the process of arising.

Furthermore, in the question, "Or rather, for whom the form-base (rūpāyatana) has arisen in a certain plane, is the nose-base (ghānāyatana) arising for that person in that plane?", it is said: "For those passing away from the sense sphere, for those without a nose-base (aghānaka) who are undergoing rebirth in the sense sphere, and for those in the fine-material sphere, the form-base has arisen in that plane, but the nose-base is not arising for them in that plane." Here, the phrase "those without a nose-base who are undergoing rebirth in the sense sphere" should be understood as referring to those who have taken rebirth through kamma that does not produce the nose-base and who will die within the first eleven weeks (sattāha). "For whom the nose-base will not cease in a certain plane..."
132:
...will the form-base (rūpāyatana) not cease for that person in that plane? For those undergoing rebirth in the sense sphere, for those without a nose-base (aghānaka) who are passing away from the sense sphere, and for those in the fine-material sphere, the nose-base does not cease in that plane, but it is not that the form-base will not cease for them in that plane. Here, the phrase "those without a nose-base who are passing away from the sense sphere" indicates that there is death for womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka) beings before the nose-base has even arisen. This is because, in the sense sphere, there is no one without a nose-base other than a womb-born being. This is also because it is not stated in the Dhammahadayavibhaṅga that "at the moment of rebirth in the sense element (kāmadhātu), eight bases appear for some."

If so, why is it not known that in the questions shown here in this Āyatana Yamaka and in the Indriya Yamaka, the answer "Āmantā (Yes)" is given with reference only to spontaneously-born (opapātika) beings? It is because a response (paṭivacana) is not given when there is the possibility of doubt in a portion of the meaning taken by the antecedent (sanniṭṭhāna) in the Yamaka. When a meaning needs to be analyzed and distinguished, a simple response is not given. If it were, it would not be a complete explanation (paripuṇṇavissajjanā).

If so, why is it not known from the statement, "For whom the pleasant-feeling faculty (somanassindriya) arises, does the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) arise for that person? Āmantā," that there is no rebirth with pleasant feeling for womb-born beings? It is because of the Vibhaṅga Pali: "At the moment of rebirth in the sense element, for whom do ten faculties appear? At the moment of rebirth for womb-born beings who are accompanied by roots (sahetuka) and associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta), ten faculties appear: the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the female faculty or the male faculty, the life-faculty, the pleasant-feeling faculty or the equanimity-faculty, the faith-faculty, etc."

In the section on cessation (nirodhavāra) regarding the future time, just as the cessation of that very consciousness is spoken of as a future event at its moment of arising (uppattikkhana), so too the cessation of that continuity of kamma-born matter (kammajasantāna) should be spoken of as a future event at its moment of arising. Therefore, in all future sections, it is spoken of in that way only for those undergoing rebirth (upappajjanta), not for those who have already arisen (uppanna). For those who have already arisen, the cessation of a different future continuity is spoken of as a future event, not the cessation of that same continuity. This is because the cessation immediately after the arising of that continuity is said to have commenced (āraddha). Therefore, even though there is the breaking up of the ear and eye for Arahants during the course of existence, the two-fold answer: "For whom the eye-base will cease, will the ear-base cease for that person? Āmantā. Or rather, for whom the ear-base will cease, will the eye-base cease for that person? Āmantā," is indeed appropriate only by way of considering the future time. Because the cessation immediately after rebirth is said to have commenced (āraddha)...
133:
Cessation (nirodha) is said to be 'begun' (āraddha). However, because it is the state of completion of that continuity (santāna), the word 'cessation' is used for the death-consciousness (cuti). Therefore, although a part of the occurring (pavatta) continuity has ceased, because it is an incomplete cessation based on the part that has not yet ceased, only death (cuti) is called the cessation (nirodha) of that continuity. Indeed, it will be stated: 'For whom the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) ceases, does the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) cease for him? Yes (āmantā).' Because of this statement, here too, only cessation at death is intended. Since the phenomenon that will cease during the occurring (pavatti) stage is said to cease only at death by virtue of completion, the answer 'Yes' (āmantā) is appropriate. In the terms 'those with eyes' (sacakkhukānaṃ) and so forth, the meaning should be understood as 'those who have obtained eyes' and so on.

'For whom the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) does not cease, will the ear-base (sotāyatana) not cease for him?' In this question, in the Pali: 'For all those being reborn (upapajjantānaṃ), and for those dying (cavantānaṃ) without eyes, the eye-base does not cease, but for them it is not that the ear-base will not cease,' it should be noted that all those being reborn and those dying without eyes are included, excluding the individuals in their final existence (pacchimabhavika) in the formless realm (arūpa). Since they are included in the second portion (koṭṭhāsa), this word 'all' (sabba) and the word 'without eyes' (acakkhuka) are 'with remainder' (sāvasesa) in consideration of them. In the phrase 'those in their final existence in the formless realm,' it should be understood that those who do not go from the formless realm to the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra) and have no rebirth elsewhere are also included as 'those in their final existence in the formless realm.' This method applies similarly in other such instances.

## The Commentary on the Occurrence Chapter is finished.

## The Commentary on the Book of Pairs of Bases (Āyatana-yamaka-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 4. Element Pairs (Dhātu-yamaka)

1-19. The phrase 'of those that are obtainable' (labbhamānānaṃ) is stated in the Occurrence Chapter with reference to the non-obtainability (alabbhamānatā) of the Yamakas related to the sound element (sadda-dhātu) and those related to the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuviññāṇa-dhātu) and so forth, by virtue of death and rebirth.

## The Commentary on the Book of Pairs of Elements (Dhātu-yamaka-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
134:
## 5. Sacca Yamaka (The Pairs of Truths)
## Commentary on the Exposition Section (Niddesavāra-vaṇṇanā)
## 1. Section on Designations (Paṇṇattivāra)
10-26. In the passage, "Is suffering the Truth of Suffering? Yes," the word 'suffering' (dukkha) applies to the three types: intrinsic suffering (dukkha-dukkha), suffering due to formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha), and suffering due to change (vipariṇāma-dukkha). The word 'suffering' also applies to birth (jāti) and so on, as in "Birth also is suffering." However, when this word 'suffering' occurs in a sense other than intrinsic suffering, it cannot occur without depending on another term (such as saṅkhāra, etc.). In this context, the pure term 'suffering' is taken without being coupled with other terms like saṅkhāra to purify the designation (paṇṇatti-sodhana). Therefore, because it is of the nature of suffering in the primary sense (nippariyāyato) and not figuratively, the word 'suffering' applies to that intrinsic suffering; and since that intrinsic suffering is certainly the Truth of Suffering, it is said, "Yes."

In the Section on Pure Truths (Suddhasaccavāra), among the origins (samudaya) taught in the Analysis of the Truths (Saccavibhaṅga), there is no factor that has the nature of a result. Among the factors that have the nature of a result, there is no such thing called cessation (nirodha). The word 'path' (magga) also occurs in the factors of fruition (phala-aṅga) because they are the results of the path, not because the function of the path is actually present. This is because those path-factors within fruition have already completed the function of deliverance from the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa). Here, the word 'path' denotes the meaning of delivering from the round, not the meaning of the result of the path that delivers from the round. Therefore, in these questions, "Is origin truth?", "Is cessation truth?", "Is path truth?", the answer is given as "Yes."

Alternatively, it should be understood that after the terms have been purified by the Section on the Purification of Terms (Padasodhana-vāra), only the words such as 'suffering' which are qualifiers (visesana) of 'Truth' are taken here. The Section on Pure Truths was taught to demonstrate that those words like 'suffering' are definitely qualifiers of Truth, and to show the specific connection of the Truths with those qualifiers. Therefore, because the qualifiers of Truth such as 'suffering' are definitely Truth, it is said: "Is suffering truth? ... [pe] ... Is path truth? Yes."

Just as intrinsic suffering and others which are qualifiers of Truth are taken here, likewise, in the Khandha Yamaka and others, in the sections on pure aggregates (Suddhakhandha-vāra), it is appropriate to take rūpa and others which are qualifiers of the aggregates. However, in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), it is stated: "Whether it be rūpa as 'agreeable and pleasant nature' or rūpa as 'great elements and derived matter,' all are included within the five aggregates; therefore, he affirms 'Yes'." By this statement, it is shown that in taking rūpa, cakkhu, dukkha, etc., in the sections on pure aggregates, meanings other than the qualifiers of the aggregates are also taken. Therefore, the other meaning was stated in accordance with that [Commentary's view].

## The Commentary on the Exposition Section is finished.
135:
## 2. Description of the Occurrence Chapter (Pavatti-vāra-vaṇṇanā)

27-164. The phrase "Even for those in the Pure Abodes" (antamaso suddhāvāsānampi) was spoken considering that since those Brahmas of the Pure Abodes are Noble Ones (Ariyas), there might be doubt regarding their rebirth through the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The phrase "of the mind dissociated from craving" (taṇhāvippayuttacittassa) should be understood as being taken only by way of the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra). By the antecedent (sanniṭṭhāna) "To whom the Truth of Suffering arises" (yassa dukkhasaccaṃ uppajjati), the following are included: all persons currently being reborn, those in the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra) during the course of existence (pavatti) who possess the arising moment (uppādakkhaṇa) of minds other than the Path and Fruition, and those in the five-constituent existence who possess the arising moment of all minds. Among those persons thus determined by the antecedent, the phrase "at the arising moment of the mind dissociated from craving during the course of existence" (pavatte taṇhāvippayuttacittassa uppādakkhaṇe) indicates some persons who possess the occurrence of a single portion, namely the portion of suffering (dukkha-koṭṭhāsa), out of the portions of suffering and origin (samudaya). Since this is a specific analysis and classification of the group already taken by the antecedent, it is appropriate to include persons of the four-constituent existence as well. This is because, among them, there is no possibility of inclusion for those possessing the arising moment of Path and Fruition, as those possessing Path and Fruition are not taken by the antecedent. By the phrase "This should not be taken here" (idaṃ idha na gahetabbaṃ), it means that the Fruition-attainment mind (phala-samāpatti-citta) in the four-constituent existence should not be taken here in the context of the arising of the Truths.

In this Chapter on Persons and Planes (pugalokāsavāra), the phrase "for all those being reborn" (sabbesaṃ upapajjantānaṃ) is spoken by way of showing the first arising of kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) which occurs continuously. Here, non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) are also included. The phrase "at the arising moment of the mind dissociated from craving during the course of existence" is spoken to show the arising of the Truth of Suffering alone, free from the arising of the Truth of Suffering mixed with the arising of the Truth of Origin. The phrase "at the arising moment of craving" (taṇhāya uppādakkhaṇe) is spoken to show the arising of the Truth of Suffering together with the arising of the Truth of Origin. The arising of the Truth of Suffering during the course of existence for those non-percipient beings is not taken in any of the preceding or succeeding portions (koṭṭhāsa). Likewise, their cessation (nirodha) is not taken. The same method applies to the Magga-sacca-yamaka. It is stated that the plane (okāsa) should be known here by way of the moment (khaṇa): at the moment of rebirth and at the moment of the arising of the mind dissociated from craving. If this were so, in the answer to the problem "To whom and where the Truth of Suffering arises, to him and there will the Truth of Origin arise?", the following answer in the latter portion would not be appropriate: "For the others being reborn into the four-constituent and five-constituent existence, and at the arising moment of the mind during the course of existence, for them there the Truth of Suffering arises and the Truth of Origin will arise." This is because at the moment of rebirth and at the moment of the arising of the mind, the Truth of Origin will not [necessarily] arise. Therefore, for persons possessing the moment of rebirth and the moment of the arising of the mind dissociated from craving, in whichever plane, such as the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), that rebirth and that arising of the mind occur, for them in that plane...
136:
...the meaning of the word 'there' (tattha) in this text is appropriate only by way of the plane (okāsa). This chapter is the Puggala-okāsa-vāra. In this Puggala-okāsa-vāra, the phrase "for all those being reborn" (sabbesaṃ upapajjantānaṃ) etc. is spoken for the purpose of showing specific persons; as for the plane (okāsa), it is simply the plane where those persons arise.

In the Pali text: "For all those passing away, at the dissolution moment (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of the mind during the course of existence, and at the arising moment of the Path and Fruition in the formless sphere (āruppa), for them the Truth of Origin does not arise and the Truth of Suffering does not arise," regarding the phrase "the Truth of Suffering does not arise at the dissolution moment of the mind during the course of existence," some teachers say that because it is an occurrence connected with the mind, only mind-born matter (cittaja-rūpa) is intended here; kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) etc. are not intended because they arise without depending on the mind. However, the person taken by the antecedent "Or to whom the Truth of Origin does not arise" is not taken by depending on the mind; rather, any person of such nature is taken. Therefore, by the consequent (saṃsaya) "to him the Truth of Suffering does not arise," it is not only the Truth of Suffering depending on the mind that is spoken of, but rather any [Truth of Suffering]. Thus, the meaning should be understood as: at the dissolution moment of the mind, no Truth of Suffering arises. This is because in the Yamaka, there is no such thing as an unanalyzed question when it ought to be analyzed.

The phrase "When the second mind is occurring for those in the Pure Abodes" (suddhāvāsānaṃ dutiye citte vattamāne) is spoken by way of showing the person and plane where the Truth of Suffering has arisen but the Truth of Origin has never yet arisen, according to the final limit of all limits. When that [second mind] is shown, because they are of the same destiny (samāna-gatika), all persons possessing all minds prior to the second unwholesome mind are also shown by that same text. For those persons also, in that Pure Abode plane, the Truth of Suffering has arisen but the Truth of Origin has never arisen. By doing so, in the text "For the others in the four-constituent and five-constituent existence" (itaresaṃ catuvokārapañcavokārānaṃ), the aforementioned Pure Abode persons are not taken. Just as in the answer to "To whom and where the Truth of Suffering arises, to him and there has the Truth of Origin arisen?", by the text "at the arising moment of the rebirth-mind of those in the Pure Abodes," those possessing the arising moment of all minds prior to the second unwholesome mind—who are of the same destiny as those possessing the arising moment of the rebirth-mind—are shown; therefore, they are not taken by the word "others" (itaresam). The same should be understood here [in the Past Chapter].

The word "others" (itaresam) serves to specify the five-constituent persons, not the four-constituent persons. This is because there are no such four-constituent persons to be excluded who were mentioned previously, unlike the aforementioned Pure Abode five-constituent persons. By the antecedent "For those who have realized [the Truths], for them there the Truth of Suffering has arisen and the Truth of Magga has arisen," persons and planes are taken as mutually delimited. Therefore, it should be noted that only those persons who have penetrated the Truths in a particular plane are taken by the word "those who have realized" (abhisametāvīnaṃ).
137:
It should be understood. Therefore, those who have realized the Four Noble Truths in the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere, and have been reborn in the fine-material or immaterial spheres, are not included here (under the term 'abhisametāvinam') as long as the realization of the Four Noble Truths has not yet arisen in that particular realm. However, they are not shown separately because they share the same destiny as those in the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes) who have not yet attained realization, as shown in the first portion: "while the second consciousness of the Suddhāvāsa inhabitants is occurring." By the term "anabhisametāvinam," those who have not yet realized the Four Noble Truths in all realms and specifically in that Suddhāvāsa realm are included. Among them, to show the specific time for taking the Suddhāvāsa inhabitants, it is said: "while the second consciousness of the Suddhāvāsa inhabitants is occurring."

By this Pali: "immediately after which consciousness they will obtain the Path of Arahatship," it should be understood that those starting from the one possessed of the consciousness preceding the purification consciousness (vodāna-citta), who share the same destiny as the one possessed of the purification consciousness, up to the one possessed of the final craving-associated consciousness, are shown. This method applies to other such Yamakas as well.

In the place where it says "at the moment of dissolution (bhanga-kkhaṇa) of the consciousness in the course of existence (pavatti)," it should be understood that the moment of dissolution of the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) is also included. Similarly, in the place where it says "at the moment of arising (uppāda-kkhaṇa) of the consciousness in the course of existence," the moment of arising of the death consciousness (cuti-citta) should also be included. In the answer to the problem: "For whom the truth of suffering does not cease, will the truth of the origin not cease for him?", in both portions, it is only said: "at the moment of dissolution of the Path and the Fruit in the immaterial sphere"; it is not specified further. Why? Because a single individual possessed of the moment of dissolution of the Path and the Fruit is included in both portions. For, among those possessed of the moment of dissolution of the Path and the Fruit in the immaterial sphere who are taken by this thesis "for whom the truth of suffering does not cease," some who are possessed of the moment of dissolution of the three Fruits and the two Paths, without letting (the Path and Fruit) arise without interval, produce insight-attachment (vipassanā-nikanti) and existence-attachment (bhava-nikanti) in between and will produce the higher Path; for them, the truth of the origin will cease. Among those very individuals, for some who produce the higher Path without letting craving arise in between, being possessed of the moment of dissolution of the Path and the Fruit, the truth of the origin will not cease. By the general statement made in the first portion, the method is shown that the meaning to be stated in the latter portion is taken by exclusion.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Course of Existence is finished.
138:
## 3. Explanation of the Section on Full Understanding (Pariññā-vāra-vaṇṇanā)
165-170. In the Section on Full Understanding... the specific statement "the three full understandings are obtained here" is said for the purpose of showing the state of all truths being fully understood, just like the state of all aggregates etc. being fully understood in the Aggregate Yamaka etc., and for the purpose of showing the non-occurrence of this section by way of realization and development. For the purpose of the full understanding of the truth of suffering and for the purpose of the abandonment of the truth of the origin, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. Therefore, to show the full understanding and abandonment in the truths, the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā) is stated regarding the truth of suffering, not the full understanding of abandonment (pahāna-pariññā). Regarding the truth of the origin, the full understanding of abandonment is stated, not the full understanding of investigation. However, the full understanding of known (ñāta-pariññā) is stated in both because it is common (to both). For the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) makes clear both suffering and the origin, thus it is the full understanding of known; because it completes the task of investigating suffering, it is the full understanding of investigation; and because it makes the origin not occur again, it is the full understanding of abandonment. Thus, all three full understandings should be applied at the moment of the Path itself.

## The Explanation of the Section on Full Understanding is finished.

## The Explanation of the Truth Yamaka is finished.

## 6. The Yamaka of Formations (Saṅkhāra-yamaka)

## 1. Explanation of the Section on Designation (Paṇṇatti-vāra-vaṇṇanā)
Just as the aggregates etc. were not analyzed previously, the bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra) etc. were also not analyzed previously (before the Saṅkhāra-yamaka). Therefore, because those bodily formations etc. are not yet known, the three formations are analyzed by such statements as "in-breathing and out-breathing is the bodily formation." In the first sense of "kāyassa saṅkhāro" (formation of the body), the genitive case (sāmī-vibhakti) is used in the sense of possession (sāmī-attha) only; in the second sense, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (kattu-attha). In the term "vacīyā saṅkhāro" (formation of speech), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (kamma-attha). In the term "cittassa saṅkhာရော" (formation of mind), it is also in the sense of the agent only. Since that sense of the agent is the sense of the instrumental case (karaṇa-vibhakti), it is said: "having made the genitive case in the sense of the instrumental."

2-7. In the phrase "suddhika-ekekapada-vasena atthābhāvato," there is a single meaning such as in-breathing and out-breathing, which is obtained by two terms and shown by the cyclic sections (cakkavāra) based on the clarification of terms (padasodhana-vāra). That meaning, by the pure terms such as body etc...
139:
Since it is not stated by the pure term 'formation' (saṅkhāra), just as in the Padasodhana-vāra (Purification of Terms section), the meaning of the term 'form' (rūpa) is shown as a part of the aggregates and the meaning of the term 'aggregate' (khandha) is shown as the collection of aggregates, thus having the intended meaning; similarly, in each individual term, there is no such intended meaning. If the compound term 'kāya-saṅkhāra' (bodily formation), without being shown separately, denotes a single meaning, then the term 'kāya-saṅkhāra' occurring in the sense of bodily formation should be qualified by the term 'kāya', just as the term 'khandha' is qualified by the term 'rūpa'. By the statement 'This is the Suddha-saṅkhāravāra' (Pure Formation Section), it shows the impropriety of the statement 'The body is the bodily formation' etc., because only the intended meanings shown by the Padasodhana-vāra of this section are taken, and those meanings are not taken by terms such as 'body' (kāya).

In this Saṅkhārayamaka, because terms such as 'body' (kāya) and the term 'formation' (saṅkhāra) are not co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa), if it were taught as 'The body is a formation, formations are the body' etc., it would result in abandoning the intended meaning and grasping an unintended meaning; therefore, the Suddha-saṅkhāra-mūla-cakkavāra is not taught. When the qualifiability of the term 'formation' (saṅkhāra) by non-co-referential terms such as 'body' (kāya) is shown by the Padasodhana-vāra-mūla-cakkavāras, a doubt arises: 'Is the bodily formation qualified by the term "body" occurring in another sense, qualified by "speech" (vacī) and "mind" (citta) occurring in other senses, or is it something else?' The same applies to the remaining terms. To show their other meanings in this section, it should be understood that the six pairs (yamakas) were taught by way of forward and reverse order (anuloma-paṭiloma) as 'Is bodily formation verbal formation?' etc. However, in the Commentary, because it is taught in the place of the Suddha-saṅkhāravāra, this method is called the Suddha-saṅkhāravāra.

## The Explanation of the Section on Designation (Paṇṇattivāra-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Section on Occurrence (Pavattivāra-vaṇṇanā)

In the Pavattivāra, because they are the locations (okāsa) for formations and persons, jhāna and the plane (bhūmi) are taken separately as locations. Therefore, in the Puggalavāra (Section on Persons), by taking the person by way of location, they are taken by way of those two locations. Thus, it is shown by qualifying the persons taken by way of location as the second and third jhānas, 'at the moment of the arising of in-breaths and out-breaths without initial and sustained application'...
140:
## Explanation of the Section on Occurrence of Formations

By the words 'those who have attained the first jhāna' (paṭhamajjhānaṃ samāpannānaṃ), the person is shown by way of the jhāna-location. By the words 'those of the sense sphere' (kāmāvacarānaṃ), the person is shown by way of the plane-location (bhūmokāsa). To qualify both types of persons, the Blessed One said: 'at the moment of the arising of in-breaths and out-breaths' (assāsa-passāsānaṃ uppādakkhaṇe). By that qualifying term, he excludes those who have attained the first jhāna in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, and those in the sense sphere such as those in the womb. This is because for sense-sphere beings such as those in the womb, initial and sustained application (vitakka-vicāra) occur without in-breaths and out-breaths. In the Commentary, however, only those of the fine-material and immaterial spheres are shown because it is certain (ekantika). By these words, 'at the moment of the arising of initial and sustained application without in-breaths and out-breaths', it should be understood that the persons shown, who have the first jhāna location and the sense-sphere location etc., are qualified by the absence of in-breaths and out-breaths. In this way, the classification of persons should be understood in all questions.

The Commentary says, 'in the first jhāna arisen in the sense-sphere plane'. If that were the meaning, then in the passage 'in the fourth jhāna, in the fine-material sphere, in the immaterial sphere, there the mental formation arises, but the bodily formation does not arise', the meaning would also be 'in the fourth jhāna arisen in the fine-material and immaterial planes'. That meaning is undesirable because it would lead to not taking the planes as locations and not taking all fourth jhānas as locations. Therefore, without mixing the jhāna-location and the plane-location, they should be applied separately as locations. For in the first jhāna location, both bodily formation and verbal formation arise, and they also arise in the sense-sphere location. Although both do not arise in every first jhāna and every sense-sphere [moment], it should be understood that this was said because both do arise there. Because they are separate locations, the statement 'here by way of mere factors' etc., should not be said. In this Yamaka, it should be understood that the second jhāna, which is merely without initial application but with sustained application, is included in the first jhāna by way of sustained application. Or, taking the second jhāna as the peak, the other is not included. In the 'Yassa-yattha' section, the term 'those attained to cessation' (nirodhasamāpannānaṃ) is not obtained. This is because those persons do not exist in a location like the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta).

By the words 'while the second consciousness of the Suddhāvāsa [beings] is occurring' (suddhāvāsānaṃ dutiye citte vattamāne), the teacher, showing that both have never arisen at the moment of the second consciousness—the functional advertence of the mind-door accompanied by initial and sustained application—which follows their first consciousness that is without initial and sustained application, [implies] also in the preceding consciousness-moments...
141:
It has already been shown that it has not occurred before. Just as it was said, "for those being reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm," to show the beginning of the mental formation (citta-saṅkhāra), it should be understood that it was also said, "at the moment when the second consciousness occurs," to show the beginning of the verbal formation (vacī-saṅkhāra).

## The Explanation of the Chapter on Occurrence (Pavatti-vāra) is finished.

## The Explanation of the Pairs of Formations (Saṅkhāra Yamaka) is finished.

## 7. Anusaya Yamaka

## The Explanation of the Chapter on the Exposition of the Delimitation of Sections

The full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā) is the discerning of causes. Having explained the full understanding of the known through the Root Pairs (Mūla Yamaka) which illustrates causes, and the full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā) through the Pairs of Aggregates (Khandha Yamaka) and so forth because of the abundance of investigative knowledge regarding the aggregates etc. as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, the Anusaya Yamaka is undertaken (expounded) to clarify the full understanding by abandonment (pahāna-pariññā), which culminates in the abandonment of latent tendencies, using the latent tendencies (anusaya) which are the pinnacle of things to be abandoned. The phrase "labbhamānavasena" means by way of what is obtainable as a latent tendency. The reason for causing the latent tendencies to be grasped in three ways is that if they were not grasped in such a way, the Pali text of the Chapter on Latent Tendencies (Anusaya-vāra) etc. would be difficult to understand.

In this context, "purimesu" means in these chapters such as the Chapter on Those with Latent Tendencies (Sānusaya-vāra). Since there is no difference in meaning, if it were not stated as "for one being reborn in the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) or for one passing away from the sense-sphere, or for one being reborn in the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu) or for one passing away from the sense-sphere," etc., how could this teaching be a Yamaka teaching? This is not a Yamaka teaching in the strict sense, but rather a demonstration of the delimitation of the location where latent tendencies reside by way of passing away and rebirth of the latent tendencies that were taught by way of Yamaka in the previous chapters. However, because of the abundance of Yamaka teachings, the entire collection of chapters should be known by the name "Anusaya Yamaka." Alternatively, although the reverse questions (paṭiloma-pucchā) are obtainable by way of meaning, they are not stated because there is no special difference in meaning; thus, this teaching should also be known as a Yamaka teaching by way of its potentiality.

By the words "they arise having obtained a suitable cause," it shows the fitness for arising when a cause is obtained. Indeed, unabandoned latent tendencies arise when a cause is obtained. And as long as the path (magga) has not yet made them unfit for arising...
142:
Because they are of such a nature, they are called 'latent tendencies' (anusaya). Such a latent tendency is grasped by the word 'uppajjati' (arises); it does not mean the actual state of currently arising as in the Khandha Yamaka and so forth. For this very reason, the Chapter on Arising (Uppajjana-vāra) is analyzed without distinction from the Chapter on Latent Tendencies (Anusaya-vāra) by saying, "To whom the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) arises, does the latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) arise to that person? Yes (āmanta)," and so on. Defilements that have arisen in the past or are currently arising in the present, having obtained a suitable cause, have reached a state of strength (thāmagata) because they have not yet been abandoned. And they have arisen and are arising solely because of their fitness to arise; there is no such thing as 'fitness to arise' other than in the past, future, and present. Therefore, all sensual lust and so forth of the past, future, and present are called 'latent tendencies.' Indeed, latent tendencies exist only in the sense of being unabandoned, and only those of the past etc. are unabandoned. The abandonment of latent tendencies occurs when the Path (magga) makes such tendencies unfit for arising. The state of being unabandoned is merely a mode of the phenomena (dhamma), not the phenomenon itself. With the intention that only the phenomenon itself arises, it is said, "It is not proper to say that the unabandoned mode arises."

In the phrase 'seven latent tendencies' (sattānusaya), if they are called latent tendencies because they lie latent in the mental continuum in the sense of being unabandoned, then why are only seven mentioned? Since other defilements besides the seven latent tendencies are also unabandoned, would they not also become latent tendencies? No, they would not. This is because the state of being a latent tendency is not stated merely by being unabandoned. For it is said: "A latent tendency is called a defilement that has reached a state of strength in the sense of being unabandoned." Therefore, it is proper to say that only a defilement that has reached a state of strength in the sense of being unabandoned is called a latent tendency. 'Reached a state of strength' (thāmagata) should be understood as a nature not shared with other defilements. For this reason, the Buddha, who realized the nature of phenomena, spoke of only these as 'latent tendencies.' 'Reached a state of strength' means being endowed with latent tendencies.

If it is argued that because the Chapter on Latent Tendencies and the Chapter on Arising follow the same course, just as the word 'anuseti' (lies latent) indicates the unabandoned mode, so should the word 'uppajjati' (arises); therefore, since the word 'uppajjati' is not used in the Chapter on Arising, it cannot be spoken? That is not so. Both are stated because of the difference in the meaning of the words. Although there is no difference in the meaning 'it arises having obtained a suitable cause,' the word 'anuseti' indicates the state of having reached strength by repeatedly lying latent in the mental continuum. If the word 'uppajjati' were to indicate that same state, there would be no special meaning, and the Chapter on Arising would not need to be stated. In fact, the word 'uppajjati' indicates the fitness for arising. Why? Because the fitness for arising is shown by the Chapter on Arising.
143:
Since its suitability for arising is shown, the term 'anusaya' is used to prevent the meaning of 'lying' as something always present without being produced by causes, and to show the intended meaning of 'lying' as the state of having reached strength due to the suitability for arising. Thus, it is said: "'Anusenti' means they arise upon obtaining a suitable cause." This statement, expressing the suitability for arising, is well-said; this is the meaning. This statement is also well-said because of these three canonical authorities (tanti); this is how it is connected. Indeed, by the collection of the three canonical texts, the state of being associated with consciousness is also shown.

## The Description of the Section on the Delimitation of the Divisions is Finished.

## Description of the Section on the Place of Arising

In the Commentary, regarding the phrase "in the two feelings in the sense element (kāmadhātu)," the word 'kāmadhātu' is stated as a qualifier for the two feelings, namely pleasant feeling (sukhavedanā) and equanimous feeling (upekkhāvedanā). If this is so, the state of the sense element being the base for the latent tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) would not be stated. However, among the two types of lust, the state of the lust for existence (bhavarāga) residing in the three elements—the fine-material element (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial element (arūpadhātu)—has been taught. Therefore, the state of the sense element being the base for sensual lust should also be taught. Indeed, the base for the latent tendencies has been shown in three ways: by way of element (dhātu), feeling (vedanā), and all that is included in the embodiment (sakkāyapariyāpanna).

Therefore, among the three elements, it is in the sense element; and among the three feelings, it is in the two feelings. Thus, the element and the feelings should be separately associated as the base, stating that "the latent tendency to sensual lust resides here in this sense element and these two feelings." This phrase "in the two feelings" is also stated only for the purpose of preventing the state of residing in all three feelings, implying that when it resides in feelings, it resides only in two, not in three. Therefore, there is no latent tendency to sensual lust that reaches the state of residing in all two feelings [in every instance]; thus, there is no special purpose in using the word 'kāmadhātu' to qualify the feeling. Indeed, it is clear that the base for the latent tendency to lust for existence, the supramundane states which are not the base for latent tendencies, and the latent tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) are not the base for the latent tendency to sensual lust. Just as when "in the two feelings" is stated, the two feelings other than the base for the latent tendency to aversion are taken, so too are those two feelings other than the base for the latent tendency to lust for existence taken.

In this context, the latent tendency to sensual lust, arising in other desirable forms and pleasant objects (piyarūpa sātarūpa) such as agreeable sights associated with the two feelings, proceeds by way of longing for pleasant physical and calm mental happiness. Therefore, its residing in the two feelings is stated. In other states...
144:
Indeed, even when that latent tendency to sensual lust arises in other things associated with pleasant and equanimous feelings, and in other desirable and pleasant objects such as agreeable forms, it resides only by following those two feelings. It only longs, saying, "It is indeed pleasant." In this way, the latent tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also arises in other things associated with painful feeling (dukkhavedanā) and in other disagreeable and unpleasant objects such as disagreeable forms; yet, because of the repulsiveness of pain, it is afflicted only as "It is indeed painful," and thus resides only by following painful feeling. Therefore, it is said that the latent tendency to aversion resides in that painful feeling.

By thus teaching that sensual lust and aversion reside in the three feelings, the arising of sensual lust and aversion is shown when desirable, neutral, and undesirable objects are grasped as 'desirable' etc., either by the nature of the object or by the power of perverted perception (viparītasaññā). Indeed, those latent tendencies arising in those objects are said to reside in the three feelings. Alternatively, the grasping of desirable objects etc. here should be understood through the medium of the three feelings. By grasping the sense element (kāmadhātu) etc., the grasping of the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) etc., which are the bases for the enjoyment of sensuality, should be understood.

Among those three elements and three feelings, when the latent tendency to sensual lust resides by way of enjoyment of existence, it resides in the sense element. When it resides by way of enjoyment of sensual pleasure, it resides in pleasant and equanimous feelings. Since aversion proceeds only by way of striking against pain, even when it strikes against various painful feelings, associated states, or undesirable objects, it resides only in painful feeling. In fine-material existence and immaterial existence, and in fine-material and immaterial states, there is no occurrence of the enjoyment of sensuality; therefore, the lust residing in those existences should be known only as "lust for existence" (bhavarāga).

By taking the three elements and the three feelings, all mundane states included in the embodiment (sakkāya) are taken. Therefore, in the answers of the Yamaka such as, "Where the latent tendency to sensual lust does not reside, does the latent tendency to wrong view (diṭṭhānusaya) not reside there?", it should be understood that the base for the latent tendency to wrong view etc., which is free from the three elements and three feelings, is not stated.

If it is objected: In one who produces longing for the peerless deliverances (Magga and Phala), the latent tendency to aversion does not reside in the displeasure (domanassa) arisen because of that longing. Similarly, in the joy (somanassa) and equanimity (upekkhā) based on renunciation (nekkhamma), the latent tendency to sensual lust should not reside.
