Therefore, are there not sense-sphere feelings that are the base for the latent tendency to wrong view, other than the base for that latent tendency to sensual lust?

Let it be so; however, there is no base for the residence of that wrong view etc. other than the three elements and the three feelings. Therefore, that [feeling based on renunciation] was not stated. Because it is said [in the Yamaka]: "Where the latent tendency to sensual lust, the latent tendency to aversion, and the latent tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) do not reside, does the latent tendency to wrong view and the latent tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya) not reside there? Yes (Amantā)," it should be understood that painful feeling is stated as the base for the latent tendency to aversion in a general sense, taken collectively. Likewise, mundane pleasant and equanimous feelings are the base for the latent tendency to sensual lust and the latent tendency to conceit.
145:
Alternatively, in the Suttanta Pāḷi, it is stated: "When shall I be able to abandon this displeasure (domanassa)?" Reflecting thus, that monk abandons aversion (paṭigha) through such reflection; in that displeasure, the latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) does not lie latent. This was spoken with reference to the total eradication of aversion by the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga), having produced displeasure based on renunciation (nekkhamma-sita domanassa), and having dispelled it by making an effort. For there is no such thing as abandoning aversion by aversion itself, or abandoning displeasure by displeasure itself. However, because it is the place where aversion arises, it should be understood that in this Anusaya Yamaka, all painful feelings (dukkha-vedanā) are called the "place where the latent tendency of aversion lies latent." This Yamaka teaching is a direct teaching (nippariyāya-desanā), whereas that Suttanta teaching is a figurative teaching (pariyāya-desanā).

For this very reason, with reference to the total eradication by the Path of Non-returning of the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) which is dispelled by the first jhāna, it is stated: "Secluded from sensual pleasures... he enters and dwells in the first jhāna; by that first jhāna, he abandons lust (rāga); therein the latent tendency of lust (rāgānusaya) does not lie latent." Similarly, with reference to the total eradication by the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga) of the latent tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya) which is dispelled by the fourth jhāna, it is stated: "With the abandoning of pleasure... he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; by that fourth jhāna, he abandons ignorance (avijja); therein the latent tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya) does not lie latent." This is because it cannot be said that the latent tendency of ignorance does not lie latent in all aspects within the equanimous feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) of the mundane fourth jhāna, as it is stated: "In all states included within the identity (sakkāya), this latent tendency of ignorance lies latent." Therefore, just as the equanimity of the fourth jhāna is the basis (vatthu) for the latent tendency of ignorance, it is not that displeasure based on renunciation is not the basis for the latent tendency of aversion (it indeed is); thus, it should be understood that those latent tendencies lie latent there as well. It is because it is not a basis by its inherent nature that lying latent is not mentioned in this Yamaka; it is not mentioned because of its being the opposite of those latent tendencies in the manner stated in the Suttas, and because of its being a powerful decisive support (balavūpanissaya) for the Path that can totally eradicate those latent tendencies.

In showing these places of latent tendencies, when the object is the place of lying latent, it cannot be said that all greed (lobha) excluding the lust for existence (bhavarāga) is the latent tendency of sensual lust. This is because greed associated with the latent tendency of views (diṭṭhānusaya) lying latent in painful feelings and in the fine-material and immaterial realms is merely greed, and not the latent tendency of sensual lust. If it were so, its place would have to be stated just like the place of the latent tendency of views. However, it is called the place of lying latent because of the inclination towards those states by way of disposition (ajjhāsaya). For example, in one who repeatedly contemplates the non-attainment of naturally pleasant objects such as visible forms, or in one who repeatedly contemplates that which was previously attained but has ceased, vanished, and changed, the aversion that arises occurs only by way of striking against pain; therefore, only pain is called the place where that aversion lies latent, not the object. Thus, in pain and so forth...
146:
Greed associated with the latent tendency of views (diṭṭhānusaya) arising by way of adherence (abhinivesa) also occurs only by way of attachment to pleasure; therefore, only the two types of happiness—pleasant happiness (sāta-sukha) and peaceful happiness (santa-sukha)—are called the place of lying latent (anusayaṭṭhāna) for that greed. This does not contradict the fact that all greed, excluding the lust for existence (bhavarāga), is the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya). Even towards the same object, some feel attachment while others feel anger (destruction). Between those two, because lust has a desire for pleasure and aversion has a desire for pain, the places where those latent tendencies of sensual lust and aversion lie latent are different.

For this reason, it was said (in the Yamaka): "Where the latent tendency of sensual lust lies latent, does the latent tendency of aversion lie latent there? No." In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, after describing the arising of displeasure (domanassa) towards the two feelings (pleasure and equanimity) and towards pleasant objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa), it is stated: "That arising is merely displeasure, not the latent tendency of aversion." Therefore, just as aversion in that context is not the latent tendency of aversion, it should be understood that greed arising together with the latent tendency of views in pain and so forth is not the latent tendency of sensual lust. In the phrase "that arising is merely displeasure, not the latent tendency of aversion," the meaning of "not the latent tendency of aversion" should be understood as "the latent tendency of aversion does not exist." This is because there is no reason to suspect displeasure of being the latent tendency of aversion.

That the teaching might seem confused means it would be as if the arising of the lust for existence was also stated by way of taking the two feelings in the sense-sphere as objects. Therefore, the intention is that this teaching was given for the purpose of showing the distinction by way of the specific object, because there is no distinction in the associated feelings.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Place of Arising is finished.

## The Great Section (Mahāvāra)

## 1. Explanation of the Section on Latent Tendencies (Anusayavāra)

The present-tense terms "anuseti" (lies latent) or "uppajjati" (arises) should be understood by way of uninterrupted occurrence (pavattāvirāma). For the cessation and cutting off of the latent tendencies occurs only by the Path, and not before that.

In the statement "They do not arise in one place, nor do they take one state as an object," there is this distinction: the former phrase prohibits arising in a single thought-moment (cittuppāda), while the latter phrase prohibits taking a single object. In the reverse (paṭiloma) of the Section on Persons and Locations (Puggalokāsavāra), regarding those various...
147:
The non-occurrence of various latent tendencies (anusaya) in various individuals should be understood both by nature and by abandonment. "For three types of individuals, the latent tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) does not underlie them in painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā), but it is not that the latent tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya) does not underlie them there (it does). For those same individuals, in the fine-material element (rūpadhātu), the immaterial element (arūpadhātu), and the supramundane (apariyāpanna), both the latent tendency of sensual lust and the latent tendency of aversion do not underlie them." This was stated with reference to the non-occurrence of sensual lust and so on in painful feeling and so on by nature. "For two types of individuals, both the latent tendency of sensual lust and the latent tendency of aversion do not underlie them in all objects." This was stated by way of the abandonment of latent tendencies. Here, in the former method, the non-occurrence of latent tendencies existing in an individual is stated with regard to the basis (okāsa). In the latter method, the state of being a non-basis for latent tendencies in the fine-material sphere and so on is stated with regard to the individual.

## End of the Commentary on the Section on Latent Tendencies (Anusayavāra).

## 2. Commentary on the Section on Those Possessed of Latent Tendencies (Sānusayavāra)

66-131. In the sections on those possessed of latent tendencies (sānusayavāra), abandoning (pajahanavāra), and full understanding (pariññāvāra), the individual is spoken of as "one possessed of latent tendencies, one who abandons, one who fully understands." For an individual, there is no such thing as being possessed or not possessed of latent tendencies by way of a specific existence, such as "one is possessed of latent tendencies in this existence," or by way of a specific existence and latent tendency, such as "one is possessed of latent tendencies by way of the latent tendency of sensual lust in this existence, and by way of some other latent tendency in that existence." Likewise, in the two feelings, the point that "one is possessed of latent tendencies by way of the latent tendency of sensual lust, but is free from latent tendencies in painful feeling" does not exist. This is because feeling is not the basis (okāsa) for the individual, but rather the basis for the latent tendencies. The respective basis where a latent tendency underlies serves as the cause (nimitta) for the individual being possessed of that respective latent tendency, and for the abandoning and full understanding of that respective latent tendency. The basis where it does not underlie is the cause for the state of being free from latent tendencies and so on. Therefore, in the sections on basis (okāsavāra), the ablative case (nissakkavacana) is used in the sense of cause as "from which, from that" (yato tato), instead of indicating with the locative case (sattami-vibhatti). Alternatively, in the sections on abandoning and full understanding, it is used only in the sense of removal (apādāna). This is because the act of removal from those respective bases and destruction is what constitutes abandoning and full understanding.

In that context (okāsavāra), "yato" means "because of which basis where latent tendencies underlie" in the forward order (anuloma), and "because of which basis where latent tendencies do not underlie" in the reverse order (paṭiloma). Only of the underlying and non-underlying of latent tendencies...
148:
To show the state of being a cause (nimitta) and a source (apādāna), in such Pāḷi passages as: "From the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere, one is possessed of latent tendencies there by way of the latent tendency of conceit (mānānusaya)" and "one abandons"; and "From painful feeling, one is free from latent tendencies there as the latent tendency of sensual lust does not exist" and "one does not abandon"; the fine-material sphere and so on are indicated only by way of locative indication (bhummaniddesa).

In the Commentary, however, since the basis for the underlying of latent tendencies is shown specifically by the answer to the fourth question, and to clarify this meaning that "yato" refers to the basis of underlying even in the initial question of that same context, it is stated: "One is possessed of latent tendencies by way of the arisen (uppanna) latent tendency of sensual lust." This statement seems as if it were written inadvertently. This is because one is not possessed of latent tendencies only by way of an anusaya that is currently arisen (uppanna), and it is not possible to use the ablative case (nissakkavacana) solely with reference to a basis that is suitable for the arising of latent tendencies. It is clear that supramundane (apariyāpanna) states are not bases suitable for the arising of latent tendencies.

In this matter, the meaning should be understood as follows: "yato uppannena" means by way of the latent tendency that would arise (is liable to arise) because of that basis of underlying. The ablative case is used for that which is liable to arise. Likewise, in the phrase "sabbadhammesu uppajjanakena," since the prohibition of arising is not made and non-arising is not intended, it is called the removal of the state of non-arising by way of the latent tendency that has reached the state of being able to arise in all phenomena. Regarding the term "sabbattha," the meaning "from all bases of latent tendencies" is not impossible. This is because grammarians allow the suffix "ttha" to be used in senses other than the locative (such as the ablative sense).

## End of the Commentary on the Section on Those Possessed of Latent Tendencies (Sānusayavāra).

## 3. Commentary on the Section on Abandoning (Pajahanavāra)

132-197. In the section on abandoning (pajahanavāra), it should not be stated as a definitive conclusion (sanniṭṭhāna) that an individual who abandons the latent tendency of sensual lust and so on with a remainder is "abandoning" them, because the latent tendencies that have not yet been abandoned are still present. Therefore, in the concluding term (sanniṭṭhānapada), only one who abandons without remainder is said to "abandon" (pajahati). Thus, it is stated: "Does one who abandons the latent tendency of conceit abandon the latent tendency of sensual lust? No." However, since the term of doubt (saṃsayapada) asks merely about the act of abandoning and does not make a definitive conclusion, it is stated with reference to whatever abandoning is evident: "Does one who abandons the latent tendency of sensual lust abandon the latent tendency of conceit? He abandons (some conceit) residing in that same individual." In the reverse order (paṭiloma), the state of not abandoning is expressed by both the concluding term and the term of doubt with the word "does not abandon"...
149:
Because it has been decided by the statement of conclusion (sanniṭṭhāna) and questioned by the statement of doubt (saṃsaya), among those who abandon without remainder, excluding those who do not abandon completely, it is said that the remaining ones "do not abandon" precisely because of the presence of unabandoned latent tendencies. It should be understood that it is not said that only those who are devoid of abandonment by the manifest Path [do not abandon].

In the Anusaya Yamaka Pali, which states: "Excluding the person possessed of the path of non-returning and the eighth person, the remaining persons do not abandon the latent tendency of sensual lust and do not abandon the latent tendency of doubt," the Commentary states: "The worldling (puthujjana) does not abandon because of the absence of full understanding as abandonment (pahānapariññā); the remaining [persons do not abandon] because those latent tendencies have already been abandoned."

In that commentary, although it is true that for some persons the latent tendency of doubt has been abandoned and for others both have been abandoned, so that for the remaining persons those latent tendencies are indeed abandoned, the fact that the latent tendency of doubt has been abandoned for Stream-enterers and others is not the reason for not abandoning both. Therefore, it cannot be said that they "do not abandon" because they have abandoned them. However, this is said to show the inclusion of those persons by the statement of conclusion, "they also do not abandon the latent tendency of sensual lust." Thus, there is no need to provide a reason for that conclusion; a reason is only required for the meaning of the doubt being questioned.

If it is asked, "In that case, should it not be said in the singular, 'because the remaining ones have abandoned that latent tendency'?" The answer is: it should not be so stated. This is because the reason must be given with reference to the latent tendency of wrong view and the latent tendency of doubt, which are questioned with a similar answer after rejecting with: "Whoever does not abandon the latent tendency of sensual lust, does that person not abandon the latent tendency of wrong view and the latent tendency of doubt?" Therefore, "because those latent tendencies have been abandoned" means that because those latent tendencies of wrong view and doubt have been abandoned, they do not abandon the latent tendencies included in the sense of the doubt. This is how the meaning should be understood.

## The Explanation of the Section on Abandoning (Pajahanavāra-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Section on What is Abandoned (Pahīnavāra-vaṇṇanā)

264-274. In the Section on What is Abandoned (Pahīnavāra), the statement that the teaching is begun only by way of those established in fruition (phalaṭṭha) is said with reference to the forward order (anuloma). This is because in the reverse order (paṭiloma), the teaching is also taken by way of the worldling (puthujjana). By the word "only" (eva) in the phrase "only by way of those established in fruition," it shows that those possessed of the path (maggasamaṅgī) are not included. For those possessed of the path, who have a single thought-moment that is the absolute opposite of the latent tendencies, no latent tendency is fit to arise, nor have they yet been brought to the state of being unfit to arise. Therefore, those persons on the path (maggasamaṅgī) are not included in the sections on latent tendency (anusaya), having latent tendency (sānusaya), what is abandoned (pahīna), and arising (uppajjana).
150:
275-296. In the Section on Occasion (Okāsavāra), when a particular latent tendency is brought to the state of non-arising in its own respective base (okāsa), it is said to be "abandoned" (pahīna). If it has not yet been brought to that state of non-arising, it is said to be "not abandoned" (appahīna). These terms "abandoned" and "not abandoned" indicate only the base (okāsa) of that latent tendency. Therefore, in a place that is not the base [of that tendency], because it is not appropriate to say either of those two, it is said to be "inexpressible" (avattabba). The statement that "it is abandoned together with that [sensual lust] in a common place" means it is abandoned in the same base as that latent tendency of sensual lust, not that it is abandoned at the same time.

## The Explanation of the Section on What is Abandoned (Pahīnavāra-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Section on Elements (Dhātuvāra-vaṇṇanā)

332-340. In the Section on Elements (Dhātuvāra), the phrase "they lie latent following the continuum (santāna)" means that as long as they are not abandoned in a certain continuum of aggregates, they follow that continuum in the state of being unabandoned and lie latent in a state of being fit to arise. Because they have the possibility of arising, the meaning that they arise when they obtain suitable causes is also appropriate here. In this Section on Elements, the six prohibitive statements (paṭinisedha) such as "sensual element" (kāmadhātu) etc., do not serve to single out the specific characteristics of the elements. When it is said, "for one who has passed away from the sensual element and does not reappear in the sensual element," etc., it is not known in which element one reappears. Therefore, in the formulations (yojanā) based on that sensual element, one first connects it as: "for one who has passed away from the sensual element and reappears in the sensual element, the fine-material element, or the immaterial element," and then subsequently the formulation is made as: "for one who does not reappear in the sensual element," etc. Only in this way is it understood that only the aforementioned elements are taken by the terms "not the sensual element" (na kāmadhātu), etc., and not just any [element].

Although in the Section on Latent Tendencies (Anusayavāra), the term "they lie latent" (anusenti) was taken with the meaning "they arise" (uppajjanti), it is not possible to take "they arise" there with reference only to what is presently arising. This is because of the statements such as: "For whom the latent tendency of sensual lust lies latent, does the latent tendency of aversion lie latent for him? Yes," etc. However, if the meaning "they arise" is taken with reference to the state of not being abandoned, that meaning is not inappropriate here in this Section on Elements; it is indeed appropriate.

"Bhaṅgā" means those that are to be divided or made into two parts. Is it not the case that there is no latent tendency that can be made into two parts—as both lying latent and not lying latent—for one arising in a certain element? Why then are the question and answer made: "How many latent tendencies are divisions (bhaṅgā)? There are no latent tendencies that are divisions"? Indeed, is it not inappropriate to have a doubt when there is no other alternative?
151:
Is it appropriate? It is not inappropriate; it is indeed appropriate. This is because if it were not stated that "there is no dissolution (bhaṅga) for the underlying tendencies (anusaya)," the absence of dissolution would not be known.

## The Explanation of the Section on Elements (Dhātuvāra-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## The Explanation of the Pairs of Underlying Tendencies (Anusayayamaka-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## 8. The Pairs of Consciousness (Cittayamaka)

## Explanation of the Section on Enumeration (Uddesavāra-vaṇṇanā)

1-62. In the explanation of the Pairs of Consciousness, it is stated that there are three pure great cycles (suddhika-mahāvāra) at the very beginning. This means that these three great cycles consist of mixed cycles (missakavāra) which are combined with terms such as "with lust" (sarāga) and "wholesome" (kusala), as well as pure cycles (suddhika) which are not mixed with terms like "with lust." Among these, it is understood that the pure cycles come first. In the mixed cycles, there are three great cycles for each consciousness mixed with lust and so forth. The statement "Sixteen Personal Cycles" (soḷasa-puggalavāra) and so forth is made by aggregating those persons mentioned in various places; it is not a continuous exposition. Because each question arises through the combination of arising (uppāda) and cessation (nirodha) with the present and future times, such as "If the consciousness of a person is arising and not ceasing, will the consciousness of that person cease and not arise?", it is called the "Cycle of the Combination of Arising, Cessation, and Time" (uppāda-nirodha-kāla-sambheda-vāra). In this same manner, the names of the remaining cycles should also be understood according to the sequence of the Pali text.

## The Explanation of the Section on Enumeration is finished.

## Explanation of the Section on Exposition (Niddesavāra-vaṇṇanā)

Regarding the phrase "referring to the consciousness of such an Arahant," it should be understood that when a person who possesses the last consciousness (pacchimacitta) at the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa) is intended, it is spoken with that very consciousness in mind. The phrase "the last consciousness of the Arahant also" is spoken referring only to the person who possesses the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa), characterized as "does not arise, but ceases."

65-82. In the explanation of the second question of the Section on Arising (uppādavāra), at the moment of dissolution of consciousness, for those who have entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpanna), and for non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), their consciousness has arisen, but their consciousness...
152:
In this context of "is arising," the meaning of the commentary "at the moment of dissolution of consciousness, their consciousness has arisen" is stated as: "Because the consciousness of all beings is only in the present moment (khana-paccuppanna) and the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa) has passed, it is said to 'have arisen'." In the commentary "at the moment of arising of consciousness, their consciousness has both arisen and is arising," it cannot be said in both ways that it "has arisen" because it has reached arising, and "is arising" because it has not yet passed. Indeed, in the present moment, the past term "has arisen" (uppajjittha) does not exist. If it were to exist, then in the question "Or else, if a consciousness has arisen, is that consciousness arising?", one would have to answer by distinguishing rather than saying "No." Similarly, in the question "If a consciousness is arising, has that consciousness arisen?", one would have to say "Yes" (āmantā) rather than "No."

In fact, by the Pali "at the moment of dissolution of consciousness," a person possessing a mind that is currently breaking up is meant; that person's past consciousness has arisen, but no consciousness is currently arising. By the Pali "at the moment of arising of consciousness," a person possessing a mind that is currently arising is meant; that person's past consciousness has also arisen, and that specific consciousness is currently arising. Thus should the meaning be understood here. For the general term "consciousness" (citta) can apply to a single specific consciousness or to many, depending on how it is taken. In the passage "Or else, if the consciousness of a person will arise, is the consciousness of that person arising? At the moment of dissolution of consciousness," the rule should be understood everywhere by the power of the premise (sanniṭṭhāna), such as "at the moment of dissolution of the consciousness of only that person who is taken by the premise 'whose consciousness will arise'." The "Cycle of What has Arisen and is Arising" (uppannuppajjamānavāra) and the "Cycle of What has Ceased and is Ceasing" (niruddhanirujjamānavāra) have been shown briefly and in detail without distinction even in the three cycles such as the Personal Cycle (puggalavāra). Among those three cycles, in the Personal Cycle, phrases like "has arisen, is arising" are spoken referring to any such person without distinction; in the Cycle of Phenomena (dhammavāra), only consciousness is spoken of; in the Cycle of Persons and Phenomena (puggaladhammavāra), both the person and the consciousness are spoken of. This distinction should be noted here.

In the Cycle of the Past Time (atikkantakālavāra), because this cycle is a Personal Cycle, the person is questioned; therefore, the answer must relate to the person only. It is not that any person is not taken by the premise "whose consciousness has arisen" (i.e., all are taken); similarly, it is not that any person is not taken by the premise "whose consciousness is the past time, having passed the moment of arising moment by moment." Indeed, there is no person whose consciousness has not passed the moment of arising, and it is not that they do not have consciousness that has passed the moment of dissolution. Therefore, the first problem should be answered as "Yes" (āmantā); likewise the second and third problems. As for the fourth problem, it should be answered: "At the moment of dissolution of the last consciousness, their consciousness has not passed the moment of dissolution, it is not that their consciousness has not passed the moment of arising; for other persons, their consciousness has not passed the moment of dissolution and has not passed the moment of arising." Why, instead of answering thus, is only consciousness mentioned in all places...
153:
Why did the Blessed One analyze only the mind? It is because the person is defined through the power of the mind. Specifically, by the statement that there is a past time because the arising moment (uppāda-kkhaṇa) has passed, a person is described as one whose mind has passed the arising moment by the power of the mind that is currently occurring (at the dissolution moment). Regarding the past mind, among those two types of persons, the mind of the former has not yet passed the dissolution moment (bhaṅga-kkhaṇa), while the mind of the latter has passed the dissolution moment, and so on. Such classification of persons is the definition of a person through the power of a certain mind. Since the classification of the person is shown by demonstrating the passing or non-passing of those various moments of that mind, the mind alone is analyzed in all answers.

Alternatively, in this section (on past time), the question is not about a person distinguished merely by the Dhamma, but rather about the mind distinguished by the person. Therefore, it should be understood that only the mind is answered. Even if the question focuses on the person, it is still primarily focused on the mind. In both ways, although "Yes" (Āmantā) should have been said in the second question, it was not said so. Instead, "the past mind" (atītaṃ cittaṃ) was said to show that being in the past due to passing the dissolution moment is not the same as being in the past due to passing the arising moment in a currently occurring mind. In the phrase "one whose mind is not arising" (yassa cittaṃ na uppajjamānaṃ), it means a person who does not have a mind whose past time has passed the moment of arising. The same method applies to the phrase "not ceasing" (na nirujjhamānaṃ).

114-116. In the Mixed Sections (Missaka-vāra), the question "If the mind with lust (sarāga) of a person is arising but not ceasing, will the mind of that person cease but not arise?" and the answer "No" (No) are shown in the Commentary. However, in the Pali Canon, because it is stated in the matrix (mātikā) as "If the mind with lust of a person is arising but not ceasing, will the mind with lust of that person cease but not arise?", the question is extracted in the answer according to the power of the mixed mind such as "with lust" in both the definitive and doubtful senses. It should be understood as being abbreviated because the answer is mostly similar to the Pure Section (Suddhika-vāra), such as: "At the arising moment of the final mind with lust, the mind with lust of those persons is arising but not ceasing, it will cease and it will not arise; at the arising moment of the mind with lust of other persons, the mind with lust of those persons is arising but not ceasing, it will cease and it will also arise."

## The Explanation of the Section of Designation (Niddesa-vāra) is finished.

## The Explanation of the Pairs of Mind (Citta-yamaka) is finished.

## 9. Dhamma-yamaka (Pairs of Phenomena)

## 1. Paṇṇatti-vāra (Section of Designation)

## Explanation of the Uddesa-vāra (Section of Synopsis)

1-16. In the opening of the Dhamma-yamaka, the phrase 'having set forth the matrix of phenomena such as the wholesome' (kusalādidhammānaṃ mātikaṃ ṭhapetvā) means: unlike the way wholesome and other phenomena were taught in the Mūla-yamaka, and unlike the way they were taught by grouping them differently such as 'the five aggregates' (pañcakkhandhā) in the Khandha-yamaka and others, here the matrix of wholesome and other phenomena starting with 'wholesome and unwholesome phenomena' (kusalākusala dhammā) is placed at the beginning of this Dhamma-yamaka and taught. This is the meaning.

## The Explanation of the Uddesa-vāra is finished.

## 2. Pavatti-vāra (Section of Occurrence)

33-34. In the answer to the question 'For whom wholesome phenomena arise, do indeterminate phenomena arise for him?', the Commentary states that 'indeterminate phenomena also (arise)' is said by the power of mind-produced matter (citta-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa). In this problem, matter such as kamma-produced matter (kamma-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa) can also be obtained. However, in the answer to the negative-reverse section (paccanika-paṭiloma-vāra), for all those who are passing away, at the dissolution moment of the mind during the course of existence (pavatti), and at the arising moment of unwholesome states in the formless realm (arūpa), it is stated that 'wholesome phenomena do not arise for them, and indeterminate phenomena do not arise for them.' Since this is stated without taking kamma-produced matter and others that are currently arising at the dissolution moment of the mind during the course of existence, only mind-produced matter is intended here. Some teachers (such as Dhamma-sirī) say that regarding matter such as kamma-produced matter, there is neither prescription nor prohibition. Similarly, intending only mind-produced matter, it is stated: 'For whom wholesome phenomena arise, do indeterminate phenomena cease for him? No.' This statement cannot be said in this way, because the prohibition of the arising of kamma-produced matter and others at the dissolution moment of the mind, and their cessation at the arising moment, is established by these very Pali texts.

Other teachers (such as Vajira-buddhi) say: 'In the Discourse on Cessation (Nirodha-kathā) of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, it should be understood as taught (by Venerable Sāriputta) that "excluding mind-produced matter, all phenomena arising at the moment of the path of stream-entry are both dispassionate (virāga) and have dispassion as their object (virāgārammaṇa), have dispassion as their range (virāgagocara), are originated from dispassion (virāgasamudāgata), and are established in dispassion (virāgapatiṭṭha)." In such passages, instead of saying "excluding matter" in general, it is said "excluding mind-produced matter" because it is connected with the mind. Similarly, in this Dhamma-yamaka, the Blessed One taught only mind-produced matter because it is connected with the mind.' This statement also cannot be possible in that manner. The reason is that for those mind-produced matters...
155:
Regarding mind-produced matter (cittaja-rūpa), it is stated: "excluding mind-originated matter" (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa). In this context, some (such as the Elder Vajirabuddhi) say that it refers only to mind-produced matter because it is connected with the mind. That statement is not so. The reason is that for those to whom the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) serves as a conascent condition (sahajāta-paccaya), and for those in whom there might be doubt regarding the arising of dispassion (virāga), etc., those states arising together with the Path of Stream-entry are taught in that (Paṭisambhidāmagga) as "states arisen at the moment of the Path of Stream-entry."

The phrase "arisen at the moment of the Path of Stream-entry" indicates being produced by the Path. Matter born of kamma (kammaja-rūpa), etc., which are produced by non-path factors, do not deserve the designation "arisen at the moment of the Path," because they do not have the Path of Stream-entry as a conascent condition at that moment. Therefore, in order to exclude what should be excluded (mind-produced matter) from the states arising together with the Path at the moment of the Path, it is stated: "excluding mind-originated matter."

In this (Dhammayamaka), however, for whichever person in whichever plane wholesome states, etc., arise and cease, the arising and ceasing of indeterminate (abyākata) states for that person in that location are considered, whether they are connected with wholesome states or not. Matter born of kamma, etc., are also not non-indeterminate (they are indeed indeterminate). Therefore, if there is arising and ceasing in the plane of the person taken by the thesis (sanniṭṭhāna), those indeterminate states should be known; if not, they should be negated. It cannot be said that indeterminate states not connected with the mind are not included here, because the arising and ceasing of those in the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) are taught.

In the fourth question, the phrase "at the moment of arising of unwholesome and indeterminate consciousness in the course of existence" (pavatte akusalābyākatacittassa uppādakkhaṇe) is stated with reference to those endowed with the moment of arising of unwholesome and indeterminate consciousness in the five-constituent plane (pañcavokāra), and those endowed only with the moment of arising of indeterminate consciousness in the four-constituent plane (catuvokāra), as taken by the thesis "or else, for whom indeterminate states arise" (yassa vā pana abyākatā dhammā uppajjanti). Thus, in all places, the distinction should be understood by the power of the thesis.

Even if it is said "arisen through a single adverting" (ekāvajjana), this characteristic—"unwholesome states will not arise for them, but it is not that wholesome states are not arising for them"—is indeed obtainable at the moment of arising of wholesome consciousness produced by various advertings in the impulsion processes (javana-vīthi) prior to that (Path process). Therefore, all (wholesome consciousness) having a characteristic similar to this characteristic should be understood as already shown by the very end of the future state of the wholesome (vodāna), namely, "at the moment of arising of that consciousness immediately after which they will attain the Path of Arahatship," because of having that same similar characteristic.

This same method applies to the places where it is stated "in the second unwholesome consciousness" and "in the second consciousness" at the beginning of the past state of the unwholesome and the past state of the indeterminate. Just as in the section on cultivation (bhāvanāvāra),
156:
by the final Path of Arahatship, the states to be abandoned by cultivation prior to that Path of Arahatship are also shown. Thus, in this Pavattivāra, those various states are shown by their respective beginnings and ends.

According to the statement "at the moment of dissolution of unwholesome states in the five-constituent plane, for them unwholesome states cease and indeterminate states also cease," it should be understood that the sixteenth consciousness from the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) occurs, and thereafter the consciousness of attachment to existence (bhavanikanti-citta) occurs; the consciousness of attachment to existence does not occur at a time prior to that.

## End of the Commentary on the Occurrence Chapter (Pavattivāra).
## End of the Commentary on the Book of Pairs of States (Dhammayamaka).
## 10. Indriyayamaka (Book of Pairs of Faculties)
## 1. Paṇṇattivāra (Chapter on Designation)
## Commentary on the Uddesavāra (Section on Enumeration)

In the Indriyayamaka, as in the Indriyavibhaṅga, the life faculty (jīvitindriya) is not indicated immediately after the mind faculty (manindriya), but is indicated after the masculinity faculty (purisindriya), following the order taught in the Sutta: "Monks, these are the three faculties. Which three? The femininity faculty, the masculinity faculty, and the life faculty" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.492). The reason is that in the Pavattivāra, the life faculty protects the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya), etc., which arise exclusively during the course of existence (pavatti) and are both kamma-born and non-kamma-born. It also protects those born of kamma that occur at the moments of death and rebirth-linking. Therefore, it should be understood that the pairs (yamaka) rooted in that life faculty should be stated in connection with the moments of death, rebirth-linking, and the course of existence. Among the faculties beginning with the eye faculty and ending with the masculinity faculty, the mind faculty is not a root at all. Excluding that mind faculty, the remaining yamaka rooted in the eye faculty, etc., should be stated only by way of death and rebirth, as in the Āyatanayamaka. Therefore, the life faculty is not indicated in the middle of those beginning with the eye faculty, but is indicated at the end.

## End of the Commentary on the Uddesavāra.
## Commentary on the Niddesavāra (Section on Exposition)

In the phrase "woman, femininity faculty" (itthi itthindriya), because there is no ultimate reality (paramattha-sabhāva) called "woman," and yet it is not that the designation "woman" does not occur based on states such as matter (rūpa), etc., (it indeed occurs), therefore, of the designation "woman"...
157:
Even though it is not manifest, because it occurs by taking it as if it were manifest, it was stated as "No" (no) instead of saying "It does not exist" (natthi) by virtue of that which is so taken (the female). By making a distinction of pleasure as "pleasure (sukha) and joy (somanassa)" and a distinction of pain as "pain (dukkha) and grief (domanassa)", the distinction is already taken that the pleasant feeling other than joy is called 'pleasure', and the painful feeling other than grief is called 'pain'. Therefore, in this context of "Is pleasure the pleasure-faculty? Is pain the pain-faculty?", it was stated as "Yes" (āmantā).

In the section on the pure faculties (Suddhindriyavāra), in the context of "Is the eye the eye-faculty?", it was stated as "Yes" (āmantā) because the divine-eye (dibba-cakkhu) and the wisdom-eye (paññā-cakkhu) are indeed the wisdom-faculty (paññindriya). By the remaining word "stream" (sota), it refers only to the stream of craving (taṇhā-sota).

## The Explanation of the Niddesavāra is concluded.

## 2. Explanation of the Pavattivāra

In the Pavattivāra (Section on Occurrence), the mind-faculty (manindriya) shown here by way of the method stated in the Sutta of the Saṃyutta Nikāya: "Monks, there are these six faculties. Which six? The eye-faculty... pe... the body-faculty, the mind-faculty," is associated with all kamma-born and non-kamma-born [faculties] occurring at death (cuti), rebirth (paṭisandhi), and during the course of existence (pavatti). It is not to be taken as depending on other phenomena like the life-faculty (jīvitindriya); it is predominant simply because it is the precursor. Therefore, just as the roof-peak is the meeting point of the rafters, the mind-faculty, which is the meeting point of all faculties, is placed and joined at the end.

Regarding the answers that proceed by taking the period of occurrence (pavatti) with the life-faculty as the root: "For whom the life-faculty is arising, for him does the pleasure-faculty arise? For all those undergoing rebirth, and at the arising moment (uppādakkhaṇa) of a consciousness dissociated from the pleasure-faculty during the course of existence, for them the life-faculty is arising, but the pleasure-faculty is not arising for them. At the arising moment of a consciousness associated with the pleasure-faculty, for them both the life-faculty is arising and the pleasure-faculty is arising," and so on—the association with the pleasure, pain, and grief faculties, and with the supramundane faculties, is obtained. Likewise, the methods rooted in the pleasure-faculty, such as "For whom the pleasure-faculty is arising, for him does the pain-faculty arise? No," are also obtained. However, it should be understood that these were not stated because they are already clear through the association with the pleasure, pain, grief, and supramundane faculties occurring only during the course of existence, and through the methods rooted in those associations, as well as through the association with the joy-faculty (somanassindriya) etc. occurring at death, rebirth, and during the course of existence, and through the methods rooted in the life-faculty.
158:
In the Commentary, the statement "For those with eyes but without joy (somanassa)" is said by virtue of the four great resultant (mahāvipāka) rebirths accompanied by equanimity. This statement should be understood as being said by way of illustrating the rebirth of those who have eyes but are devoid of joy. A restriction such as "only the four" was not made; by that statement, the small resultant (paritta-vipāka/ahetuka) and fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) rebirths which have similar characteristics are also shown.

In that Commentary, among the sense-sphere rebirths, an illustration is made with the four great resultants because of their similarity to the rebirth accompanied by joy. By this illustration, it is shown that just as those with rebirth accompanied by joy are not without eyes, so too those with other great resultant (equanimity) rebirths are not without eyes. Among womb-born (gabbhaseyyaka) beings, the state of those with rootless rebirth (ahetuka-paṭisandhi) who pass away before the eye etc. have arisen is already shown by showing the state of sense-sphere beings with rooted rebirth (sahetuka-paṭisandhi) as always having eyes.

Indeed, even with reference to a womb-born being, the statement "For whom the joy-faculty (somanassindriya) arises, for him does the eye-faculty (cakkhundriya) arise? Yes (āmantā)" is shown in the Āyatana Yamaka in such a way that it is appropriate. This is because there is no reason to exclude womb-born beings who are included by the definitive term (sanniṭṭhāna); and in the Pali texts such as "For women, for those without the nose-faculty who are being reborn," those very womb-born beings are spoken of.

In the context of "For those without eyes, with equanimity," which is said by virtue of rootless rebirth (ahetuka-paṭisandhi), it should be understood that the equanimity-accompanied rootless rebirth in the sense-sphere also illustrates the immaterial-sphere (arūpa) rebirth which has similar characteristics. However, in some manuscripts, the reading "ahetukārūpapaṭisandhivasena" (by virtue of rootless and immaterial rebirth) is seen; that reading is indeed better.

It is stated: "Therein, certainly, faith (saddhā), mindfulness (sati), and wisdom (paññā) do not exist; but concentration (samādhi) and energy (vīriya) do not reach the status of faculties (indriya)." If concentration and energy were present, it would not be possible to say "they do not reach the status of faculties," because of the statements: "Is concentration the concentration-faculty? Yes," and "Is energy the energy-faculty? Yes." Just as there is a trace of concentration, namely one-pointedness (ekaggatā), in the rootless rebirth consciousness, there is no such trace of energy. Therefore, it should be stated here: "Therein, certainly, faith, energy, mindfulness, and wisdom do not exist; but one-pointedness is merely a trace of concentration."

In this context, the intention would be: just as in some other rootless consciousnesses, concentration and energy exist and reach the status of faculties, so here (in this rootless rebirth) concentration and energy do not reach the status of faculties. Wishing to show the very absence of the concentration and energy faculties, it is shown by distinguishing it from other rootless consciousnesses.
159:
It is distinguished from other rootless consciousnesses (mind-door adverting and the smile-producing consciousness). In the text, "But concentration and energy do not reach the status of faculties," although it could be said "But concentration and energy exist," the phrase "reach the status of faculties" is used because of the presence of one-pointedness (ekaggatā) which has not reached the state of the concentration faculty (samādhindriya), which is the enhancement of concentration; it is not said because of the absence of the enhancement of energy. For a qualifying attribute (visesana) applies only to the object to be qualified (visesya). In some books, there is the reading, "Therein, certainly, faith, energy, mindfulness, and wisdom do not exist"; that reading is indeed better.

With the intention that the state of being eyeless exists for those in the womb as long as the eye faculty has not yet arisen, it is said: "Root-accompanied eyeless persons are spoken of by way of those in the womb and by way of the formless beings." However, it should be noted that those in the womb are not included here because they will certainly have eyes that will arise. "Those with eyes who are dissociated from knowledge" is said by way of those with two-rooted rebirth in the sense sphere; and in this text, rootless eyeless persons with rebirth are also included. The arising of the female faculty continuum and the male faculty continuum in relation to rebirth, and their cessation in relation to death, are mostly shown. For sometimes, the arising and cessation of these female and male faculty continua occur even during the course of existence (pavatti), as in the case of the first beings of the aeon. In these Root Yamakas of the Faculties ending with the male faculty, because they are marked by the eye faculty etc. which arise by way of rebirth and death as taken by the antecedent (sanniṭṭhāna) in the first questions, it should be understood that the life faculty etc., although obtainable by way of the course of existence, are taken by the antecedent in the second questions only in connection with rebirth and death.

The physical life faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya) has a course similar to the eye faculty etc., and proceeds only by way of death and rebirth; because the arising and cessation of the continuum are seen, it is said that "at the moment of arising of a consciousness dissociated from joy during the course of existence" is spoken with reference to the mental life faculty (arūpa-jīvitindriya). In the phrase "by way of the availability of these life faculties etc. and the other five faculties," the availability should be noted thus: for these life faculties etc. in death, rebirth, and the course of existence; and for the other eye faculties etc. in death and rebirth. In the phrase "This is only a cutting (cheda)," the name "cutting" should be noted as the cutting of the latter portion (pacchima-koṭṭhāsa) in the answer given by demonstrating the specific nature of each complete question.

Or else: For whom the joy faculty does not arise, does the life faculty not arise for that person? For those being reborn without joy, at the moment of arising of a consciousness dissociated from joy during the course of existence, the joy faculty does not arise for them, but not...
160:
In saying that the life faculty does not arise for them, the non-mention of "those attained to cessation and the non-percipient beings" indicates that the physical life faculty has a course similar to the eye faculty etc. The arising of that physical life faculty is spoken of only at the time of rebirth. In saying "those being reborn without joy," the non-percipient beings are included, but those non-percipient beings and those attained to cessation are not mentioned by way of the course of existence. The non-arising of this physical life faculty is also spoken of only at the times of death and rebirth, not during the course of existence. In the latter portion, "For all those who are dying, and at the moment of dissolution of consciousness during the course of existence, the joy faculty does not arise for them and the life faculty does not arise," in this phrase "for all those who are dying," the non-percipient beings are included, but those non-percipient beings and those attained to cessation are not mentioned by way of the course of existence. The meaning is that in the section on "for whom and where" (yassa-yatthaka), those attained to cessation should not be shown or taken. For the phrase "those attained to cessation" does not indicate a plane like the phrase "non-percipient beings," nor does it indicate the moment of non-arising of the joy faculty etc. like the phrases "at the moment of arising of a consciousness associated with equanimity, at the moment of dissolution of all consciousness," etc.; rather, it is a term that indicates only the person.

In the division of past time, when it is said, "At the moment of arising of the rebirth-consciousness of the beings in the Pure Abodes, the joy faculty had not arisen for them there and the life faculty had not arisen there," why is it said "at the moment of arising of the rebirth-consciousness"? Should it not be said "for those being reborn," as in "For those being reborn in the Pure Abodes, for the non-percipient beings, the joy faculty had not arisen for them there and the mind faculty had not arisen there"? It should not be said so. Just as persons being reborn by way of joy and the mind faculty are those possessed of rebirth-consciousness, they are not only those possessed of rebirth-consciousness by way of joy and the life faculty. By way of the life faculty, as long as the first physical life faculty lasts, they are called "those being reborn." At that time, from the second consciousness onwards, it cannot be said that "the life faculty had not arisen," because the mental life faculty has already arisen and ceased. Therefore, both are indicated by the moment of arising. Just as the characteristic "had not ceased" is obtainable in both moments of the rebirth-consciousness but is indicated by the very first moment of dissolution of the rebirth-consciousness, so should it be understood here.

In the division of future time, having made an antecedent of a faculty that will arise, only the future arising of another faculty is questioned. Therein, just as in the division of present time, because only the person who is currently arising is taken by the divisions of antecedent and doubt, and thus only the person being reborn is questioned by "For whom the eye faculty etc. arise...", and their arising is possible only at the time of rebirth and not at any other time; so too in this future section, it is questioned: "For whom the eye faculty etc. will arise, will the life faculties arise for that person who is being reborn?"
161:
In the Present Portion (Paccuppannavāra), because it is asked, "The eye-faculty, etc., are arising; for that person currently undergoing rebirth, the life-faculty, etc., are arising," the arising of these faculties can only occur at the moment of rebirth, and not at other times (during the course of existence). In this Future Portion (Anāgatavāra), however, although it is asked, "For whom the eye-faculty, etc., will arise, will the life-faculty, etc., arise for that person currently undergoing rebirth?", it is not the case that the arising of these faculties cannot occur at times other than the moment of rebirth (i.e., it can indeed occur). Therefore, in the question, "For whom the eye-faculty will arise, will the joy-faculty (somanassindriya) arise for that person?", it is stated, "Yes (Āmantā)."

In this same manner, in the Cessation Portion (Nirodhavāra), it is stated, "For whom the eye-faculty will cease, will the joy-faculty cease for that person? Yes (Āmantā)." It is not the case that for whom the eye-faculty will cease, the joy-faculty will not cease (it will indeed cease). Even for a person in their last existence (pacchimabhavika) who has a rebirth-linking accompanied by equanimity, the joy-faculty will still cease. This is because it is not impossible for the cessation of the joy-faculty to occur in the period (during the course of existence) prior to the death-consciousness (cuti) of that person currently undergoing rebirth.

In these first questions of the Future Portion, the meaning of the antecedent (sanniṭṭhāna) is the basis (nissaya) for the meaning of the doubt-term (saṃsaya) being asked. Whether it is one whose faculties arise at the moment of rebirth, or one whose faculties arise in both (rebirth and the course of existence), that meaning is the basis for the meaning being asked even in reverse. With this intention, in the second questions, only the meaning of the antecedent is determined. In those first questions, the doubt-meaning of arising or cessation, taken in its specific form (sarūpa) merely by being a future state, is not determined as the basis. Because there is such a determination of the antecedent meaning, it is said: "Or else, for whom the joy-faculty will arise, will the eye-faculty arise for that person? Yes (Āmantā)." This method is the same in the Cessation Portion.

In the Negative (Paṭiloma) section, however, unlike in the Positive (Anuloma) where "will arise, will cease" are stated in their specific future forms, it is not stated so here. Therefore, the arising and cessation in the course of existence (pavatti) of the faculty taken by the doubt-term in the Positive section, which were connected to the eye-faculty as the root, should not be connected in the same way here. This is because, just as arising and cessation can occur by passing beyond or not yet reaching the moment, it is not so with non-arising and non-cessation (anuppāda-anirodha). The non-existence (abhāva) of the non-existence of what is not present (abhūta) cannot occur by passing beyond or not yet reaching it. In the Negative section, the non-existence of the arising and cessation of faculties that are not present is asked. Therefore, for that non-existence (abhūtābhāva) which has no distinction, because there is no connection with another time like the arising that is currently occurring, the basis of the meaning being asked by the non-existence of the arising and cessation of the eye-faculty, etc., is decided by the antecedent. Based on that basis, the non-arising and non-cessation of the life-faculty, etc., which have arising and cessation as future rebirth and death...
162:
...are asked by the doubt-term. Thus it is said: "For whom the eye-faculty will not arise, will the joy-faculty not arise for that person? Yes (Āmantā)," and "For whom the eye-faculty will not cease, will the joy-faculty not cease for that person? Yes (Āmantā)." A specific explanation (sarūpadassana vissajjanā) like "Those who, having been reborn in the formless realm, will attain final Nibbāna," as seen in the case of the life-faculty and equanimity-faculty, etc., is not stated here.

In the passage, "For those who, having been reborn in the fine-material realm, will attain final Nibbāna, the nose-faculty will not arise, but it is not that the joy-faculty will not arise for them," those who will have rebirth-linking with equanimity are included in the latter group "those who, having been reborn in the formless realm, will attain final Nibbāna" because they share the same characteristic. Therefore, it should be understood that here, only those who will have rebirth-linking with joy (somanassa) are meant.

In some early manuscripts of the Commentary, it is written: "In the Past-Future Portion (Atītānāgatavāra), at the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa) of the rebirth-consciousness of the Suddhāvāsa deities, the mind-faculty had not arisen before; not taking the meaning by way of passing the moment of arising as in the Dhammayamaka..." This is merely a clerical error (pamādalikhita). However, in the manuscripts where the text appears as: "In the Present-Past Portion (Paccuppannātītavāra), at the moment of dissolution of the rebirth-consciousness of the Suddhāvāsa deities, the mind-faculty had not arisen before... the meaning should be taken by way of it not having arisen before in that life," this version is much better.

## The Explanation of the Portion on the Occurrence of Processes (Pavatti-vāra) is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Portion on Full Understanding (Pariññā-vāra)

435-482. In the Portion on Full Understanding (Pariññā-vāra), by the phrase "and the mixed mundane indeterminate states," because they are mixed with mundane indeterminate states which are exclusively to be fully understood (ekantapariññeyya) and included within the Truth of Suffering, the state of being "to be fully understood" of the mind-faculty, etc., is stated based on those states, just like the feeling-aggregate, etc. If it is said that they are "to be fully understood" because they are mixed with states to be fully understood, why in the Dhammayamaka are the pairs (yamaka) not stated by connecting with the term "indeterminate" (abyākata), such as "He who develops a wholesome state, fully understands an indeterminate state"? Just as it is said, "I develop the wholesome, I abandon the unwholesome"...
163:
In wholesome and unwholesome states, there is the firm application of mind regarding development and abandonment. Similarly, there is the firm application of mind regarding full understanding in the aggregates and so forth, such as 'the aggregate of feeling is impermanent, the base of mental objects is impermanent.' Among those indeterminate states, the aggregate of feeling and others should be fully understood as 'impermanent' and so on. Furthermore, these should be fully understood by taking them as the aggregate of feeling and so forth, not by taking them as indeterminate states.

Why, in this detailed analysis of the Truth of Suffering, is only the abandonment of grief (domanassa) mentioned and not its full understanding? Is it not true that although the aggregate of feeling and others included in the Truth of Suffering are not taken as wholesome or unwholesome, wholesome and unwholesome states are also to be fully understood? It is true. Just as the nature of the aggregate of feeling and others can exist even without the nature of being developed or abandoned, the nature of the faculty of grief (domanassindriya) does not exist without the nature of being abandoned. To show this distinction, only the abandonment of the faculty of grief is mentioned here. It should be understood that this is not because the nature of full understanding is absent. By the statement 'the unwholesome is strictly to be abandoned,' it should be understood that it only prohibits the nature of not being abandoned, meaning it is only to be abandoned; it does not prohibit the nature of full understanding.

The faculty of final knowledge (aññindriya) is the culmination of things to be developed, but not the culmination of things to be realized. Therefore, only its nature of being developed is taken. The statement beginning with 'two persons' should be written after the Pali beginning with 'does not fully understand the faculty of the eye'; it should be understood as being written out of sequence. Having bypassed the section based on the faculty of the eye, this was stated in the section based on the faculty of grief: 'Two persons do not abandon the faculty of grief and do not develop the faculty of final knowledge.'

In this context, there are nine persons: the worldling (puthujjana) and the eight noble ones (ariya). Among those nine persons, the worldling is of two kinds: the capable (bhabba) and the incapable (abhabba). In places where 'worldling' appears, and in places such as 'six persons have not fully understood the faculty of the eye and have not abandoned the faculty of grief,' the worldling is taken without distinction. In places where 'those worldlings who will attain the path' appears, and in places such as 'five persons will fully understand the faculty of the eye and will abandon the faculty of grief,' only the capable worldling is taken distinctly. In places where 'those worldlings who will not attain the path' appears, and in places such as 'three persons will not abandon the faculty of grief and will not fully understand the faculty of the eye,' only the incapable worldling is taken. The Arahant is also of two kinds: the one endowed with the highest fruit (aggaphalasamaṅgī) and the [established] Arahant. That person also, in places where 'Arahant' appears, and in places such as 'three persons... the faculty of one who will know the unknown...'
164:
"...have developed and have abandoned the faculty of grief," and so forth, [the person] is taken without distinction. In places such as "he who realizes the highest fruit," and in places such as "three persons have abandoned the faculty of grief but have not realized the faculty of one who has final knowledge," and so forth, the first type, the person endowed with the highest fruit, is taken distinctly. In places such as "he who has realized the highest fruit," the other [Arahant] person is taken. Thus, having known the classification of persons, one should apply the answer by extracting the persons taken by the concluding statement in those respective Pali passages.

## The Explanation of the Chapter on Full Understanding is finished.

## The Explanation of the Book of Pairs of Faculties is finished.

## The Mūlaṭīkā on the Yamaka is completed.
